uses.sentence: The power was shown for the rustics who had not yet heard the name of Christ, and a catechumen not yet baptized saw Christ in a dream.
uses.paragraph: Who counts as outside? A man who has left the consent of the universal and ancient Church under his own name is to be cut off by bishops' sentence, lest one sick sheep infect the flock. But Martin went to Trier to protect even heretics from the sword, and the Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. The power was shown for the rustics who had not yet heard the name of Christ, and a catechumen not yet baptized saw Christ in a dream.
uses.record_text: At Tours, the unconverted countryside of Gaul. It was Martin's mission field. There he halted the veiled idols, burned temples, felled a sacred pine, and built churches where they fell.

use_note.means: Heathen rustics meant, at Tours, the unconverted Gallic countryside where Martin halted idols, burned temples and built churches where they fell.
not_for: pagan as a neutral identity, or temple burning as intolerance to be judged

uses.sentence: A single teacher, be he a bishop, be he a Confessor, be he a martyr, holds only a private fancy of his own.
uses.paragraph: Vincent, on the island, set it down plainly. The canon of Scripture is complete, and more than enough. But Scripture still needs the Church's own line of interpretation, because nearly everyone reads it his own way. So within the Catholic Church itself we take care to hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part of the Church, or a novelty, or a few men dissent, we prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council's decree, or the ancients collated - the doctors whose agreed writings form "a consentient council". A single teacher, be he a bishop, be he a Confessor, be he a martyr, holds only a private fancy of his own.
uses.record_text: But suppose a teacher holds something that differs from what all hold, or goes against it. He may be holy and learned. He may be a bishop, a Confessor, or a martyr. Even so, let that be regarded as a private notion of his own. And let it be separated from the authority of common, public, general belief

use_note.means: Vincent, in chapter 28 of the Commonitory, says any teacher's view held against all, even a bishop's, confessor's or martyr's, is to be treated as a private fancy.
not_for: a separate witness from gallic.quote.private-fancy-of-his-own, which carries this same sentence in full
a rejection of bishops' authority in general, when the rule targets a lone opinion against consent
a rule aimed at a named opponent, which the passage does not name

uses.sentence: Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again.
uses.paragraph: What his death meant to us we kept at the hours, not in a treatise. At the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, and took away the debt that could not be paid, nailing it to his cross. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. And Vincent on the island wrote it as the faith believed everywhere, always, by all: in Christ two substances but one Person, the Word not changing into flesh, so that Mary is truly the mother of God.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

use_note.means: This witness says this world knew Jesus as the crucified one met in the poor, kept his death and rising at the hours, and preached grace drawing the unwilling.
not_for: a Gallic treatise on the atonement, which no one in this world wrote
the Christ with wounds as independently witnessed, when one author reports Martin's word
the resurrection as argued rather than confessed at the hours
the question of Christ's divinity, which sits in gallic.dw.one-person-two-substances

uses.sentence: Martin pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared.
uses.paragraph: And when the sword was drawn? Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics in the Spains. He held that bishops declaring men heretics and casting them out was enough, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a Church cause was a foul and unheard-of thing. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and others would follow, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When anger failed, the emperor named executioners. Martin pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared. It was granted. He left in grief, felt his power lessened, and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: Meanwhile, the bishops Martin would not share communion with went to the king in terror. They complained that they had been condemned in advance. It was all over for the standing of every one of them, they said, if Martin's authority now backed the stubbornness of Theognitus. He alone had so far condemned them by a sentence given in public. They said the man should never have been let inside the walls. He was now not just the heretics' defender but their champion. And nothing had really been gained by Priscillian's death if Martin was going to play the part of his avenger. At last they threw themselves down, weeping and wailing, and begged the emperor to use his power against this one man. The emperor came close to being forced to give Martin, too, the fate of heretics. Still, although he was inclined to favor the bishops too much, he knew Martin surpassed all others in faith, holiness, and excellence. So he tried another way to get the better of the holy man. First he sent for him in private and spoke to him very kindly. He assured Martin that the heretics had been condemned by regular public trials, not by the priests' persecution. He said there was no reason for Martin to think communion with Ithacius and the rest of that party was something to condemn. He added that Theognitus had caused division out of personal hatred rather than for the cause he stood for. In fact, he said, Theognitus was the only one who had so far cut himself off from communion. The rest had changed nothing. He also pointed out that a synod held a few days before had ruled that Ithacius could not be charged with any fault. When these arguments hardly moved Martin, the king grew furious and hurried out of his presence. Without delay, executioners were appointed for the people Martin had pleaded for. When Martin learned of this, he rushed to the palace, though it was already night. He promised that if these people were spared, he would take communion. He asked only that the tribunes already sent to the Spanish provinces to destroy the churches be called back. There was no delay: Maximus granted everything he asked. The next day, the ordination of Felix as bishop was being arranged. Felix was without doubt a man of great holiness, truly worthy of being made a priest in happier times. Martin took part in the communion that day. He judged it better to give way for the moment than to ignore the safety of those with a sword hanging over their heads. Even so, he would not confirm his communion by signing his name, though the bishops tried their very hardest to make him. The next day he hurried away from that place. On the way back he was filled with grief and mourning that he had been mixed up, even for an hour, in the evil communion. Not far from a village named Andethanna, remote woods stretch far and wide in deep solitude. There he sat down, while his companions went on a little way ahead of him. He sank into deep thought, by turns accusing and defending the cause of his grief and what he had done. Suddenly an angel stood beside him and said, "Martin, you are right to feel remorse, but you had no other way out of your difficulty. Renew your strength and take up your courage again. Otherwise you will put at risk not only your good name now, but your very salvation." So from then on he took great care never to be mixed up in communion with the party of Ithacius. But once he cured some of the possessed more slowly than usual, and with less of the grace he usually had. At once he confessed to us in tears that he felt his power had lessened. He said it was because of the evil of that communion. He had taken part in it for a moment out of necessity, not with his whole heart. He lived sixteen years after this. But he never again attended a synod, and he kept well away from all gatherings of bishops.

use_note.means: Gallus narrates how Martin, to stop the tribunes, took communion with the Ithacian bishops, was answered by an angel, and afterwards felt his healing power diminished.
not_for: the angel's speech and the lessened power as established fact, when they rest on Martin's tearful report through Gallus
the earlier petition at the palace over the tribunes, which sits in gallic.quote.gallus-on-the-tribunes-for-the-spains
a separate witness from gallic.quote.aloof-from-assemblies-of-bishops, whose sentence closes this passage

uses.sentence: That grammar - received, not invented - ran through everything we held.
uses.paragraph: What we can say is this. We were two households inside one shared grammar of reception, and the two never wrote to each other. Nothing a man made up binds anyone; our customs were the fathers', our faith what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. That grammar - received, not invented - ran through everything we held. Whether any present church holds itself to exactly that measure, in exactly our form, is not a question our own record can answer.
uses.record_text:
Antiquity, the Fathers, and consent are the test of legitimacy, set against novelty - applied by all three founding voices to monastic custom, doctrine, and cult alike.
Cassian holds that allegiance is owed not to customs a few people have introduced, but to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement (Inst. I.2). He calls his own Institutes not his but the fathers' (Conf. Pref. I). And he holds up, as a warning, the monk who trusted his own judgment over the Elders' tradition and in the end forsook the desert (Conf. II.24).
Vincent holds that the Catholic faith is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all - tested by universality, antiquity, and consent (Comm. ch. 2). He quotes Pope Stephen's own rule that there should be no innovation, nothing but what has been handed down (ch. 6). And he holds that a guardian of doctrine is not an author but a keeper, not a teacher but a disciple, not a leader but a follower (ch. 22).
Sulpitius tells that Martin, asked to venerate a supposed martyr's tomb, would not lend his own authority to popular opinion, because no reliable tradition about it reached back to antiquity (Vita XI).
This same standard also became a battleground. Prosper reports that the Massilians defended their own obstinacy by antiquity; Celestine, as later editors read him, answered that novelty must cease to assail antiquity; and Vincent read that same letter for his own side (Comm. ch. 32). The rule that was meant to settle disputes became, in the grace controversy, one more thing both sides claimed for themselves.

use_note.means: Antiquity, the fathers and consent are the test of legitimacy against novelty in custom, doctrine and cult, applied by all three founding voices though they never cite one another.
not_for: a conservatism that forbids all growth
the test as consistently applied, when that is contested in gallic.contested.who-holds-antiquity
Cassian's customs as a written Rule
Martin's refusal of an unattested tomb as an application of Vincent's formulated test, which sits in gallic.term.the-rule

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles we kept his hours: at the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world and took away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints; dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit, and no one took his life from him - he laid it down himself and took it again.
uses.paragraph: Jesus was the one we called Lord and Saviour, and we said it as a thing already believed, not argued. At Tours he was the Christ who came showing his wounds. Our saint, alone in his cell, refused a purple-robed visitor who said *I am Christ* - and answered that he would believe only in one who came in the form in which he suffered, bearing the marks of his wounds. That was the Lord we knew - the crucified one. Among the brethren at Marseilles we kept his hours: at the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world and took away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints; dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit, and no one took his life from him - he laid it down himself and took it again.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.
not_for: a penal substitution doctrine, when the sixth-hour sentence is near it but not the same
anything from Cassian's books against Nestorius, which are unread
the bare formula, which sits in gallic.quote.one-substance-three-persons
a private confession of Jesus as personal Lord, which the record lacks

uses.sentence: At Tours the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes.
uses.paragraph: So among the brethren at Marseilles the life was built to keep the wheel fed. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers as brought down from heaven by an angel, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. At Tours the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk at Tours and Marseilles, served at Marseilles by a received Egyptian system of psalms at fixed hours said to be an angel's.
not_for: the Divine Office as one settled book that all monks everywhere recited
prayer as private devotion and feeling
the eucharist as a rite, which sits in gallic.term.communion

He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.

At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? uses.sentence: Yet it needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way and almost as many senses are extracted from it as there are readers.
uses.paragraph: Our approach and purpose in reading the Scriptures is what Cassian set down for the hours and what Vincent held as the rule of understanding. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, and after the psalms came two lessons - one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body. The hours themselves were received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to them by an angel's ministry. Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than sufficient for all things. Yet it needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way and almost as many senses are extracted from it as there are readers. So what we held was this: the Scriptures are read at the hours, daily, by heart, as prayer - not first as a text to be studied but as the voice we speak back to God. And where doctrine is contested, the rule is universality, antiquity, and consent - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, the old, and the consent of the Fathers collated. The Apostle's words were on a monk's lips at the moment he felt his labour had done something: not I, but the grace of God with me. That is purpose: to be turned into prayer, held as one body, and read by the Fathers' consent, never by a man inventing his own sense alone.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

use_note.means: The rule meant Vincent's test of the faith, what has been believed everywhere, always, by all, preferring the whole, the old and consent to the part, the new and few.
not_for: the Vincentian canon as a slogan in later polemic over which communion holds the faith

uses.sentence: The steward kept them in his cupboard, and if the man was seen once to cool toward the rule he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own.
uses.paragraph: The process among the brethren at Marseilles is Egypt's, and Cassian set it down as the fathers' own. A man came to the door. He was put off and scorned there ten days or more, of set purpose, to prove he meant it. When he was let in, he was searched for even a single hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the garments of the house. Then he was lodged a year under the guest-elder. After that he was handed to a dean over ten, and taught the alphabet, as it were, in the direction of perfection. His old clothes were not thrown away. The steward kept them in his cupboard, and if the man was seen once to cool toward the rule he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own.
uses.record_text: But the clothes he took off are handed over to the care of the steward. They are kept until the excellence of his progress, his life and his endurance can be recognized through different kinds of temptations and trials.

use_note.means: Cassian explains in Institutes IV.6 that a novice's worldly clothes are kept by the steward until trials have proven his progress.
not_for: a claim that the clothes are kept permanently, when the chapter says they are given away once progress is proven
Gallic practice, when Cassian describes the Egyptian coenobia

uses.sentence: We carry only its edges: the founder's arrival, his going off to a see, and Vincent's remembrancer written there.
uses.paragraph: And of the island's own day - a rule kept, a novice received, an elder's saying, an office sung - nothing. The house the churches came to for so many of their bishops is the one our record cannot enter. We carry only its edges: the founder's arrival, his going off to a see, and Vincent's remembrancer written there.
uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

use_note.means: The record attests that everything it holds about this world's places and daily life comes from texts, and cannot supply any excavation, material find or account of the island's days.
not_for: a claim that nothing has ever been dug up, when the build has not searched that literature

uses.sentence: Cassian brought the customs of the monasteries from Egypt as delivered to us by the fathers - received, not invented.
uses.paragraph: We never settled it by one judge or one seat. What we held is this: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. That is Vincent's test, on the island, and it runs on three things at once - universality, antiquity, and consent. When part of the Church dissents, prefer the whole; when novelty arises, prefer antiquity; when a few teach something, prefer the consent of many. And consent means an ancient council's decree, or the writings of the fathers collated - never one teacher alone, be he bishop or confessor or martyr, for one teacher alone has only a private fancy of his own. Novelty is suspect for being new; what was handed down from antiquity is held fast. That grammar runs through all three of our founding voices. Cassian brought the customs of the monasteries from Egypt as delivered to us by the fathers - received, not invented. Martin would not honor a tomb without steady tradition from antiquity. And Vincent wrote the test itself.
uses.record_text: For us tradition is what has been received from predecessors and must be passed on unchanged. Vincent's second criterion of truth after Scripture, "the Tradition of the Catholic Church." Pope Stephen's rule, "nothing but what has been handed down." Cassian's "traditions of the Elders" by which thoughts are judged. And the "steady tradition ... from antiquity" without which Martin will not honour a tomb.

use_note.means: Tradition meant what has been received and must be passed on unchanged, the ground on which Vincent's rule, Cassian's elders and Martin's refusal of a tomb are all judged.
not_for: a rival authority to Scripture in a confessional debate

uses.sentence: The twelve was fixed by that, he says, and the two lessons the fathers added by their own appointment afterward.
uses.paragraph: At Marseilles, Cassian wrote out the customs of the monasteries of Egypt and Palestine for a bishop's new house - customs, he said, not a written rule of his own, delivered to us by the fathers, not ours. The twelve psalms at evening and at night came from an angel, not from us. In those days, Cassian says, only a few were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men - the fathers of Egypt argued whether the psalms should be fifty or sixty, and one of them rose to sing at Vespers, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The twelve was fixed by that, he says, and the two lessons the fathers added by their own appointment afterward. Egypt was our measure, the place the customs came from.
uses.record_text: In those days only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. The perfection of the earliest Church still stood unbroken. The burning faith of the few had not yet cooled by being spread among the many. At that time the honored fathers watchfully made plans for those who would come after them. They met to discuss what plan to adopt for daily worship across the whole community of brothers. A dispute might send out a poisonous root of error, or jealousy, or division among those who came after. Each man judged by the measure of his own zeal, paying no heed to how weak others were. Some were for fifty, others for sixty. Some, not satisfied with that number, thought they really ought to go beyond it. They held a holy difference of opinion in their devout debate over the rule of their religious life. It was so great that the hour for their evening service came before the sacred question was settled. One stood up in their midst to sing the Psalms to the Lord. They were all sitting, their minds closely fixed on the words of the singer. He sang eleven Psalms, with prayers placed between them, each verse sung in an even voice. He ended the twelfth with the response "Alleluia." Then he suddenly vanished from the sight of all. At once this ended both their debate and their service. At this the honored assembly of the Fathers understood that, by God's providence, the angel's guidance had set a general rule for the brothers' communities. So they decreed that this number should be kept in both their evening and their night services. What they added, they added simply as extras, by their own decision.

use_note.means: Cassian, in Institutes II, relates the Egyptian tradition that an angel chanting twelve psalms settled the fathers' dispute over how many psalms the offices should hold.

uses.sentence: How both are true cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man.
uses.paragraph: What we never settled, on purpose, was how God's will toward all and a man's own perishing both stay true. Free will always remains in a man to neglect or delight in the grace of God. Grace goes before, works with the will, and crowns it; and still our effort is required. How both are true cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.record_text: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.

uses.sentence: Not the two houses at Marseilles.
uses.paragraph: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like — only as far as those pages say, and no further.
uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

uses.sentence: A discharged soldier told Caesar he was now the soldier of Christ and may not fight.
uses.paragraph: The path those books took to reach us, our record does not trace. They were already in the churches and the monasteries when Martin first gathered brethren. What our own life added was not the books but what they were read for. A newcomer at Marseilles was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. A week's cook was judged a pilferer for three lentils left on the floor, because everything in the house is consecrated to the Lord. A discharged soldier told Caesar he was now the soldier of Christ and may not fight. The books were read inside that frame - a renunciation of marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter service of Christ. And they were read to be said. The psalter learned by heart, said at the work, kept a man's wheel fed. That is the path as our record keeps it: books received, not invented, read at fixed hours in a house built to hold a man to them.

uses.sentence: That was our own test for everything we kept - doctrine, a monastic custom, a cult, the dress itself - and it was how we refused what we refused.
uses.paragraph: The question is exactly ours. What among us is handed down, and what is made up? That was our own test for everything we kept - doctrine, a monastic custom, a cult, the dress itself - and it was how we refused what we refused. If novelty is profane, antiquity is sacred. So the answer begins with what we claimed as handed down, and where we admitted we had nothing to claim.
uses.record_text: The axis on which all three of our founding voices judge what is legitimate. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever "has been handed down" from antiquity is to be held fast. "If novelty is profane, antiquity is sacred."

use_note.means: Novelty and antiquity named the axis on which all three founding voices judged legitimacy: the new is suspect for being new, and what was handed down is held fast.

uses.sentence: Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body.
uses.paragraph: The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. That is what we had of him: the apostles' witness, received as Scripture, kept in the cells, and said at prayer.
uses.record_text: What did we have of Jesus? The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

use_note.means: The record attests that this world's books never claim a witness to the Lord and never argue the resurrection to a doubter, and it cannot supply either.

uses.sentence: What is done to the least of these is done to him.
uses.paragraph: He was also the one we met in the poor. At a city gate a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed - until a soldier cut his one cloak in two. That night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The fathers of Egypt taught the same: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What is done to the least of these is done to him.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.sentence: The work itself was held sacred: a cook who left three lentils on the floor during his week of duty was judged a pilferer of the Lord's property and suspended from prayer until he did penance, because everything in the house is consecrated to God.
uses.paragraph: A mill-wheel fed and a body held still - that is the shape of a day among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set it down from Egypt. The whole was built to serve one aim: prayer that never stops, the way a blacksmith beats his anvil between strokes. Twelve psalms at evening, learned by heart, and twelve at night - the number an angel fixed when the fathers of Egypt could not settle it themselves. Between those hours, labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. The psalms at the work, too. A man rarely went out except for prayer. The work itself was held sacred: a cook who left three lentils on the floor during his week of duty was judged a pilferer of the Lord's property and suspended from prayer until he did penance, because everything in the house is consecrated to God. That whole order was Egypt's, received from the fathers, not ours. Cassian wrote it out for a bishop's new house and said plainly that no one who joined our monasteries had kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even for a year. What a house in Gaul did instead, day by day, he never wrote.
uses.record_text: A steward finds three lentils on the floor during a brother's week as cook, the abbot judges him a pilferer of sacred property, and he is suspended from prayer until public penance - because everything in the house is "consecrated to the Lord."

uses.sentence: We spoke of a debt that could not be paid, taken out of the way by Christ's cross.
uses.paragraph: We spoke of a debt that could not be paid, taken out of the way by Christ's cross. We spoke of free will that always remains in a man, weak but real, able to neglect or delight in the grace of God. And we spoke of God calling us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, drawing us toward salvation. Whether a child not yet able to choose carries guilt from birth - that question as you shape it is not in our record the way it stands in yours.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

uses.sentence: All three are God's gift.
uses.paragraph: We never argued it as a formula, and where Cassian touched it he touched it as Egypt's fathers touched it - as a thing held, not debated. Here is what our record keeps. Among the brethren at Marseilles, Abbot Chaeremon named three stages of the grace by which we are saved: the first kindles our desire toward salvation, the second enables us in the good we wish for, the third preserves us to the end in the virtues. All three are God's gift. And he taught plainly that a newborn has no merits before him - he spoke of "the case even of infants, who have as yet done nothing either good or bad". That is the nearest our record comes to your question's shape: infants with no works of their own, and grace going before every stage. But whether they bear guilt from birth, by what they are rather than what they have done, Cassian does not say. What he does say is this: the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; he does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and it is grievous blasphemy to think otherwise. Free will always remains in a man, and it is weak, and the help of God is necessary to it every day and hour. How both are true - how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. The inherited guilt as a thing confessed apart from the grace that answers it is not in our record to give you.

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that every itching thought is laid bare to him the moment it rises.
uses.paragraph: Within the house the place belongs to the senior whose judgment stands in for the junior's own. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that every itching thought is laid bare to him the moment it rises. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. Abbot is the title of every Egyptian father Cassian reports. At Tours the same place was held by one master, Martin, who himself consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the practice of laying every "itching thought" bare to the senior as soon as it arises. It is "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection." The elders' rule: "a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it." So "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered."

use_note.means: Disclosure of thoughts meant laying every rising thought bare to the senior before any deed, the first lesson of Cassian's monastic life and not the later sacrament.
not_for: sacramental confession of sins to a priest with absolution
therapy or optional spiritual accountability
public penance for a committed fault, which sits in gallic.term.penance-satisfaction
a documented Gallic practice, when whether any Gallic house kept it is unrecorded

uses.sentence: Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt men in the Spains, where a man could be counted a heretic for the clothes he wore.
uses.paragraph: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was - not underground, but in the courts, among bishops who had given way with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue. The violence we knew was heretics driving a bishop into exile, and later bishops handing heretics to the sword. Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt men in the Spains, where a man could be counted a heretic for the clothes he wore. But that was the sword drawn in the Church's cause by bishops, not a persecution that drove believers into hiding. What some of us did hide was different. Martin kept one thing hidden because of the times: that he had gone to the court and yielded once to a communion he abhorred, to save men from being killed. He hid that out of grief, not fear. The hiddenness we valued was the monk's own cell, where a man kept himself from the world he had left. Not catacombs. Wooden cells and caves.
uses.record_text: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

use_note.means: Gallus recounts how Maximus shielded Ithacius after Priscillian's death and how Martin went to court to stop tribunes being sent into the Spains.
not_for: a doctrinal ruling on heresy, when Martin's petition concerned lives
the forced communion and the angel, which sit in gallic.quote.gallus-on-the-forced-communion-and-the-angel
an event corroborated outside Sulpitius's own writings

uses.sentence: At Tours the saint himself began as a soldier still in the ranks, regarded as a monk though he had not yet professed.
uses.paragraph: And now the limits. At Tours the saint himself began as a soldier still in the ranks, regarded as a monk though he had not yet professed. A citizen threw himself at Martin's knees, Martin was escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and he became a bishop who kept the objects and virtues of a monk. Whether Tours kept any testing at its own door, no one wrote. Of the island's own reception of a newcomer - a rule kept, a novice received - nothing. Not one man who came to our door left an account of how he was met there.
uses.record_text: A monk, for us, is a man who has cut himself off from marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter life in Christ's service. The cut shows in his body and his dwelling. But at Tours a soldier still in the ranks could be "regarded as a monk," and so could a bishop in his see.

use_note.means: A monk meant a man cut off from marriage, kin, property and the world for stricter service of Christ, a name a soldier or bishop could bear at Tours.
not_for: a cloistered professional religious under a written Rule and an abbot
someone who by definition is not a soldier, a bishop or a city dweller
Benedictine or later medieval monasticism
why monks became bishops, which sits in gallic.term.monk-bishop

uses.sentence: Cassian never told how he came to believe.
uses.paragraph: So our record does not argue belief into anyone. It says the Lord sought the unpitied, that he draws the unwilling, and that a man came to faith by seeing Christ in the half of a soldier's cloak. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness says Jesus sought the unpitied, citing Martin's cloak, the guest received as Christ and grace calling the unwilling, while naming its thin personal testimony.
not_for: a personal conversion testimony from anyone but Martin, which the record lacks
evidence that Gallic houses broke fasts for guests, which Cassian does not say
a settled reading of Conference XIII on grace, which is contested
who Christ was and what his death meant, which sit in gallic.dw.the-christ-who-bears-the-wounds

uses.sentence: Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh.
uses.paragraph: On the island Vincent wrote what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.
not_for: a penal substitution doctrine, when the sixth-hour sentence is near it but not the same
anything from Cassian's books against Nestorius, which are unread
the bare formula, which sits in gallic.quote.one-substance-three-persons
a private confession of Jesus as personal Lord, which the record lacks

uses.sentence: Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers as brought down from heaven by an angel, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule.
uses.paragraph: So among the brethren at Marseilles the life was built to keep the wheel fed. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers as brought down from heaven by an angel, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. At Tours the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk at Tours and Marseilles, served at Marseilles by a received Egyptian system of psalms at fixed hours said to be an angel's.
not_for: the Divine Office as one settled book that all monks everywhere recited
prayer as private devotion and feeling
the eucharist as a rite, which sits in gallic.term.communion
later Benedictine or Roman hours, whose names Lauds, Prime and Compline are the editor's

uses.sentence: Vincent on the island held that bishops and ancient councils guard the faith.
uses.paragraph: Authority came, for us, from two directions at once. Vincent on the island held that bishops and ancient councils guard the faith. And Martin at Tours refused them communion, judged their yielding to the royal court degenerate submissiveness, held it a foul thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church, and lived sixteen years after Treves without entering a synod again. We never reconciled the two. Bishops and synods guard the truth, yet the saint keeps fleeing them.
uses.record_text:
Antiquity, the Fathers, and consent are the test of legitimacy, set against novelty - applied by all three founding voices to monastic custom, doctrine, and cult alike.
Cassian holds that allegiance is owed not to customs a few people have introduced, but to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement (Inst. I.2). He calls his own Institutes not his but the fathers' (Conf. Pref. I). And he holds up, as a warning, the monk who trusted his own judgment over the Elders' tradition and in the end forsook the desert (Conf. II.24).
Vincent holds that the Catholic faith is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all - tested by universality, antiquity, and consent (Comm. ch. 2). He quotes Pope Stephen's own rule that there should be no innovation, nothing but what has been handed down (ch. 6). And he holds that a guardian of doctrine is not an author but a keeper, not a teacher but a disciple, not a leader but a follower (ch. 22).
Sulpitius tells that Martin, asked to venerate a supposed martyr's tomb, would not lend his own authority to popular opinion, because no reliable tradition about it reached back to antiquity (Vita XI).
This same standard also became a battleground. Prosper reports that the Massilians defended their own obstinacy by antiquity; Celestine, as later editors read him, answered that novelty must cease to assail antiquity; and Vincent read that same letter for his own side (Comm. ch. 32). The rule that was meant to settle disputes became, in the grace controversy, one more thing both sides claimed for themselves.

use_note.means: Antiquity, the fathers and consent are the test of legitimacy against novelty in custom, doctrine and cult, applied by all three founding voices though they never cite one another.
not_for: a conservatism that forbids all growth
the test as consistently applied, when that is contested in gallic.contested.who-holds-antiquity
Cassian's customs as a written Rule
Martin's refusal of an unattested tomb as an application of Vincent's formulated test, which sits in gallic.term.the-rule

uses.sentence: What we had instead was the books, read at the hours.
uses.paragraph: Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the books, read at the hours. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.
uses.record_text: What did we have of Jesus? The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

use_note.means: The record attests that this world's books never claim a witness to the Lord and never argue the resurrection to a doubter, and it cannot supply either.
not_for: a proof of the resurrection written by this world for a doubter, which the record says is absent
the cloak vision or the raised catechumen as evidence that the Lord rose, when they show the saint's power, as in gallic.story.the-cloak-at-amiens and gallic.story.raising-of-the-catechumen
the content of Cassian's seven books against Nestorius, which is unread
a chain of witnesses, when the world's floor stands more than three centuries after the events

uses.sentence: So what the test gave us was a way to name what binds and what does not, and the refusal of one man's novelty - not one answer forced through to the end.
uses.paragraph: The evidence that it worked is also the evidence that it did not. On the grace question itself - does our good will begin with us or with God's mercy? - Vincent read the Apostolic See's own letter as written for the side of antiquity, and held that we kept the faith of the fathers. But whether Vincent's reading of that letter stands as ours, or as one voice's act inside an argument still live, our record leaves contested. The fathers of Egypt left it open on purpose: our teacher Chaeremon answered on both sides with Scripture and said no one can fully grasp it. We stopped where the fathers stopped. So what the test gave us was a way to name what binds and what does not, and the refusal of one man's novelty - not one answer forced through to the end.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

use_note.means: The rule meant Vincent's test of the faith, what has been believed everywhere, always, by all, preferring the whole, the old and consent to the part, the new and few.
not_for: the Vincentian canon as a slogan in later polemic over which communion holds the faith
a monastic Rule, whether Cassian's customs or Benedict's
a formula consistently applied, when its use in the live grace dispute is contested in gallic.contested.who-holds-antiquity
novelty as a value in itself, which sits in gallic.term.novelty-antiquity

uses.sentence: Sulpitius said Martin had apostolic authority, the apostles' own power over death, demons, and emperors.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the same question sat elsewhere. Martin foreknew his own death and still travelled to Condate to restore peace among quarrelling clergy, counting reconciliation a crown for his virtues. He kept, as bishop, a monk's own habits - the objects and virtues of a monk in a see. Sulpitius said Martin had apostolic authority, the apostles' own power over death, demons, and emperors. That was the highest word spoken for him, and it was a claim of direct likeness to the first, not to a custom passed through stages.
uses.record_text: At Tours, the highest thing said of Martin - having the apostles' power over death, demons, and emperors. At Marseilles, the perfection of love, and the first Church's common life.

use_note.means: Apostolic authority meant, at Tours, Martin's apostle-like power over death, demons and emperors, and at Marseilles the perfection of love and the first Church's common life.
not_for: apostolic succession as a doctrine of validly ordained bishops
Martin's apostolic authority as jurisdiction
Rome as such, which sits in gallic.term.apostolic-see-pope
the saint's power as such, which sits in gallic.term.virtus

uses.sentence: Pope Stephen's own rule, as Vincent quoted it: let nothing new be brought in - nothing except what has been handed down.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles Cassian held the same grammar. We owe unhesitating loyalty not to what a few people made up, but to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement. At Tours Martin would not honour a tomb without steady tradition from antiquity to warrant it. Pope Stephen's own rule, as Vincent quoted it: let nothing new be brought in - nothing except what has been handed down.
uses.record_text: Let nothing new be brought in - nothing except what has been handed down.

use_note.means: Vincent quotes Pope Stephen's rule, written to Africa in the dispute over rebaptism, that nothing be innovated beyond what has been handed down.
not_for: a verified text of Stephen's letter, which survives only through Vincent's and Cyprian's citations
Pope Celestine's letter to Gaul, which sits in gallic.quote.vincent-celestines-letter-and-its-reading
Vincent's own keeper-not-author teaching, which sits in gallic.quote.not-an-author-but-a-keeper

uses.sentence: What the disciples did who gathered in the caves around his wooden cell, our record does not say beyond that they were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the record dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap - never on what the brethren around him sang, or at what hours. Martin kept his mind on prayer even at other work. What the disciples did who gathered in the caves around his wooden cell, our record does not say beyond that they were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master.
uses.record_text:
Authority to teach or narrate rests on having seen and heard a named master, and formation happens by imitation of a named exemplar. Sulpitius writes 'the life of a most holy man, which shall serve in future as an example to others' (Vita I), and Marmoutier's disciples are 'disciplined after the example of the saintly master' (Vita X), and Martin's last saying is 'I have sinned if I leave you a different example' (Ep. III), and Gallus can say 'I myself am a witness' (Dial. II.4). Cassian writes that 'these things cannot be taught save by one who has had experience of them' (Inst. Pref.). The Conferences are reported speech of named elders whom God 'has deemed us worthy both to see ... and to dwell with'. The novice takes his examples 'from a very few or indeed from one or two only' (Inst. IV.40). At Lérins the value is present as writings collated (Comm. ch. 3, ch. 28). It is also present as a disciple's Life of his master (Hilary's Life of Honoratus, Gennadius ch. LXX).
The texts raise no concern about attestation, but they do raise one about convention: a shared late-antique literary convention, which weakens what convergence proves. The value passes every test applied to it. It repeats across the kinds of evidence tested, one of them by existence alone. The form of both nodes' literature depends on it. The Dialogues are built as eyewitness testimony, and the Conferences are built as heard conferences, and each corpus defends its authority on that ground, while imitation of a named exemplar is the stated way that formation works at both nodes. It explains why Sulpitius writes a Life and why Hilary writes a Life, why Cassian writes reported speech, and why this world's stories are almost entirely first-person-attested. The value persists across nodes, 'with Vincent transforming the value from heard to read.' In the interaction test it passes with one negative cell.
Is this one value? As far as the evidence allows, in the sense the tests measure, yes. It is also a convention shared far beyond this world: 'two unconnected Latin monastic communities in 400 could each have inherited it separately.' The link across nodes is confirmed, but it is discounted as evidence of unity. The value is supporting, not primary. It organizes the literature's form and the formation mechanism, but it works within the context that the monk-bishop and Egypt-as-measure gravities establish, since the exemplar is a monk-bishop or an Egyptian father. A convention that the world shares with its neighbours does not meet the primary bar. The record's confidence and its gravity standing agree.
It held, but it fractured at the edge through transmission. In the grace controversy it becomes a weapon. Cassian's authority is that he heard Chaeremon. Prosper attacks 'a man of priestly rank' without naming him. The eyewitness-teacher's standing survives the attack. The fracture came in transmission, since the excision of Conferences XII and XXII removed two eyewitness conferences from this world's own English text. Gennadius gives 'two divisions' against the three Dialogues in this world's text. This shows that copying split the eyewitness frame itself again.

use_note.means: Authority to teach rests on having seen and heard a named master, so formation is imitation of a named exemplar, shifting at Lerins from men seen to writings read.
not_for: Vincent's collated writings as men seen
an impersonal institution or rule as the carrier of formation
the two eyewitness conferences removed from the vendored edition, which are absent
imitation as a mechanism in itself, which sits in gallic.term.example-imitation

uses.sentence: Before he gathered his first brethren, the violence of heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder.
uses.paragraph: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. Martin's road began by leaving Caesar's service at a donative: I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. Before he gathered his first brethren, the violence of heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder. The trouble was not soldiers hunting believers. It was bishops bowing to the royal court, and a secular ruler made judge in a cause of the Church.
uses.record_text: At a donative on the eve of battle a soldier tells Caesar he is now the soldier of Christ and may not fight, offers to stand unarmed before the enemy line - and the enemy surrenders before morning.

use_note.means: Sulpitius records Martin, at a donative before battle, telling Julian Caesar that he is now Christ's soldier and offering to stand unarmed, whereupon the enemy surrenders.
not_for: the earlier cloak scene, which sits in gallic.story.the-cloak-at-amiens
Cassian's dress-mysticism soldier, which sits in gallic.term.soldier-of-christ
the editors' identification of Julian and Worms as the text's own
a general Christian refusal of military service, when it is one saint's act

uses.sentence: He held that it was punishment enough for the bishops to declare men heretics and put them out of the churches, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing.
uses.paragraph: The power claimed by bishops when they made common cause with an emperor's court, and the man we remember is the one who said it was a foul thing. Here is what our record holds. At Treves the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, and in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics by bishops in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court. The accuser there was himself a bishop. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. He held that it was punishment enough for the bishops to declare men heretics and put them out of the churches, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went, our record says, to protect even heretics themselves. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin pledged that night that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: He said the bishops had already declared them heretics. Being driven out of the churches, he held, was punishment enough. Besides, he said, it was a foul and unheard-of disgrace for a secular ruler to judge a church case.

use_note.means: Sulpitius, in his own voice in the Sacred History, states Martin's position that expulsion sufficed for the heretics and that a secular judge in a church cause was unheard of.
not_for: a separate witness from gallic.quote.secular-ruler-judge-in-ecclesiastical-cause, which carries the same sentence
independent corroboration of the Dialogues' Treves account, when both come from the same author
a claim that Martin thought the condemned were not heretics

uses.sentence: His disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the record is one named man - Martin, master and bishop both, who kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office. Authority rested where the power was felt. He needed no title. Sulpitius calls him "our master" and says it was unlawful to do anything but acquiesce to him. His disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Yet Martin himself, on a question touching whether a tradition had come down from antiquity, consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics, and would not honour a tomb where no steady tradition supported it. One of those presbyters was Brictio, whom Martin had raised from boyhood and who stormed into the courtyard in a fury. The man had sat down on his wooden seat one day, and Brictio came raging that he was holier than the master who brought him up, calling his visions ridiculous fancies and dreaming that he himself deserved the episcopate. Martin held that demons were driving him, but said he would bear with Brictio the way Christ bore with Judas. He would not remove him. That presbyter's rank came from somewhere, not from Martin alone, but where and how the record does not say.
