The novice takes his examples 'from a very few or indeed from one or two only' (Inst. IV.40). At Lérins the value is present as writings collated (Comm. ch. 3, ch. 28). It is also present as a disciple's Life of his master (Hilary's Life of Honoratus, Gennadius ch. LXX).
The texts raise no concern about attestation, but they do raise one about convention: a shared late-antique literary convention, which weakens what convergence proves. The value passes every test applied to it. It repeats across the kinds of evidence tested, one of them by existence alone. The form of both nodes' literature depends on it. The Dialogues are built as eyewitness testimony, and the Conferences are built as heard conferences, and each corpus defends its authority on that ground, while imitation of a named exemplar is the stated way that formation works at both nodes. It explains why Sulpitius writes a Life and why Hilary writes a Life, why Cassian writes reported speech, and why this world's stories are almost entirely first-person-attested. The value persists across nodes, 'with Vincent transforming the value from heard to read.' In the interaction test it passes with one negative cell.
Is this one value? As far as the evidence allows, in the sense the tests measure, yes. It is also a convention shared far beyond this world: 'two unconnected Latin monastic communities in 400 could each have inherited it separately.' The link across nodes is confirmed, but it is discounted as evidence of unity. The value is supporting, not primary. It organizes the literature's form and the formation mechanism, but it works within the context that the monk-bishop and Egypt-as-measure gravities establish, since the exemplar is a monk-bishop or an Egyptian father. A convention that the world shares with its neighbours does not meet the primary bar. The record's confidence and its gravity standing agree.
It held, but it fractured at the edge through transmission. In the grace controversy it becomes a weapon. Cassian's authority is that he heard Chaeremon. Prosper attacks 'a man of priestly rank' without naming him. The eyewitness-teacher's standing survives the attack. The fracture came in transmission, since the excision of Conferences XII and XXII removed two eyewitness conferences from this world's own English text. Gennadius gives 'two divisions' against the three Dialogues in this world's text. This shows that copying split the eyewitness frame itself again.

use_note.means: Authority to teach rests on having seen and heard a named master, so formation is imitation of a named exemplar, shifting at Lerins from men seen to writings read.
not_for: Vincent's collated writings as men seen
an impersonal institution or rule as the carrier of formation
the two eyewitness conferences removed from the vendored edition, which are absent

uses.sentence: A citizen threw himself at Martin's knees, Martin was escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and he became a bishop who kept the objects and virtues of a monk.
uses.paragraph: And now the limits. At Tours the saint himself began as a soldier still in the ranks, regarded as a monk though he had not yet professed. A citizen threw himself at Martin's knees, Martin was escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and he became a bishop who kept the objects and virtues of a monk. Whether Tours kept any testing at its own door, no one wrote. Of the island's own reception of a newcomer - a rule kept, a novice received - nothing. Not one man who came to our door left an account of how he was met there.
uses.record_text: A monk is lured out of his monastery by a citizen pretending his wife is ill, escorted to the city under a kind of guard, objected to by bishops for his mean clothes and disgusting hair, and answered by a psalm opened at random.

use_note.means: Sulpitius reports that Martin was lured from his monastery by a pretext, escorted under guard, and made bishop of Tours though some bishops objected to his mean clothes.
not_for: a neutral account of the objecting bishops, when Sulpitius is hostile to them
the southern counterpart, which sits in gallic.story.bishop-archebius
later canonical procedure for episcopal election
Martin's reluctance as proven fact, a claim contested in gallic.contested.election-as-capture

uses.sentence: A brother judged at fault lay on the ground until the abbot bade him rise, or was barred from prayer with the brethren.
uses.paragraph: The discipline for a fault is kept. A brother judged at fault lay on the ground until the abbot bade him rise, or was barred from prayer with the brethren. A steward found three lentils on the floor during one brother's week as cook, and the abbot judged him a pilferer of sacred property and suspended him from prayer until public penance. But that is a house's discipline turned on its own member for a fault, not a reckoning for what the house itself did wrong.
uses.record_text: The public discipline of our house. For a fault, a monk lies on the ground until the Abbot bids him rise, or is barred from prayer with the brethren. No priest is needed to restore him.

use_note.means: Penance meant the house's public discipline: lying on the ground until the Abbot bids rise, or barred from prayer, with no priest needed to restore the monk.
not_for: sacramental penance as private confession with absolution by formula
penance as self-punishment, or satisfaction as a scholastic category
the disclosure of thoughts before sin, which sits in gallic.term.disclosure-of-thoughts
documented Gallic practice, when whether any Gallic house kept the graded scale is not recorded

uses.sentence: In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person - that was Vincent's word on the island, and it was not debated among us but confessed as what the Church believes.
uses.paragraph: God as we held him is the Lord who never lets go of the tiller and whose hand is on everything. In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person - that was Vincent's word on the island, and it was not debated among us but confessed as what the Church believes. The Word of God does not change into flesh, and we do not worship a Quaternity. What we called him in our prayers was this: not only Protector and Saviour but Helper and Sponsor - Saviour, because he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. He wills all men to be saved, and to think otherwise was for us grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. He does not will only some instead of all. His grace always works together with our will, going before it and following it, inspiring the first desire and crowning the last perseverance. And at the same time the will always remains free in man, to neglect or delight in that grace, so that a monk's fasting and watching are truly his and truly required. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself; and God does not send rich crops to the idle. Both are held. How he works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. He is the God who judges now, not only at the end - a teaching one of us held, not all. And he is the one met in the beggar at the gate, wearing the half of a cloak.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.
not_for: a penal substitution doctrine, when the sixth-hour sentence is near it but not the same
anything from Cassian's books against Nestorius, which are unread
the bare formula, which sits in gallic.quote.one-substance-three-persons
a private confession of Jesus as personal Lord, which the record lacks

uses.sentence: Martin kept his mind on prayer even at other work.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the record dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap - never on what the brethren around him sang, or at what hours. Martin kept his mind on prayer even at other work. What the disciples did who gathered in the caves around his wooden cell, our record does not say beyond that they were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk at Tours and Marseilles, served at Marseilles by a received Egyptian system of psalms at fixed hours said to be an angel's.
not_for: the Divine Office as one settled book that all monks everywhere recited
prayer as private devotion and feeling

uses.sentence: Martin was a soldier under oath, a catechumen not yet baptized.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the story is one man's. Martin was a soldier under oath, a catechumen not yet baptized. At a donative on the eve of battle he told Caesar that he was now the soldier of Christ and it was not lawful for him to fight, and offered to stand unarmed before the enemy line. He left the army, gathered brethren around him in wooden cells and caves, and kept the habits of a monk even after he was made a bishop against his wish.
uses.record_text: A catechumen soldier has nothing left but his cloak. He cuts it in two for a naked beggar at a city gate. That night he sees Christ wearing the half he gave away.

use_note.means: Sulpitius tells that Martin, a catechumen soldier, cut his cloak in two for a beggar at a city gate and that night saw Christ wearing the half he gave.
not_for: evidence that the vision really happened, which the record does not assess
the discharge scene, which sits in gallic.story.discharge-before-caesar
a proof that anyone saw the Lord in the flesh, which gallic.limit.no-one-who-saw-him says is not held
the editors' identification of Amiens as the text's own

uses.sentence: The empire was Christian in our day.
uses.paragraph: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was - not underground, but in the courts, among bishops who had given way with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue. The violence we knew was heretics driving a bishop into exile, and later bishops handing heretics to the sword. Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt men in the Spains, where a man could be counted a heretic for the clothes he wore. But that was the sword drawn in the Church's cause by bishops, not a persecution that drove believers into hiding. What some of us did hide was different. Martin kept one thing hidden because of the times: that he had gone to the court and yielded once to a communion he abhorred, to save men from being killed. He hid that out of grief, not fear. The hiddenness we valued was the monk's own cell, where a man kept himself from the world he had left. Not catacombs. Wooden cells and caves.
uses.record_text: Hiding in the catacombs? No. Our age had no persecutor. Sulpitius says of Martin that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack; without them, he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding his blood - in hunger, in watchings, in nakedness, in fasting. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was. Did it change what we were? Martin's road began by leaving Caesar's service at a donative: I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. Before he gathered his first brethren, the violence of heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder. And at Treves, where the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place; he held it a foul and unheard-of thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church. He yielded there once, to save lives, and never sat with bishops again. What would an outsider have found strangest? We can only tell you what they laughed at. Some bystanders at a city gate laughed at a soldier walking in half a cloak. Bishops at the election said Martin's person was despicable, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting. Cassian says the Egyptians' sheepskin and little hoods would be a subject for derision in Gaul, so we did not wear them. Our own presbyter, raging in the courtyard, called the saint's visions ridiculous fancies. And what were we accused of? Sulpitius says that some of Martin's calumniators, though very few, were reported to be bishops. Others reported the brethren at Marseilles to Africa and to Rome for what they held about grace. A man of Marseilles wrote that at Carthage a monk, pale, with his hair shaved to the skin, could hardly be looked at without curses, and that servants of God from Egypt were met in the street with hissing. That was Africa, not Gaul. But it is the nearest our record comes to a crowd's own voice.

use_note.means: This witness says the Gallic monks met no persecution but faced derision at dress, hair and visions, and accusation by bishops and reporters to Africa.
not_for: the Carthage crowd's derision as a Gallic town's reaction, when it is Salvian's report of Africa
the objecting bishops as fairly heard, when only Sulpitius speaks for them
persecution or hiding in their own time, which the witness denies
the election as plainly a capture, which is weighed in gallic.contested.election-as-capture

uses.sentence: On the island Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and sufficient.
uses.paragraph: On the island Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and sufficient. And he held at the same time that Scripture's authority needs the Church's tradition, because of the great depth of Holy Scripture itself - almost everyone does not understand it in one and the same way, so that the same words are understood differently by different people. What guards against that is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. The whole Church's understanding, not one man's.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness says Jesus sought the unpitied, citing Martin's cloak, the guest received as Christ and grace calling the unwilling, while naming its thin personal testimony.
not_for: a personal conversion testimony from anyone but Martin, which the record lacks
evidence that Gallic houses broke fasts for guests, which Cassian does not say
a settled reading of Conference XIII on grace, which is contested
who Christ was and what his death meant, which sit in gallic.dw.the-christ-who-bears-the-wounds

uses.sentence: The fathers taught that the number of psalms, twelve at evening and twelve at night, was fixed by an angel's own singing - not invented by men, but received.
uses.paragraph: Our record of the hours kept among us comes from Cassian's own hand, written for a bishop's new monastery: the reason for the third hour, the sixth, the ninth, and the rest, drawn from what he learned in Egypt. The fathers taught that the number of psalms, twelve at evening and twelve at night, was fixed by an angel's own singing - not invented by men, but received. At Tours the hours themselves are not described, but Martin's practice is: prayer without a gap, like a blacksmith who beats his anvil between strokes.
uses.record_text: In those days only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. The perfection of the earliest Church still stood unbroken. The burning faith of the few had not yet cooled by being spread among the many. At that time the honored fathers watchfully made plans for those who would come after them. They met to discuss what plan to adopt for daily worship across the whole community of brothers. A dispute might send out a poisonous root of error, or jealousy, or division among those who came after. Each man judged by the measure of his own zeal, paying no heed to how weak others were. Some were for fifty, others for sixty. Some, not satisfied with that number, thought they really ought to go beyond it. They held a holy difference of opinion in their devout debate over the rule of their religious life. It was so great that the hour for their evening service came before the sacred question was settled. One stood up in their midst to sing the Psalms to the Lord. They were all sitting, their minds closely fixed on the words of the singer. He sang eleven Psalms, with prayers placed between them, each verse sung in an even voice. He ended the twelfth with the response "Alleluia." Then he suddenly vanished from the sight of all. At once this ended both their debate and their service. At this the honored assembly of the Fathers understood that, by God's providence, the angel's guidance had set a general rule for the brothers' communities. So they decreed that this number should be kept in both their evening and their night services. What they added, they added simply as extras, by their own decision.

use_note.means: Cassian, in Institutes II, relates the Egyptian tradition that an angel chanting twelve psalms settled the fathers' dispute over how many psalms the offices should hold.
not_for: an attested event, when Cassian names no witness and points to ecclesiastical history
a custom already kept in Gaul, when Cassian writes it for Castor's new house
the two added lessons as angelic, when the fathers added them by their own appointment

uses.sentence: Martin yielded once - pledged he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled - and it was granted.
uses.paragraph: Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent into the Spains, and found the bishops there in daily fellowship with the accuser, a bishop himself. He held that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing, and went to protect even heretics. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and others would follow, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin yielded once - pledged he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled - and it was granted. Afterward an angel told him his compunction was just, he felt his power lessened, and he never sat with bishops again. That unsettled us because the saint himself never called it right, and because it showed how the bishops could act when power was near.
uses.record_text: To stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics in the Spains, Martin yields once to a communion he abhors, is told by an angel that his compunction is just, feels his power diminished, and never attends a synod again.

use_note.means: Gallus tells that Martin yielded once to communion with the Ithacian bishops to save men from the tribunes, then lost power, was told his compunction was just, and shunned synods.
not_for: Priscillianism as a movement, which belongs to another world
the south's valuing of councils as guarantors, which sits in gallic.term.council-synod
Martin's rejection of synods as a general principle, when it follows one forced act
the earlier phase told in Sulpitius's own voice as one account with the Dialogues, when the two accounts remain distinct

uses.sentence: And of the women's houses at both our places, not one woman left her own word - not even the one our record praised most, and she is praised for not being seen.
uses.paragraph: But hear this limit. On the island - the house the churches came to for so many of their bishops - our record carries the founder's arrival and his going off to a see, and Vincent's own rule against forgetting, and nothing of what a day there actually held. And of the women's houses at both our places, not one woman left her own word - not even the one our record praised most, and she is praised for not being seen.
uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

use_note.means: The record attests that everything it holds about this world's places and daily life comes from texts, and cannot supply any excavation, material find or account of the island's days.
not_for: a claim that nothing has ever been dug up, when the build has not searched that literature
what the island kept day by day, which the record does not hold
Cassian's Egyptian customs as how Gallic houses lived, when he admits no one in our monasteries kept Egypt's perseverance even for a year, as in gallic.term.customs-of-the-monasteries
the editorial place-names as the world's own words

uses.sentence: Between them, labour in the cell without ceasing - basket-work, rope-work, whatever the hands can do while the heart says the psalms learned by heart.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set down what he had received from Egypt, the day was built around the hours and the cell. Twelve psalms at evening, twelve at night, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. Between them, labour in the cell without ceasing - basket-work, rope-work, whatever the hands can do while the heart says the psalms learned by heart. The wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. A brother may not go out without the elder's leave. Every thought is laid bare to the senior the moment it arises, before any deed. At the sixth hour comes the danger: a monk hates his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set. The remedy is to stay. All of it serves one mark: purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, at which every fast and vigil is aimed.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk at Tours and Marseilles, served at Marseilles by a received Egyptian system of psalms at fixed hours said to be an angel's.
not_for: the Divine Office as one settled book that all monks everywhere recited
prayer as private devotion and feeling
the eucharist as a rite, which sits in gallic.term.communion

uses.sentence: Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore.
uses.paragraph: The power claimed by bishops when they made common cause with an emperor's court, and the man we remember is the one who said it was a foul thing. Here is what our record holds. At Treves the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, and in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics by bishops in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court. The accuser there was himself a bishop. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. He held that it was punishment enough for the bishops to declare men heretics and put them out of the churches, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went, our record says, to protect even heretics themselves. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin pledged that night that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

use_note.means: Gallus recounts how Maximus shielded Ithacius after Priscillian's death and how Martin went to court to stop tribunes being sent into the Spains.

uses.sentence: A man rarely went out except for prayer.
uses.paragraph: A mill-wheel fed and a body held still - that is the shape of a day among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set it down from Egypt. The whole was built to serve one aim: prayer that never stops, the way a blacksmith beats his anvil between strokes. Twelve psalms at evening, learned by heart, and twelve at night - the number an angel fixed when the fathers of Egypt could not settle it themselves. Between those hours, labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. The psalms at the work, too. A man rarely went out except for prayer. The work itself was held sacred: a cook who left three lentils on the floor during his week of duty was judged a pilferer of the Lord's property and suspended from prayer until he did penance, because everything in the house is consecrated to God. That whole order was Egypt's, received from the fathers, not ours. Cassian wrote it out for a bishop's new house and said plainly that no one who joined our monasteries had kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even for a year. What a house in Gaul did instead, day by day, he never wrote.
uses.record_text: The monk's own dwelling, and the place where everything happens to him. There Martin prays, receives saints, and is tempted by a purple-robed devil behind a closed door. There Cassian's junior may not go out without leave, stays all day at his work, and is assailed at noon by the disease that makes him hate the cell itself.

use_note.means: The cell meant the monk's own hut or cave, rarely left except for prayer, where saints and devils come and the wandering heart is held still.

uses.sentence: A man leaves Caesar's service for Christ's.
uses.paragraph: The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man leaves Caesar's service for Christ's. He fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.record_text: At a donative on the eve of battle a soldier tells Caesar he is now the soldier of Christ and may not fight, offers to stand unarmed before the enemy line - and the enemy surrenders before morning.

uses.sentence: Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point.
uses.paragraph: All of it served one mark. The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. The archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the immediate goal of the whole monastic life, as distinct from its end, the kingdom of heaven. uses.sentence: Two old men who had lived apart forty years met again; one said the sun had never seen him eating, the other said nor me angry.
uses.paragraph: The shape of the discretion was this. Two old men who had lived apart forty years met again; one said the sun had never seen him eating, the other said nor me angry. Discretion was the virtue that kept every other virtue from destroying itself, the royal road between excess and slackness, gained only by humility and by showing one's thoughts to the elders. It judged the thought, not the man who brought it. A brother who spilled three lentils during his week as cook was suspended from prayer until he did penance, because everything in the house belonged to the Lord. That severity sat beside a patience for the thought laid bare.
uses.record_text: Two old men meet after forty years apart; the abbot of many says the sun has never seen him eating, and the hermit answers, "nor me angry."

uses.sentence: And Cassian says in the same breath that no one who came to our monasteries kept it unbroken even for a year.
uses.paragraph: That was Egypt's order. And Cassian says in the same breath that no one who came to our monasteries kept it unbroken even for a year. What a house in Gaul did instead, he never wrote. The fathers of Egypt remembered a man who had fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that forced turning into a willing one. So even at the door a man's past was not the bar; his perseverance was.
uses.record_text: In this, too, I will try to satisfy your directions. To that end, suppose I happen to find that something in those countries has been either taken away or added. And suppose the change does not follow the example of the elders, set by ancient custom, but the whim of whoever founded a monastery. Then I will faithfully add it or leave it out. I will do so by the rule I have seen kept in the monasteries founded long ago throughout Egypt and Palestine. For I do not believe a new foundation in the West, in Gaul, could find anything more reasonable or more perfect than those customs. The monasteries founded by holy and spiritually minded fathers since the apostles first preached keep those customs. In keeping them, they have lasted even to our own time. In my work, however, I will venture to use my own judgment in this way. I may find something in the rule of the Egyptians that is impossible in these countries, or hard and difficult. The cause may be the harsh climate, or some difficulty or difference in habits. In that case, I will balance it to some extent with the customs of the monasteries found throughout Pontus and Mesopotamia. For if we take proper account of what is possible, keeping the rule is just as perfect, though strength may be unequal.

uses.sentence: So within the Catholic Church itself we take care to hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all.
uses.paragraph: Vincent, on the island, set it down plainly. The canon of Scripture is complete, and more than enough. But Scripture still needs the Church's own line of interpretation, because nearly everyone reads it his own way. So within the Catholic Church itself we take care to hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part of the Church, or a novelty, or a few men dissent, we prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council's decree, or the ancients collated - the doctors whose agreed writings form "a consentient council". A single teacher, be he a bishop, be he a Confessor, be he a martyr, holds only a private fancy of his own.
uses.record_text: Within the Catholic Church, we must take great care to hold only what has been believed everywhere, always, by everyone. That is what "Catholic" truly means: it takes in everyone. The word itself says so, and so does plain logic. We follow this rule by holding to universality, antiquity, and agreement.

use_note.means: Vincent states in the Commonitory that true Catholic faith is what has been believed everywhere, always and by all, tested by universality, antiquity and consent.

uses.sentence: He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized.
uses.paragraph: How did Martin come to believe? Sulpitius told it, and it is our one whole story. At ten, against his parents' wish, Martin went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Why he went at ten, what moved him, Sulpitius never said. The one thing given is that he went before he believed it, and stayed there years.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness says Jesus sought the unpitied, citing Martin's cloak, the guest received as Christ and grace calling the unwilling, while naming its thin personal testimony.

uses.sentence: But he never described a room or named a site, and the island's own day was never told.
uses.paragraph: In the south, Cassian wrote for a bishop's new monastery in a province without one, and founded two houses himself, one for men and one for women. But he never described a room or named a site, and the island's own day was never told.
uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

use_note.means: The record attests that everything it holds about this world's places and daily life comes from texts, and cannot supply any excavation, material find or account of the island's days.

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that the first stage of a monk's turning was giving up goods, family, and the world's honours - and that this, though it is called leaving all things, was only the first and easiest stage.
uses.paragraph: Marriage was a thing left behind, and its leaving was the renunciation. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that the first stage of a monk's turning was giving up goods, family, and the world's honours - and that this, though it is called leaving all things, was only the first and easiest stage. The act that made a monk was figured as death, and the monk was dead to the world and its deeds and desires. At Tours Martin left Caesar's service at a donative and never married; he gathered brethren, and the bishops who objected to his election said his clothes were mean and his hair disgusting, not that he had taken a wife. The whole of what we marked was the cut, not the bond. For a woman the cut had its own form. A girl was devoted by her father to perpetual virginity, and the bishop placed on her the dress characteristic of that state. At Martin's funeral the consecrated virgins walked as a choir. Cassian taught that marriage may be excused; virginity points to glory. The completed victory is not to be seen.
uses.record_text: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."

use_note.means: Renunciation meant the act that makes a monk, a death to the world of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest of three stages.

uses.sentence: That is where the trouble was - not underground, but in the courts, among bishops who had given way with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue.
uses.paragraph: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was - not underground, but in the courts, among bishops who had given way with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue. The violence we knew was heretics driving a bishop into exile, and later bishops handing heretics to the sword. Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt men in the Spains, where a man could be counted a heretic for the clothes he wore. But that was the sword drawn in the Church's cause by bishops, not a persecution that drove believers into hiding. What some of us did hide was different. Martin kept one thing hidden because of the times: that he had gone to the court and yielded once to a communion he abhorred, to save men from being killed. He hid that out of grief, not fear. The hiddenness we valued was the monk's own cell, where a man kept himself from the world he had left. Not catacombs. Wooden cells and caves.
uses.record_text: Hiding in the catacombs? No. Our age had no persecutor. Sulpitius says of Martin that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack; without them, he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding his blood - in hunger, in watchings, in nakedness, in fasting. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was. Did it change what we were? Martin's road began by leaving Caesar's service at a donative: I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. Before he gathered his first brethren, the violence of heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder. And at Treves, where the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place; he held it a foul and unheard-of thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church. He yielded there once, to save lives, and never sat with bishops again. What would an outsider have found strangest? We can only tell you what they laughed at. Some bystanders at a city gate laughed at a soldier walking in half a cloak. Bishops at the election said Martin's person was despicable, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting. Cassian says the Egyptians' sheepskin and little hoods would be a subject for derision in Gaul, so we did not wear them. Our own presbyter, raging in the courtyard, called the saint's visions ridiculous fancies. And what were we accused of? Sulpitius says that some of Martin's calumniators, though very few, were reported to be bishops. Others reported the brethren at Marseilles to Africa and to Rome for what they held about grace. A man of Marseilles wrote that at Carthage a monk, pale, with his hair shaved to the skin, could hardly be looked at without curses, and that servants of God from Egypt were met in the street with hissing. That was Africa, not Gaul. But it is the nearest our record comes to a crowd's own voice.

use_note.means: This witness says the Gallic monks met no persecution but faced derision at dress, hair and visions, and accusation by bishops and reporters to Africa.
not_for: the Carthage crowd's derision as a Gallic town's reaction, when it is Salvian's report of Africa

uses.sentence: Cassian wrote for a bishop founding a new monastery in a province that did not have one, and he wrote of Egypt's customs, not of Gaul's construction.
uses.paragraph: I cannot say. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Where we gathered is named by place, never described as a building. At Tours, a wooden cell for the saint and caves for the brethren. The island where Honoratus went and Vincent dwelt is a harbour, a camp of God, and a place no one would live before he came - never floor, wall, or roof. Cassian wrote for a bishop founding a new monastery in a province that did not have one, and he wrote of Egypt's customs, not of Gaul's construction. Where the brethren stood to sing the twelve psalms that an angel fixed for the fathers, what covered them or what they stood on - that is not in our record. The one procession we are told of moved on the road, between Tours and the monastery, with two thousand monks and a choir of virgins following the body. If you dug, we could not tell you what you would find.
uses.record_text:
This world holds Egypt up as the standard of real monastic life. But the two houses relate to that standard in opposite ways.
In the south, the tie is receptive. Bishop Castor wanted the customs of the East, and especially of Egypt, set up in a province of Gaul that had no monasteries at all. Cassian promises to fix anything founded on one person's own whim, rather than on the Egyptian rule. He will adapt the letter of that rule only where Gaul's climate or circumstances make it truly impossible (Inst. Pref.). Gallic monks are told to take the authors of the Conferences into their own cells, as living teachers (Conf. Pref. III). At Lérins, Eucherius names two Egyptian fathers as the pattern of a life already lived, in effect, in heaven.
In the north, the tie is comparative, even competitive. Gennadius says plainly that the Dialogues set the life of the Eastern monks side by side with the life of Martin. One speaker in the Dialogues concedes to another that Martin surpasses every hermit and solitary of the East. Another passage sends word all the way to Egypt itself. However proud Egypt is of its many saints, Europe need not yield to it, or to all of Asia, since Europe has Martin alone. Gaul is the poorer, colder partner in this comparison.
Both houses organize themselves around the same point: Egypt, as the standard of real monastic life. But they differ in kind. The south receives that standard as a rule to keep. The north measures itself against it as a rival to match. This split shows up everywhere the idea is tested. It repeats across every voice in this world's own literature. The Institutes' whole structure, the Conferences' whole frame, and the shape of the Dialogues all depend on it. In the south, formation itself is nothing but this act of reception. In the north, the fit is only partial. It explains the north's competitive language and the south's own talk of adapting to climate. It explains why Cassian's own text is, at once, desert monasticism's Latin transmission and this world's own founding literature. And it holds up across both houses, in these two different modes, wherever it meets this world's other core ideas. Both halves rest on strong, direct evidence. So this record finds no real doubt about the finding itself. The only open question is what it means for whether this is one world or two - and this record leaves that question open.
The tie to Egypt held steady across this world's whole span. But what Egypt was needed for kept changing. Before Cassian ever wrote, Tours answered the Egyptian standard with rivalry. Marseilles and Lérins answered it, a generation later, with reception and careful adaptation. Once the fight over grace broke out, the receptive mode hardened further. Egypt itself became an authority to plead against Augustine and Rome - the whole line of orthodox teachers on the heart's own perfection, as Cassian frames it. Under the barbarian collapse, Egypt survives as little more than a byword for holiness, in the one place Salvian mentions it. The standard itself never moved. What moved was what this world needed it for.

use_note.means: Egypt stands as the measure of real monastic life, received in the south as a rule from the fathers and matched at Tours by a saint said to outdo it.

So "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered."

uses.sentence: God, as we held him, is the one who calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation.
uses.paragraph: God, as we held him, is the one who calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He wills all to be saved, and those who perish, perish against his will - to think otherwise is grievous blasphemy. That is the first thing: his will reaches for every man, not only some instead of all.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. uses.sentence: Two old men met after forty years apart; the abbot of many said the sun had never seen him eating, and the hermit answered, "nor me angry".
uses.paragraph: There was a place inside the fence for someone who had not yet believed, and a patience kept for the one who lost heart. At Tours a boy named Martin went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. The catechumen who belonged to the Church but had not yet been baptized was not outside; he was still learning. And among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, knew the monk's own trouble. A man's bright early days cool. He comes to hate his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a pious reason to leave. That cooling was the professed man's own fear, not a beginner's stumble - a disease of temperature that damns. The remedy was not argument but staying. The senior held him in his cell as in a secure harbour, and taught him to lay bare every thought. A thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to tell it, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. What was shown was not belief as an achieved state but labour and patience. Two old men met after forty years apart; the abbot of many said the sun had never seen him eating, and the hermit answered, "nor me angry". They proved perseverance, not perfection. At Tours the presbyter who stormed into the courtyard, called his master's visions ridiculous fancies, and repented within the hour was not removed. Martin bore with him afterward, asking why he should not bear with the man if Christ bore with Judas.

The books exist to be that example when the man himself is absent.

uses.sentence: We never argued it as a formula, and where Cassian touched it he touched it as Egypt's fathers touched it - as a thing held, not debated.
uses.paragraph: We never argued it as a formula, and where Cassian touched it he touched it as Egypt's fathers touched it - as a thing held, not debated. Here is what our record keeps. Among the brethren at Marseilles, Abbot Chaeremon named three stages of the grace by which we are saved: the first kindles our desire toward salvation, the second enables us in the good we wish for, the third preserves us to the end in the virtues. All three are God's gift. And he taught plainly that a newborn has no merits before him - he spoke of "the case even of infants, who have as yet done nothing either good or bad". That is the nearest our record comes to your question's shape: infants with no works of their own, and grace going before every stage. But whether they bear guilt from birth, by what they are rather than what they have done, Cassian does not say. What he does say is this: the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; he does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and it is grievous blasphemy to think otherwise. Free will always remains in a man, and it is weak, and the help of God is necessary to it every day and hour. How both are true - how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. The inherited guilt as a thing confessed apart from the grace that answers it is not in our record to give you.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. Grace "always co-operates with our will"; it goes before the will and follows it; it inspires the first desire and crowns the last perseverance. We hold it together, on purpose, with a will that stays free - in a relation "that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man."

use_note.means: Grace meant, for Cassian's Marseilles, God's help without which no effort reaches its goal, going before the will and crowning it, held on purpose with a will that stays free.

uses.sentence: That grammar of reception runs through everything: the psalter's number came from an angel the fathers received it from, not from us; the office was not sought but seized; and at the moment a man felt his labour had accomplished something, our discipline taught him to say Not I, but the grace of God with me.
uses.paragraph: What we held was received, not invented. The customs of the monasteries were the fathers' own, brought from Egypt, not ours. The faith was what had been believed everywhere, always, by all. We were keepers, not authors - disciples, not teachers - followers, not leaders. That grammar of reception runs through everything: the psalter's number came from an angel the fathers received it from, not from us; the office was not sought but seized; and at the moment a man felt his labour had accomplished something, our discipline taught him to say Not I, but the grace of God with me.
uses.record_text: The fathers of Egypt argue whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupts them. One father rises to sing, finishes the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanishes. The number is fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel.

uses.sentence: The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity.
uses.paragraph: All of it served one mark. The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers as brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. Prayer that never stops - the aim of every monk, and a fixed system of psalms at set hours built to serve that aim.

uses.sentence: The hours kept the Lord's death and rising: at the third hour the Spirit came down; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints.
uses.paragraph: What we carry of our worship is this. At Tours the saint prayed without a gap, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. At Marseilles Cassian handed us the hours from Egypt - twelve psalms at evening, twelve at night, the number fixed by an angel who sang the twelfth with Alleluia and vanished. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. The hours kept the Lord's death and rising: at the third hour the Spirit came down; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. That is what our own books say of it.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

uses.paragraph: He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. The girdle, the hood, the tunic - each was a mystery of the inner life. But his old clothes were not thrown away. The steward kept them in his cupboard against the day he grew cold. They waited there as long as his body advanced in goodness and his mind in humility, and they were kept until the excellence of his progress and his long perseverance in it gave certain proof that he would never return to the world.

We were taught not to invent, but to hold what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. That meant Scripture was heard through the fathers, not against them. uses.sentence: The Lord we knew was the crucified one who came in the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak, whose death at the sixth hour took away a debt that could not be paid, and whose grace calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling.
uses.paragraph: By what path they arrived, our record does not say. We were formed more than three hundred years after the Lord's days. No one in our record claims a chain of hands back to an apostle, and we never asked for one. What we held was what the Church held - the books believed everywhere, always, by all, against the few and the new. The Lord we knew was the crucified one who came in the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak, whose death at the sixth hour took away a debt that could not be paid, and whose grace calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling. That reached us as the fathers' faith, kept in the churches and carried into the monasteries - received, not invented, never traced hand to hand as though legitimacy were a claim to prove.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness says Jesus sought the unpitied, citing Martin's cloak, the guest received as Christ and grace calling the unwilling, while naming its thin personal testimony.
not_for: a personal conversion testimony from anyone but Martin, which the record lacks

uses.sentence: Of the island's own day, not a line.
uses.paragraph: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like — only as far as those pages say, and no further.
uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

use_note.means: The record attests that everything it holds about this world's places and daily life comes from texts, and cannot supply any excavation, material find or account of the island's days.

uses.sentence: That the grace argument has one Catholic answer - Vincent read the Apostolic See's letter for his side, and we never settled which of Chaeremon's two phrasings on the beginning of a good will was his own.
uses.paragraph: What would not survive is any claim we made past the record's edge. That Martin's reluctance was total - Sulpitius is no neutral witness, and the objecting bishops never answered. That the island kept what Vincent taught - nothing shows a day there. That Gallic houses lived by Cassian's customs - he says they did not. That a miracle happened as told - our record has reported experience, not assessed fact. That the grace argument has one Catholic answer - Vincent read the Apostolic See's letter for his side, and we never settled which of Chaeremon's two phrasings on the beginning of a good will was his own.
uses.record_text: Meanwhile, the bishops Martin would not share communion with went to the king in terror. They complained that they had been condemned in advance. It was all over for the standing of every one of them, they said, if Martin's authority now backed the stubbornness of Theognitus. He alone had so far condemned them by a sentence given in public. They said the man should never have been let inside the walls. He was now not just the heretics' defender but their champion. And nothing had really been gained by Priscillian's death if Martin was going to play the part of his avenger. At last they threw themselves down, weeping and wailing, and begged the emperor to use his power against this one man. The emperor came close to being forced to give Martin, too, the fate of heretics. Still, although he was inclined to favor the bishops too much, he knew Martin surpassed all others in faith, holiness, and excellence. So he tried another way to get the better of the holy man. First he sent for him in private and spoke to him very kindly. He assured Martin that the heretics had been condemned by regular public trials, not by the priests' persecution. He said there was no reason for Martin to think communion with Ithacius and the rest of that party was something to condemn. He added that Theognitus had caused division out of personal hatred rather than for the cause he stood for. In fact, he said, Theognitus was the only one who had so far cut himself off from communion. The rest had changed nothing. He also pointed out that a synod held a few days before had ruled that Ithacius could not be charged with any fault. When these arguments hardly moved Martin, the king grew furious and hurried out of his presence. Without delay, executioners were appointed for the people Martin had pleaded for. When Martin learned of this, he rushed to the palace, though it was already night. He promised that if these people were spared, he would take communion. He asked only that the tribunes already sent to the Spanish provinces to destroy the churches be called back. There was no delay: Maximus granted everything he asked. The next day, the ordination of Felix as bishop was being arranged. Felix was without doubt a man of great holiness, truly worthy of being made a priest in happier times. Martin took part in the communion that day. He judged it better to give way for the moment than to ignore the safety of those with a sword hanging over their heads. Even so, he would not confirm his communion by signing his name, though the bishops tried their very hardest to make him. The next day he hurried away from that place. On the way back he was filled with grief and mourning that he had been mixed up, even for an hour, in the evil communion. Not far from a village named Andethanna, remote woods stretch far and wide in deep solitude. There he sat down, while his companions went on a little way ahead of him. He sank into deep thought, by turns accusing and defending the cause of his grief and what he had done. Suddenly an angel stood beside him and said, "Martin, you are right to feel remorse, but you had no other way out of your difficulty. Renew your strength and take up your courage again. Otherwise you will put at risk not only your good name now, but your very salvation." So from then on he took great care never to be mixed up in communion with the party of Ithacius. But once he cured some of the possessed more slowly than usual, and with less of the grace he usually had. At once he confessed to us in tears that he felt his power had lessened. He said it was because of the evil of that communion. He had taken part in it for a moment out of necessity, not with his whole heart. He lived sixteen years after this. But he never again attended a synod, and he kept well away from all gatherings of bishops.

use_note.means: Gallus narrates how Martin, to stop the tribunes, took communion with the Ithacian bishops, was answered by an angel, and afterwards felt his healing power diminished.
not_for: the angel's speech and the lessened power as established fact, when they rest on Martin's tearful report through Gallus

uses.sentence: Leadership was not established among us; it overtook the man who fled it.
uses.paragraph: Leadership was not established among us; it overtook the man who fled it. At Tours a monk was lured from his monastery by a citizen pretending his wife was ill, escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and made bishop though some of the bishops summoned for it said his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, and his hair disgusting. Then the new bishop kept a monk's habits inside the office - the same humility in his heart, sitting on a rude little stool such as those in use by the lowest of servants. Each of our houses told its founder's rise the same way. On the island the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive. And the one Egyptian bishop Cassian chose to tell us of had been carried off from the anchorites and complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it.
uses.record_text:
Renunciation kept producing bishops. Men renounced the world to become monks, and then the office of bishop overtook them.

Martin shows the pattern. He kept up the position of a bishop properly, yet he did not lay aside the aims and virtues of a monk.

Of the eighty disciples at Marmoutier, numbers were afterwards made bishops (Vita, ch. X). The disciples were trained after their master's example.

Everything Cassian wrote was addressed to bishops, or to men who became bishops. His formation writing was for a bishop's new monastery. Honoratus moves from monk to bishop between two of his dedications (Conferences, prefaces II and III).

Archebius is the Egyptian counter-case. He counted his appointment as expulsion from the monastic system, as unworthy of it. Cassian carried his story west (Conferences XI.2).

Hilary of Arles preached on Honoratus in the south's own Latin. He tells how the priest's headband fastened on a man who fled from it, and how the honor came to him. The Latin is there in the source, but this English wording of it is rated Inferential/Thin.

What sets this world apart is a seminary that looked like a monastery. Every primary voice attests this pattern, and Gennadius confirms it independently. It holds in both north and south, more strongly than any other pattern in this world. It is the only one that a Latin insider in the south, Hilary, attests apart from Cassian.

It explains three things. The withdrawal stayed close to the city. The grace argument reached Rome. The ending was a change in how the institution spoke, not a collapse.

The controversy over grace did not break the pattern. It strengthened it into the Lérins network of bishops. Celestine's letter named Venerius, Cassian's own bishop, first (Gibson's editorial introduction). It warned that priests ought not to teach so as to invade the bishops' rights.

By the 470s a bishop formed at Lérins, Faustus, carried the argument at the commission of synods. Under barbarian pressure this was the institution left standing. Gennadius, writing from the same city about 495, reports two monasteries still standing.

These pressures did not change the pattern. They made it the way the world ended.

use_note.means: Renunciation kept producing bishops, so this world's monks were repeatedly seized into the office they were taught to flee and kept a monk's virtues inside the see.
not_for: a bishop's career as promotion or sell-out
