uses.sentence: Under him were deans, each over ten brothers.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles leadership was the fathers' structure, received from Egypt. Cassian handed us not a written rule of his own but the customs of the monasteries he had seen kept there, as they were delivered by the Fathers. A congregation was governed by the direction of a single Elder, called Abbot - the Egyptian fathers' own title. Under him were deans, each over ten brothers. Every thought was laid bare to the senior. The junior had no cell key of his own; he could not go out without leave; and it was the Abbot's hands that stripped a newcomer of his old clothes and dressed him in the house's dress. Where that Abbot's own authority came from - election, appointment, seniority - Cassian never says. He gives us the Egyptian fathers' unanimous decision on customs, not the mechanism by which one house chose its own.

"Abbot" is the title of every Egyptian father Cassian reports. At Tours the same place is held by one master, Martin, who himself consults "his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics."

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles, Abbot Chaeremon named three stages of the grace by which we are saved: the first kindles our desire toward salvation, the second enables us in the good we wish for, the third preserves us to the end in the virtues.
uses.paragraph: We never argued it as a formula, and where Cassian touched it he touched it as Egypt's fathers touched it - as a thing held, not debated. Here is what our record keeps. Among the brethren at Marseilles, Abbot Chaeremon named three stages of the grace by which we are saved: the first kindles our desire toward salvation, the second enables us in the good we wish for, the third preserves us to the end in the virtues. All three are God's gift. And he taught plainly that a newborn has no merits before him - he spoke of "the case even of infants, who have as yet done nothing either good or bad". That is the nearest our record comes to your question's shape: infants with no works of their own, and grace going before every stage. But whether they bear guilt from birth, by what they are rather than what they have done, Cassian does not say. What he does say is this: the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; he does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and it is grievous blasphemy to think otherwise. Free will always remains in a man, and it is weak, and the help of God is necessary to it every day and hour. How both are true - how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. The inherited guilt as a thing confessed apart from the grace that answers it is not in our record to give you.
uses.record_text: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.

use_note.means: Cassian reports Chaeremon teaching that grace kindles desire, enables virtue and preserves it without destroying free will, and that their union exceeds human reason.

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles, men held that grace and effort work together.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, men held that grace and effort work together. The will stays free; grace goes before it, works with it, and crowns it; and still God asks real labour of us. Others reported that teaching to Africa and to Rome. Vincent read the Apostolic See's own letter as written for his own side, for antiquity. But he never said the question was closed. Our own teacher Chaeremon had answered on both sides with Scripture's own cases and said that how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.record_text:
Human effort and free choice are real, and they matter. This world argues that point under pressure from Augustine's own later teaching on grace.
Cassian's own text states the position directly. He gives it through the teaching he attributes to Abbot Chaeremon. God's grace always works together with a person's own will, for that will's own good. But it sometimes waits on some real effort from the person before it is given (Conf. XIII.13). To deny that God wants everyone saved, and not just some, Chaeremon says, would be a grave blasphemy (Conf. XIII.7). Neither side of the argument should be pushed too far, Chaeremon warns. Exactly how grace and free will fit together, in the end, is a question human reason cannot fully answer (Conf. XIII.11, XIII.18). Elsewhere, Cassian's own manual for monks, in its climactic book, gives plain advice. A monk who feels he is making progress should credit it all to God's grace, and not to himself (Inst. XII.9).
What the wider Church heard about this teaching came mostly at second hand. Augustine himself reports that the Gallic monks he is answering already grant one point: that God's grace goes ahead of the human will. But they remain unsettled on the question of predestination. That is a report from the other side, not this world's own voice. What is known of Rome's own reply survives only at a distance - Prosper's appeal to the Pope, Celestine's letter to the Gallic bishops, a Roman critique of Cassian's own thirteenth Conference. None of it comes from a text this world wrote itself; it comes through a modern editor's own account of that history. Gennadius, writing on his own, confirms only that a dispute between Cassian and Prosper existed at all. At Tours, there is simply nothing on this question. The corpus there closed before it was ever raised.
At Lérins, the current runs the other way, though how far Vincent himself took part is genuinely disputed. He quotes Pope Celestine's own words, that novelty must give way to old and settled teaching. He reads those words as backing his own side. But nothing in his surviving text names Augustine, or the fight itself, outright.
This argument is Cassian's own, within this world's own voices. No other Native voice in this world independently holds it. Yet it matters enormously wherever it appears. Several other parts of this world's own literature depend on it. It turned one whole Conference, out of twenty-four, into a direct answer to a crisis in formation. And it explains a great deal of what survives about Prosper, Celestine, and a Roman critique of Cassian himself. But it does not appear evenly across this world's whole span. Tours has nothing to say about it, for reasons of plain timing, not disagreement. For that reason, this record calls it a supporting idea at the level of the whole world. Within the southern house alone, though, it is treated as the leading concern. The evidence for the position is strong. Yet its reach across the whole world stays narrow. That gap is itself a real and disclosed tension in how this record is classified. A reader should not mistake the modest classification for any doubt about what Cassian and Chaeremon actually taught.
Under pressure from Rome, the argument grew stronger, and who carried it changed too. It began as monks writing for other monks. It ended, a generation later, with a bishop, trained at Lérins, writing at the order of a church council. Inside this world's own literature, though, it began as something much simpler. It was a remedy for the pride of a monk who feels, at last, that he is making progress - offered long before anyone outside gave it any name at all.

use_note.means: Human effort and free choice are held real and to matter while grace goes before and crowns them, argued under Augustine's pressure in a relation Cassian says reason cannot grasp.

uses.sentence: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find.
uses.paragraph: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like — only as far as those pages say, and no further.
uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

uses.sentence: The senior held him in his cell as in a secure harbour, and taught him to lay bare every thought.
uses.paragraph: There was a place inside the fence for someone who had not yet believed, and a patience kept for the one who lost heart. At Tours a boy named Martin went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. The catechumen who belonged to the Church but had not yet been baptized was not outside; he was still learning. And among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, knew the monk's own trouble. A man's bright early days cool. He comes to hate his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a pious reason to leave. That cooling was the professed man's own fear, not a beginner's stumble - a disease of temperature that damns. The remedy was not argument but staying. The senior held him in his cell as in a secure harbour, and taught him to lay bare every thought. A thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to tell it, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. What was shown was not belief as an achieved state but labour and patience. Two old men met after forty years apart; the abbot of many said the sun had never seen him eating, and the hermit answered, "nor me angry". They proved perseverance, not perfection. At Tours the presbyter who stormed into the courtyard, called his master's visions ridiculous fancies, and repented within the hour was not removed. Martin bore with him afterward, asking why he should not bear with the man if Christ bore with Judas.
uses.record_text: The monk's own dwelling, and the place where everything happens to him. There Martin prays, receives saints, and is tempted by a purple-robed devil behind a closed door. There Cassian's junior may not go out without leave, stays all day at his work, and is assailed at noon by the disease that makes him hate the cell itself.

use_note.means: The cell meant the monk's own hut or cave, rarely left except for prayer, where saints and devils come and the wandering heart is held still.

uses.sentence: He held that bishops declaring men heretics and casting them out was enough, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a Church cause was a foul and unheard-of thing.
uses.paragraph: And when the sword was drawn? Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics in the Spains. He held that bishops declaring men heretics and casting them out was enough, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a Church cause was a foul and unheard-of thing. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and others would follow, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When anger failed, the emperor named executioners. Martin pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared. It was granted. He left in grief, felt his power lessened, and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: To stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics in the Spains, Martin yields once to a communion he abhors, is told by an angel that his compunction is just, feels his power diminished, and never attends a synod again.

use_note.means: Gallus tells that Martin yielded once to communion with the Ithacian bishops to save men from the tribunes, then lost power, was told his compunction was just, and shunned synods.

uses.sentence: The Word of God does not change into flesh, and we do not worship a Quaternity.
uses.paragraph: God as we held him is the Lord who never lets go of the tiller and whose hand is on everything. In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person - that was Vincent's word on the island, and it was not debated among us but confessed as what the Church believes. The Word of God does not change into flesh, and we do not worship a Quaternity. What we called him in our prayers was this: not only Protector and Saviour but Helper and Sponsor - Saviour, because he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. He wills all men to be saved, and to think otherwise was for us grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. He does not will only some instead of all. His grace always works together with our will, going before it and following it, inspiring the first desire and crowning the last perseverance. And at the same time the will always remains free in man, to neglect or delight in that grace, so that a monk's fasting and watching are truly his and truly required. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself; and God does not send rich crops to the idle. Both are held. How he works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. He is the God who judges now, not only at the end - a teaching one of us held, not all. And he is the one met in the beggar at the gate, wearing the half of a cloak.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

uses.sentence: What we held about how a man comes to faith is this: the beginning of it is not ours.
uses.paragraph: What we held about how a man comes to faith is this: the beginning of it is not ours. uses.sentence: The canon of Scripture is perfect and more than sufficient in itself for everything - and yet every man reads it his own way, so that it seems capable of yielding as many meanings as there are readers.
uses.paragraph: Scripture was not our sole authority. We held three things together: the canon of Scripture, the tradition of the Church, and the consent of the ancients. Vincent, on the island, wrote it plainly. The canon of Scripture is perfect and more than sufficient in itself for everything - and yet every man reads it his own way, so that it seems capable of yielding as many meanings as there are readers. What guards it is the tradition of the Catholic Church, and within that tradition the test is threefold: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and the consent of the ancients. By "consent" Vincent meant an ancient council where one had spoken, or else the collated writings of the fathers - not one teacher alone, however great, but many together.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

uses.sentence: Martin had the apostles' own power - over death, over demons, over emperors.
uses.paragraph: We held what Egypt handed us and never claimed it went back unbroken to the first days. The psalms and the hours had a story. Among the fathers of Egypt only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. They argued whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupted them. One father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel. That is the rule Cassian brought to Gaul as the fathers' own, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. It is a beginning claimed in Egypt, not in Jerusalem. We never said we had it from the apostles. What we said of ourselves is that we received it from the fathers and kept it where Gaul's cold allowed. Egypt was our measure, in the south. At Tours the highest word spoken was different. Martin had the apostles' own power - over death, over demons, over emperors. That named the kind of power the saint showed, not a line of customs kept. And the test of what was legitimate ran through everything we held. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever has been handed down from antiquity is to be held fast. We did not invent a proof that our hours went back to the first believers. We said Egypt gave them to us, and that an angel gave them to Egypt. The authority was in whose they were, not in how old.
uses.record_text: At Tours, the highest thing said of Martin - having the apostles' power over death, demons, and emperors. At Marseilles, the perfection of love, and the first Church's common life.

uses.paragraph: His mercy is real patience. Martin bore with a presbyter he had raised who called his visions ridiculous fancies, because, he said, if Christ bore with Judas he should bear with this man. God's own bearing with us is longer still.
uses.record_text: Then the holy man explained, both to him and to all of us, how he had seen demons driving him on. He declared that the insults heaped on him did not move him. In fact, they had hurt the man who spoke them instead. Later, this same Brictio was often accused before Martin of many serious crimes. Yet Martin could not be persuaded to remove him from the priesthood. He did not want to be suspected of taking revenge for the wrong done to himself. And he often repeated this saying: ‘If Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio?’

uses.sentence: And in the same book he said plainly that no one who joined our monasteries kept that perseverance unbroken even for a year.
uses.paragraph: That is the order Cassian wrote. And in the same book he said plainly that no one who joined our monasteries kept that perseverance unbroken even for a year. So the formation passed by watching a named man. Martin's eighty disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Cassian wrote the conferences so that our monks might receive the fathers into their cells, talking with them after a fashion by daily questions and answers. The books exist to be that example when the man himself is absent.
uses.record_text: I will certainly not try to weave a tale of God's miracles and signs. It is true that we have heard of many such things among our elders, things beyond belief. We have also seen them fulfilled before our very eyes. Yet I will leave out all these things. They give the reader nothing but astonishment, and no instruction in the perfect life. Instead, as far as I can and with God's help, I will try to explain faithfully only their institutions and the rules of their monasteries. Above all, I will explain the origin and causes of the principal faults. They count eight of these. I will also explain the remedies for them, following their traditions. For my purpose is to say a few words, not about God's miracles, but about how to improve our character and reach the perfect life. In this I follow what we received from our elders.

use_note.means: Cassian declares in the Institutes preface that he will not narrate the miracles he has heard and seen, but only the fathers' rules and remedies for faults.

uses.sentence: The accuser there was himself a bishop.
uses.paragraph: The power claimed by bishops when they made common cause with an emperor's court, and the man we remember is the one who said it was a foul thing. Here is what our record holds. At Treves the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, and in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics by bishops in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court. The accuser there was himself a bishop. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. He held that it was punishment enough for the bishops to declare men heretics and put them out of the churches, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went, our record says, to protect even heretics themselves. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin pledged that night that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

uses.sentence: That unsettled me - that bishops could make such common cause with a court, that a secular ruler could sit as judge in an ecclesiastical cause, and that the man who went to stop it paid for it with diminished power and never sat with bishops again.
uses.paragraph: That unsettled me - that bishops could make such common cause with a court, that a secular ruler could sit as judge in an ecclesiastical cause, and that the man who went to stop it paid for it with diminished power and never sat with bishops again. Two limits belong with this. The accuser is heard only through the man who called him worthless. And at Marseilles we had no Martin to go to court; whether any voice there spoke against what happened at Treves, no one kept.

uses.sentence: When part of the Church dissents, prefer the whole; when novelty arises, prefer antiquity; when a few teach something, prefer the consent of many.
uses.paragraph: We never settled it by one judge or one seat. What we held is this: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. That is Vincent's test, on the island, and it runs on three things at once - universality, antiquity, and consent. When part of the Church dissents, prefer the whole; when novelty arises, prefer antiquity; when a few teach something, prefer the consent of many. And consent means an ancient council's decree, or the writings of the fathers collated - never one teacher alone, be he bishop or confessor or martyr, for one teacher alone has only a private fancy of his own. Novelty is suspect for being new; what was handed down from antiquity is held fast. That grammar runs through all three of our founding voices. Cassian brought the customs of the monasteries from Egypt as delivered to us by the fathers - received, not invented. Martin would not honor a tomb without steady tradition from antiquity. And Vincent wrote the test itself.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

use_note.means: The rule meant Vincent's test of the faith, what has been believed everywhere, always, by all, preferring the whole, the old and consent to the part, the new and few.

uses.sentence: Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.
uses.paragraph: No, never that phrase. What we kept for conversion is one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness says Jesus sought the unpitied, citing Martin's cloak, the guest received as Christ and grace calling the unwilling, while naming its thin personal testimony.

uses.sentence: A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered.
uses.paragraph: Within the house the place belongs to the senior whose judgment stands in for the junior's own. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that every itching thought is laid bare to him the moment it rises. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. Abbot is the title of every Egyptian father Cassian reports. At Tours the same place was held by one master, Martin, who himself consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the practice of laying every "itching thought" bare to the senior as soon as it arises. It is "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection." The elders' rule: "a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it." So "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered."

use_note.means: Disclosure of thoughts meant laying every rising thought bare to the senior before any deed, the first lesson of Cassian's monastic life and not the later sacrament.

uses.sentence: No one in our record claims to have known someone who saw him.
uses.paragraph: What connected us to Jesus, and by what path it came, is in the books and the practices they carried. The books were read at the hours. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough - and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Those books were not inventions of ours. They were already the faith believed everywhere, always, by all when our own span opened. More than three hundred years lay between the Lord's days and ours. No one in our record claims to have known someone who saw him. What we had instead was what those books gave us: the cloak story as Sulpitius told it, with the Lord's own words set beside it - what is done to the least of these is done to him. The Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me, which the fathers of Egypt taught a monk to say when he felt his fast had done something. The hours of prayer themselves, built around the hours of the Lord's passion - the third hour when the Spirit came down, the sixth when the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, the ninth when he went down into hell.
uses.record_text: What did we have of Jesus? The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

use_note.means: The record attests that this world's books never claim a witness to the Lord and never argue the resurrection to a doubter, and it cannot supply either.
not_for: a proof of the resurrection written by this world for a doubter, which the record says is absent

uses.sentence: He fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ.
uses.paragraph: The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man leaves Caesar's service for Christ's. He fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

uses.sentence: He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all - a man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused the novelty and innovated nothing.
uses.paragraph: Our faith in Jesus as truly God is held as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, set it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all - a man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused the novelty and innovated nothing. That is the formula as Vincent held it, and it is the whole of our own direct witness on the Trinity as such.
uses.record_text: Vincent's example against Nestorius. In Christ there are two substances but one Person, so Mary is truly "the mother of God." Ephesus had refused the new teaching three years before.

use_note.means: Theotocos appears as Vincent's example against Nestorius: two substances and one Person in Christ, so that Mary is truly the mother of God, a proof-case for his rule.

uses.paragraph: And for the monk the turning had stages. Renunciation - death to the world and its desires - came in three acts, not one. Giving up goods was only the first and easiest. uses.sentence: By "consent" Vincent meant an ancient council where one had spoken, or else the collated writings of the fathers - not one teacher alone, however great, but many together.
uses.paragraph: Scripture was not our sole authority. We held three things together: the canon of Scripture, the tradition of the Church, and the consent of the ancients. Vincent, on the island, wrote it plainly. The canon of Scripture is perfect and more than sufficient in itself for everything - and yet every man reads it his own way, so that it seems capable of yielding as many meanings as there are readers. What guards it is the tradition of the Catholic Church, and within that tradition the test is threefold: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and the consent of the ancients. By "consent" Vincent meant an ancient council where one had spoken, or else the collated writings of the fathers - not one teacher alone, however great, but many together.
uses.record_text: Vincent's word for an authorized teacher in the Church. What binds is the consent of such teachers; one teacher's own view, "be he a bishop, be he a Confessor, be he a martyr," is "a private fancy."

uses.sentence: And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation.
uses.paragraph: And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. Grace goes before the will, kindles the first desire, and crowns the last perseverance. The help of God without which no effort reaches its goal - that is what we meant by grace.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.sentence: The honest limit here is that we wrote no treatise on it.
uses.paragraph: The honest limit here is that we wrote no treatise on it. Vincent's formula was his test-case for refusing heresy, not a doctrine dwelt on for itself. What we held of the Trinity we held as already settled - one substance, three Persons - and our own life pressed hardest not there but at grace and effort, the cooling of monks, and whether power should be shown or hidden.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

use_note.means: This witness says this world knew Jesus as the crucified one met in the poor, kept his death and rising at the hours, and preached grace drawing the unwilling.

uses.sentence: Cassian wrote it out for a bishop's new house and said plainly that no one who joined our monasteries had kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even for a year.
uses.paragraph: A mill-wheel fed and a body held still - that is the shape of a day among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set it down from Egypt. The whole was built to serve one aim: prayer that never stops, the way a blacksmith beats his anvil between strokes. Twelve psalms at evening, learned by heart, and twelve at night - the number an angel fixed when the fathers of Egypt could not settle it themselves. Between those hours, labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. The psalms at the work, too. A man rarely went out except for prayer. The work itself was held sacred: a cook who left three lentils on the floor during his week of duty was judged a pilferer of the Lord's property and suspended from prayer until he did penance, because everything in the house is consecrated to God. That whole order was Egypt's, received from the fathers, not ours. Cassian wrote it out for a bishop's new house and said plainly that no one who joined our monasteries had kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even for a year. What a house in Gaul did instead, day by day, he never wrote.
uses.record_text:
Antiquity, the Fathers, and consent are the test of legitimacy, set against novelty - applied by all three founding voices to monastic custom, doctrine, and cult alike.
Cassian holds that allegiance is owed not to customs a few people have introduced, but to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement (Inst. I.2). He calls his own Institutes not his but the fathers' (Conf. Pref. I). And he holds up, as a warning, the monk who trusted his own judgment over the Elders' tradition and in the end forsook the desert (Conf. II.24).
Vincent holds that the Catholic faith is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all - tested by universality, antiquity, and consent (Comm. ch. 2). He quotes Pope Stephen's own rule that there should be no innovation, nothing but what has been handed down (ch. 6). And he holds that a guardian of doctrine is not an author but a keeper, not a teacher but a disciple, not a leader but a follower (ch. 22).
Sulpitius tells that Martin, asked to venerate a supposed martyr's tomb, would not lend his own authority to popular opinion, because no reliable tradition about it reached back to antiquity (Vita XI).
This same standard also became a battleground. Prosper reports that the Massilians defended their own obstinacy by antiquity; Celestine, as later editors read him, answered that novelty must cease to assail antiquity; and Vincent read that same letter for his own side (Comm. ch. 32). The rule that was meant to settle disputes became, in the grace controversy, one more thing both sides claimed for themselves.

uses.sentence: That grammar runs through all three of our founding voices.
uses.paragraph: We never settled it by one judge or one seat. What we held is this: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. That is Vincent's test, on the island, and it runs on three things at once - universality, antiquity, and consent. When part of the Church dissents, prefer the whole; when novelty arises, prefer antiquity; when a few teach something, prefer the consent of many. And consent means an ancient council's decree, or the writings of the fathers collated - never one teacher alone, be he bishop or confessor or martyr, for one teacher alone has only a private fancy of his own. Novelty is suspect for being new; what was handed down from antiquity is held fast. That grammar runs through all three of our founding voices. Cassian brought the customs of the monasteries from Egypt as delivered to us by the fathers - received, not invented. Martin would not honor a tomb without steady tradition from antiquity. And Vincent wrote the test itself.
uses.record_text: The axis on which all three of our founding voices judge what is legitimate. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever "has been handed down" from antiquity is to be held fast. "If novelty is profane, antiquity is sacred."

uses.sentence: At a donative on the eve of battle he told Caesar that he was now the soldier of Christ and it was not lawful for him to fight, and offered to stand unarmed before the enemy line.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the story is one man's. Martin was a soldier under oath, a catechumen not yet baptized. At a donative on the eve of battle he told Caesar that he was now the soldier of Christ and it was not lawful for him to fight, and offered to stand unarmed before the enemy line. He left the army, gathered brethren around him in wooden cells and caves, and kept the habits of a monk even after he was made a bishop against his wish.
uses.record_text: At a donative on the eve of battle a soldier tells Caesar he is now the soldier of Christ and may not fight, offers to stand unarmed before the enemy line - and the enemy surrenders before morning.

uses.sentence: Where we said the record is thin - the island's day, the women's voices, the body's teaching cut from our English text - that honesty would survive whole.
uses.paragraph: And one thing more. Where we said the record is thin - the island's day, the women's voices, the body's teaching cut from our English text - that honesty would survive whole. A record's silence, plainly named, is not a claim a scholar can refute.
uses.record_text:
Miracle, exorcism, and blessed objects hold together the northern literature. The south's teacher refuses this whole approach on principle.
At Tours, power is something Martin bears, and is known by. He prays over a dead catechumen. He senses that God's power is present, and raises the man back to life (Vita VII). Gallus reports that Martin himself used to say something else, too. He sensed less of that power as bishop than he remembered having before he held the office (Dial. II.4). One of Sulpitius's letters defends that same power against a skeptic. Gennadius, writing later, calls Martin a man famous for signs, wonders, and virtues.
Cassian refuses this on principle. He says plainly that he will not try to tell stories about God's wonders, however many he has witnessed himself. Such stories teach a reader nothing about how to live well (Inst. Pref.). Abbot Nesteros goes further still. No one who declared himself an exorcist before an admiring crowd was ever counted a good monk. Whether the devils obeyed him was beside the point (Conf. XV.7). This is the sentence that sets the two literatures directly against each other. Inside the south itself, Eucherius still admires the Egyptian fathers' visible signs of grace. So the real argument runs between Cassian and Sulpitius, not between south and north as a whole. Neither names the other; whether Cassian's refusal is a veiled answer to Sulpitius is not settled.
This gravity organizes the north's literature completely. The Vita, the Letters, and the Dialogues are all built from acts of power. The north's account of the episcopate, power lost through office, depends on it too. But it rests mostly on one voice, Sulpitius's alone. Gennadius confirms only that Martin was famous for signs, not that power organizes a monk's whole life. Cassian refuses the whole approach outright. For that reason, this record holds virtus as a tensional gravity, not a primary one. It is real and unresolved, resting on one voice rather than broad agreement. It is the steady counter-force that keeps this ecology from being reduced to the south's interior program alone. One house's literature is made of exactly what the other house's teacher says a good monk must never proclaim. It does not organize the whole world. But the world cannot be described without it. This record finds no demonstrated link between this gravity and the grace controversy.
Under institutional pressure the gravity shifts rather than holds steady. Martin felt less power as bishop than as monk, by his own account. He felt a further loss after a forced communion with bishops he distrusted. Office itself, in this literature, registers as a real cost to the saint's body. Under barbarian pressure the gravity is touched only twice, and thinly. At the north's ending, it passed from a living saint's power to a relic's, and to a psalm's.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. uses.sentence: Cassian handed us not a written rule of his own but the customs of the monasteries he had seen kept there, as they were delivered by the Fathers.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles leadership was the fathers' structure, received from Egypt. Cassian handed us not a written rule of his own but the customs of the monasteries he had seen kept there, as they were delivered by the Fathers. A congregation was governed by the direction of a single Elder, called Abbot - the Egyptian fathers' own title. Under him were deans, each over ten brothers. Every thought was laid bare to the senior. The junior had no cell key of his own; he could not go out without leave; and it was the Abbot's hands that stripped a newcomer of his old clothes and dressed him in the house's dress. Where that Abbot's own authority came from - election, appointment, seniority - Cassian never says. He gives us the Egyptian fathers' unanimous decision on customs, not the mechanism by which one house chose its own.
uses.record_text: What Cassian carried from Egypt and Palestine to a Gallic bishop's "new monastery." Not a written Rule of his own. Rather, "the customs of the monasteries which we have seen observed" there, "as they were there delivered to us by the Fathers." We keep them where Gaul's cold and our weak bodies allow. Where they do not, we balance them from Pontus and Mesopotamia.

use_note.means: The customs of the monasteries meant what Cassian carried from Egypt to Gaul, received from the fathers and not written as a Rule, kept as far as the cold allowed.

uses.paragraph: I cannot say. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Where we gathered is named by place, never described as a building. At Tours, a wooden cell for the saint and caves for the brethren. The island where Honoratus went and Vincent dwelt is a harbour, a camp of God, and a place no one would live before he came - never floor, wall, or roof. Cassian wrote for a bishop founding a new monastery in a province that did not have one, and he wrote of Egypt's customs, not of Gaul's construction. Where the brethren stood to sing the twelve psalms that an angel fixed for the fathers, what covered them or what they stood on - that is not in our record. The one procession we are told of moved on the road, between Tours and the monastery, with two thousand monks and a choir of virgins following the body. If you dug, we could not tell you what you would find.
uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

uses.sentence: The senior held him in his cell as in a secure harbour, and taught him to lay bare every thought.
uses.paragraph: There was a place inside the fence for someone who had not yet believed, and a patience kept for the one who lost heart. At Tours a boy named Martin went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. The catechumen who belonged to the Church but had not yet been baptized was not outside; he was still learning. And among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, knew the monk's own trouble. A man's bright early days cool. He comes to hate his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a pious reason to leave. That cooling was the professed man's own fear, not a beginner's stumble - a disease of temperature that damns. The remedy was not argument but staying. The senior held him in his cell as in a secure harbour, and taught him to lay bare every thought. A thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to tell it, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. What was shown was not belief as an achieved state but labour and patience. Two old men met after forty years apart; the abbot of many said the sun had never seen him eating, and the hermit answered, "nor me angry". They proved perseverance, not perfection. At Tours the presbyter who stormed into the courtyard, called his master's visions ridiculous fancies, and repented within the hour was not removed. Martin bore with him afterward, asking why he should not bear with the man if Christ bore with Judas.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the practice of laying every "itching thought" bare to the senior as soon as it arises. It is "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection." The elders' rule: "a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it." So "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered."

use_note.means: Disclosure of thoughts meant laying every rising thought bare to the senior before any deed, the first lesson of Cassian's monastic life and not the later sacrament.
not_for: sacramental confession of sins to a priest with absolution
therapy or optional spiritual accountability

a documented Gallic practice, when whether any Gallic house kept it is unrecorded

uses.sentence: Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way.
uses.paragraph: The second is this. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. We were taught not to invent, but to hold what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. That meant Scripture was heard through the fathers, not against them. When a man at our door came in troubled by one sentence - that striving cannot make a man master of the good - the elder answered him with the husbandman and the rain, and told him the initiative comes from God. The question was about what Paul said; the answer was in the elder's mouth, not on the page. You are reading it as though you had to settle it yourself, and we were not formed that way.
uses.record_text: What did we have of Jesus? The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

use_note.means: The record attests that this world's books never claim a witness to the Lord and never argue the resurrection to a doubter, and it cannot supply either.
not_for: a proof of the resurrection written by this world for a doubter, which the record says is absent
the cloak vision or the raised catechumen as evidence that the Lord rose, when they show the saint's power, as in gallic.story.the-cloak-at-amiens and gallic.story.raising-of-the-catechumen

uses.sentence: When a monk feels his fasting has accomplished something, he is taught to say *Not I, but the grace of God with me*.
uses.paragraph: And he was the one without whom we can do nothing. When a monk feels his fasting has accomplished something, he is taught to say *Not I, but the grace of God with me*. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. He calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. Those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness says Jesus sought the unpitied, citing Martin's cloak, the guest received as Christ and grace calling the unwilling, while naming its thin personal testimony.
not_for: a personal conversion testimony from anyone but Martin, which the record lacks

uses.sentence: Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent into the Spains, and found the bishops there in daily fellowship with the accuser, a bishop himself.
uses.paragraph: Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent into the Spains, and found the bishops there in daily fellowship with the accuser, a bishop himself. He held that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing, and went to protect even heretics. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and others would follow, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin yielded once - pledged he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled - and it was granted. Afterward an angel told him his compunction was just, he felt his power lessened, and he never sat with bishops again. That unsettled us because the saint himself never called it right, and because it showed how the bishops could act when power was near.
uses.record_text: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

use_note.means: Gallus recounts how Maximus shielded Ithacius after Priscillian's death and how Martin went to court to stop tribunes being sent into the Spains.
not_for: a doctrinal ruling on heresy, when Martin's petition concerned lives

uses.sentence: The books were read inside that frame - a renunciation of marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter service of Christ.
uses.paragraph: The path those books took to reach us, our record does not trace. They were already in the churches and the monasteries when Martin first gathered brethren. What our own life added was not the books but what they were read for. A newcomer at Marseilles was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. A week's cook was judged a pilferer for three lentils left on the floor, because everything in the house is consecrated to the Lord. A discharged soldier told Caesar he was now the soldier of Christ and may not fight. The books were read inside that frame - a renunciation of marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter service of Christ. And they were read to be said. The psalter learned by heart, said at the work, kept a man's wheel fed. That is the path as our record keeps it: books received, not invented, read at fixed hours in a house built to hold a man to them.
uses.record_text: A monk, for us, is a man who has cut himself off from marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter life in Christ's service. The cut shows in his body and his dwelling. But at Tours a soldier still in the ranks could be "regarded as a monk," and so could a bishop in his see.

use_note.means: A monk meant a man cut off from marriage, kin, property and the world for stricter service of Christ, a name a soldier or bishop could bear at Tours.

uses.sentence: At Tours the hours themselves are not described, but Martin's practice is: prayer without a gap, like a blacksmith who beats his anvil between strokes.
uses.paragraph: Our record of the hours kept among us comes from Cassian's own hand, written for a bishop's new monastery: the reason for the third hour, the sixth, the ninth, and the rest, drawn from what he learned in Egypt. The fathers taught that the number of psalms, twelve at evening and twelve at night, was fixed by an angel's own singing - not invented by men, but received. At Tours the hours themselves are not described, but Martin's practice is: prayer without a gap, like a blacksmith who beats his anvil between strokes.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk at Tours and Marseilles, served at Marseilles by a received Egyptian system of psalms at fixed hours said to be an angel's.

uses.sentence: And Salvian, who wrote from one of the houses at Marseilles, named those who had taken our way of life as the ones who chose to be lowly, poor, and unesteemed.
uses.paragraph: Everything, we said - and proved the claim by the life the brethren kept. Among the brethren at Marseilles a man was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the clothing of the house. That is the sign, not the whole list. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, named three renunciations, and giving up one's goods was only the first. Leaving behind bodily wealth and riches - possessions, kin, the life one had in the world - is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the man who has renounced. The second renunciation is of habits, vices, and the mind's former affections - the whole interior road of the faults. The third is drawing the mind away from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come. So the claim was this: marriage, property, honours, secular business, kin. Martin was a soldier in Caesar's service who left it at a donative, saying he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight. The fathers remembered a man who fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that compelled turning into a willing one. And Salvian, who wrote from one of the houses at Marseilles, named those who had taken our way of life as the ones who chose to be lowly, poor, and unesteemed.
uses.record_text: Salvian's plain name for those who have taken our way of life. A class of people, seen from the city, who chose to be lowly and poor.

use_note.means: The religious was Salvian's plain name, from the city, for those who took the monastic way, a class who chose to be lowly and poor.
not_for: religious as an adjective of general piety

uses.sentence: A steward found three lentils on the floor during one brother's week as cook, and the abbot judged him a pilferer of sacred property and suspended him from prayer until public penance.
uses.paragraph: The discipline for a fault is kept. A brother judged at fault lay on the ground until the abbot bade him rise, or was barred from prayer with the brethren. A steward found three lentils on the floor during one brother's week as cook, and the abbot judged him a pilferer of sacred property and suspended him from prayer until public penance. But that is a house's discipline turned on its own member for a fault, not a reckoning for what the house itself did wrong.
uses.record_text: A steward finds three lentils on the floor during a brother's week as cook, the abbot judges him a pilferer of sacred property, and he is suspended from prayer until public penance - because everything in the house is "consecrated to the Lord."

use_note.means: Cassian relays that a cook who left three lentils on the floor was judged a pilferer of sacred property and barred from prayer, because the house's goods are the Lord's.

uses.sentence: First, the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, taught that God does not will only some to be saved instead of all.
uses.paragraph: First, the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, taught that God does not will only some to be saved instead of all. He does not want even one of his little ones to perish, and to think otherwise is grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. That is Abbot Chaeremon's own word, and we held it.
uses.record_text: For if He wills none of His little ones to perish, how can we, without grievous blasphemy, imagine He does not will all people's salvation? That He wills only some to be saved, instead of all people in general?

use_note.means: Chaeremon, in Cassian's Conference XIII, argues it would be grievous blasphemy to imagine God wills only some, rather than all, to be saved.
