uses.sentence: Grace goes before the will, kindles the first desire, and crowns the last perseverance.
uses.paragraph: And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. Grace goes before the will, kindles the first desire, and crowns the last perseverance. The help of God without which no effort reaches its goal - that is what we meant by grace.
uses.record_text: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.

uses.sentence: One father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished.
uses.paragraph: We held what Egypt handed us and never claimed it went back unbroken to the first days. The psalms and the hours had a story. Among the fathers of Egypt only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. They argued whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupted them. One father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel. That is the rule Cassian brought to Gaul as the fathers' own, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. It is a beginning claimed in Egypt, not in Jerusalem. We never said we had it from the apostles. What we said of ourselves is that we received it from the fathers and kept it where Gaul's cold allowed. Egypt was our measure, in the south. At Tours the highest word spoken was different. Martin had the apostles' own power - over death, over demons, over emperors. That named the kind of power the saint showed, not a line of customs kept. And the test of what was legitimate ran through everything we held. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever has been handed down from antiquity is to be held fast. We did not invent a proof that our hours went back to the first believers. We said Egypt gave them to us, and that an angel gave them to Egypt. The authority was in whose they were, not in how old.

uses.sentence: At the sixth hour we confessed that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross.
uses.paragraph: What sits beside it is how we spoke of Jesus in the voice of formation. Cassian calls him the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. At the sixth hour we confessed that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. That was kept at the hours: the divine substance, the saving death, and the rising. And the Lord we knew was the crucified one met in the poor - Martin refused a Christ without wounds.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

uses.sentence: He went, our record says, to protect even heretics themselves.
uses.paragraph: The power claimed by bishops when they made common cause with an emperor's court, and the man we remember is the one who said it was a foul thing. Here is what our record holds. At Treves the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, and in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics by bishops in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court. The accuser there was himself a bishop. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. He held that it was punishment enough for the bishops to declare men heretics and put them out of the churches, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went, our record says, to protect even heretics themselves. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin pledged that night that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

uses.sentence: Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen.
uses.paragraph: No, never that phrase. What we kept for conversion is one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.sentence: Every thought is laid bare to the senior the moment it arises, before any deed.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set down what he had received from Egypt, the day was built around the hours and the cell. Twelve psalms at evening, twelve at night, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. Between them, labour in the cell without ceasing - basket-work, rope-work, whatever the hands can do while the heart says the psalms learned by heart. The wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. A brother may not go out without the elder's leave. Every thought is laid bare to the senior the moment it arises, before any deed. At the sixth hour comes the danger: a monk hates his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set. The remedy is to stay. All of it serves one mark: purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, at which every fast and vigil is aimed.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the practice of laying every "itching thought" bare to the senior as soon as it arises. It is "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection." The elders' rule: "a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it." So "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered."

use_note.means: Disclosure of thoughts meant laying every rising thought bare to the senior before any deed, the first lesson of Cassian's monastic life and not the later sacrament.

uses.sentence: Brictio, a presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood, stormed into the courtyard and called his master's visions ridiculous fancies.
uses.paragraph: One man's raging hour is kept, and the saint's reply. Brictio, a presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood, stormed into the courtyard and called his master's visions ridiculous fancies. He was back within the hour, at Martin's feet, and Martin bore with him afterward and would not remove him. Martin asked why he should not bear with the man, if Christ bore with Judas. But that is a saint bearing with a presbyter's rage in a moment when the presbyter repented - not a house answering for its own failure toward someone outside its wall.
uses.record_text: These things filled the wretched man with bitter rage. And, I believe, the urging of those demons drove him most of all. He attacked Martin so fiercely that he barely held back from striking him. The holy man, for his part, kept a calm face and a peaceful mind. With gentle words he tried to hold back the unhappy man's madness. But the spirit of evil had such a grip on him that he could not control even his own mind. That mind was a very foolish one even at the best of times. His lips trembled, and his face changed, pale with rage. He poured out sinful words. He claimed he was a holier man than Martin, who had raised him. From his earliest years, he said, he had grown up in the monastery, trained in the Church's holy ways. Martin, he said, had first been stained by a soldier's life, as Martin could not deny. And now, he said, Martin had sunk completely into old age's foolishness. His groundless superstitions and ridiculous fancies about visions had brought him to it.

use_note.means: Gallus describes Brictio nearly assaulting Martin and claiming to be holier for growing up in the monastery, while Martin answered with gentle words.
not_for: a neutral report of Brictio's case, when it comes from men hostile to him
the reproof that provoked the outburst, which sits in gallic.quote.brictio-horses-and-slaves
a claim that Martin argued back, when the text gives him only gentle restraint

uses.sentence: We did not read them the way you are reading them now.
uses.paragraph: We did not read them the way you are reading them now. The difference is not what we saw in them but what we did with them. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer was held to it by a rule. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The words were not read once and set aside. They were the grain the mill turned. A man kept praying even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The Apostle's word not I, but the grace of God with me was taught to a monk at the moment he felt his own fasting had done something. At Tours the saint took the Apostle's least of these as the beggar at the gate. And at the election a bystander seized the psalter, read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. So what you are missing is not a key to the text. It is the use the text was put to. You read it to understand it. We said it to feed the wheel that cannot stop turning, and heard it speak into the hour we were standing in.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk at Tours and Marseilles, served at Marseilles by a received Egyptian system of psalms at fixed hours said to be an angel's.

uses.sentence: Then he was given for a year to the elder who kept the gate for guests.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, the way a newcomer was received was Egypt's way, set down by Cassian as the fathers' own. The man lay outside the doors ten days or more, put off and scorned on purpose, to give proof that he meant it. He was searched for a single hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. Then he was given for a year to the elder who kept the gate for guests.
uses.record_text:
Antiquity, the Fathers, and consent are the test of legitimacy, set against novelty - applied by all three founding voices to monastic custom, doctrine, and cult alike.
Cassian holds that allegiance is owed not to customs a few people have introduced, but to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement (Inst. I.2). He calls his own Institutes not his but the fathers' (Conf. Pref. I). And he holds up, as a warning, the monk who trusted his own judgment over the Elders' tradition and in the end forsook the desert (Conf. II.24).
Vincent holds that the Catholic faith is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all - tested by universality, antiquity, and consent (Comm. ch. 2). He quotes Pope Stephen's own rule that there should be no innovation, nothing but what has been handed down (ch. 6). And he holds that a guardian of doctrine is not an author but a keeper, not a teacher but a disciple, not a leader but a follower (ch. 22).
Sulpitius tells that Martin, asked to venerate a supposed martyr's tomb, would not lend his own authority to popular opinion, because no reliable tradition about it reached back to antiquity (Vita XI).
This same standard also became a battleground. Prosper reports that the Massilians defended their own obstinacy by antiquity; Celestine, as later editors read him, answered that novelty must cease to assail antiquity; and Vincent read that same letter for his own side (Comm. ch. 32). The rule that was meant to settle disputes became, in the grace controversy, one more thing both sides claimed for themselves.

use_note.means: Antiquity, the fathers and consent are the test of legitimacy against novelty in custom, doctrine and cult, applied by all three founding voices though they never cite one another.
not_for: a conservatism that forbids all growth
the test as consistently applied, when that is contested in gallic.contested.who-holds-antiquity

uses.sentence: What he does say is this: the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; he does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and it is grievous blasphemy to think otherwise.
uses.paragraph: We never argued it as a formula, and where Cassian touched it he touched it as Egypt's fathers touched it - as a thing held, not debated. Here is what our record keeps. Among the brethren at Marseilles, Abbot Chaeremon named three stages of the grace by which we are saved: the first kindles our desire toward salvation, the second enables us in the good we wish for, the third preserves us to the end in the virtues. All three are God's gift. And he taught plainly that a newborn has no merits before him - he spoke of "the case even of infants, who have as yet done nothing either good or bad". That is the nearest our record comes to your question's shape: infants with no works of their own, and grace going before every stage. But whether they bear guilt from birth, by what they are rather than what they have done, Cassian does not say. What he does say is this: the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; he does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and it is grievous blasphemy to think otherwise. Free will always remains in a man, and it is weak, and the help of God is necessary to it every day and hour. How both are true - how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. The inherited guilt as a thing confessed apart from the grace that answers it is not in our record to give you.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

uses.sentence: Martin kept silence a long time.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. That is one man's own confession, made alone.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

use_note.means: This witness says this world knew Jesus as the crucified one met in the poor, kept his death and rising at the hours, and preached grace drawing the unwilling.
not_for: a Gallic treatise on the atonement, which no one in this world wrote
the Christ with wounds as independently witnessed, when one author reports Martin's word
the resurrection as argued rather than confessed at the hours

uses.sentence: The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of the mind as a mill that cannot stop turning.
uses.paragraph: Yes. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of the mind as a mill that cannot stop turning. Thoughts will come - from God, from the devil, from ourselves - and a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. The mind is a wheel turned by a stream, and the miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, thoughts are the raw material of the interior struggle. "It is impossible for the mind not to be approached by thoughts, but it is in the power of every earnest man either to admit them or to reject them." They come "from God, from the devil, and from ourselves." The mind is a mill-wheel that must grind something; the miller decides "whether he will have wheat or barley or darnel ground by it."

use_note.means: Thoughts meant the raw material of the interior struggle, which cannot stop arriving from God, the devil or ourselves, the monk answering for which he admits.
not_for: intrusive thoughts as symptoms to be managed

uses.sentence: What connected us to Jesus, and by what path it came, is in the books and the practices they carried.
uses.paragraph: What connected us to Jesus, and by what path it came, is in the books and the practices they carried. The books were read at the hours. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough - and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Those books were not inventions of ours. They were already the faith believed everywhere, always, by all when our own span opened. More than three hundred years lay between the Lord's days and ours. No one in our record claims to have known someone who saw him. What we had instead was what those books gave us: the cloak story as Sulpitius told it, with the Lord's own words set beside it - what is done to the least of these is done to him. The Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me, which the fathers of Egypt taught a monk to say when he felt his fast had done something. The hours of prayer themselves, built around the hours of the Lord's passion - the third hour when the Spirit came down, the sixth when the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, the ninth when he went down into hell.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness says Jesus sought the unpitied, citing Martin's cloak, the guest received as Christ and grace calling the unwilling, while naming its thin personal testimony.
not_for: a personal conversion testimony from anyone but Martin, which the record lacks
evidence that Gallic houses broke fasts for guests, which Cassian does not say
a settled reading of Conference XIII on grace, which is contested

uses.sentence: So the claim was this: marriage, property, honours, secular business, kin.
uses.paragraph: Everything, we said - and proved the claim by the life the brethren kept. Among the brethren at Marseilles a man was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the clothing of the house. That is the sign, not the whole list. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, named three renunciations, and giving up one's goods was only the first. Leaving behind bodily wealth and riches - possessions, kin, the life one had in the world - is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the man who has renounced. The second renunciation is of habits, vices, and the mind's former affections - the whole interior road of the faults. The third is drawing the mind away from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come. So the claim was this: marriage, property, honours, secular business, kin. Martin was a soldier in Caesar's service who left it at a donative, saying he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight. The fathers remembered a man who fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that compelled turning into a willing one. And Salvian, who wrote from one of the houses at Marseilles, named those who had taken our way of life as the ones who chose to be lowly, poor, and unesteemed.
uses.record_text: For us "the world" is what a monk has left - kin, property, honours, delights, "secular business." We name it from the far side of the renunciation, as a warfare one has been discharged from and a sea one has come out of. We never name it as a place from which God is absent.

use_note.means: The world meant what a monk has left, kin, property, honours and business, named from the harbour as a warfare one was discharged from, never as a place without God.
not_for: secular in the modern sense of non-religious or secular government
contempt for the created order, or misanthropy

uses.sentence: What we argued was this: does the beginning of a good will come from us, or from God?
uses.paragraph: What we argued was this: does the beginning of a good will come from us, or from God? Two friends came back to morning service troubled because an old man had said a man cannot make himself master of the good by his own toil. The elder cut the office short and answered with a field. The husbandman ploughs, sows, and weeds - all truly his labour - and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself alone, yet God does not send it to the idle. From that morning came the teaching: God's grace goes before our will, inspires the beginning, works with us, and crowns the end - and it asks real effort of us every day and hour. Both halves held together. Our labour is truly ours and truly required. The grace that makes it reach its goal is God's.
uses.record_text: Two friends come back to morning service troubled by one sentence an old man added the night before - that striving cannot make a man master of the good - and the elder shortens the office to answer them with a husbandman, the rain, and "the initiative ... comes from God."

use_note.means: Cassian records that Germanus's scruple over one sentence of Chaeremon's led the elder to shorten the office and answer that the initiative comes from God.

uses.sentence: Eighty of them were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the record is thinner still. Martin himself began as a soldier under oath, still a catechumen, who cut his one cloak in two at a city gate. At ten he had gone to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen, then stayed one for years. After the cloak he was baptized. The brethren gathered around him as disciples around a master. Eighty of them were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. But what a man did to become one of them - whether he too lay outside, whether he was reclothed, how long he was tested - Sulpitius never told.
uses.record_text: Our formative bond is a named man and those formed by watching him. Martin's "eighty disciples, who were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master"; Clarus, "a disciple of Martin's"; Sulpitius mourning "our master, Martin." The south keeps it as elder and junior. Vincent turns it on doctrine: the true Catholic is "not a teacher but a disciple, not a leader but a follower."

use_note.means: Disciple and master named the bond between a named man and those formed by watching him, which Vincent turned on doctrine: the Catholic is a disciple, not a leader.

uses.sentence: That cut showed in his body and his dwelling.
uses.paragraph: Here is what the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, said about it. Renunciation has three stages. The first is giving up one's goods - "of what is not our own," they said, because all things are God's. But that stage alone is not enough to make a man perfect. The second is giving up one's former way of life, its vices and passions of soul and flesh. The third is withdrawing the mind from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come. A professed man had cut himself off from marriage, kin, property, and the life of the world for a stricter life in Christ's service. That cut showed in his body and his dwelling.
uses.record_text: A monk, for us, is a man who has cut himself off from marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter life in Christ's service. The cut shows in his body and his dwelling. But at Tours a soldier still in the ranks could be "regarded as a monk," and so could a bishop in his see.

use_note.means: A monk meant a man cut off from marriage, kin, property and the world for stricter service of Christ, a name a soldier or bishop could bear at Tours.

uses.sentence: Our record keeps the stories a house tells of itself - the saint's own life told by a disciple who mourned him; the elders' words carried from Egypt; the island's remembered founder; the faith believed everywhere, always, by all.
uses.paragraph: I cannot tell you what you are asking for. Our record keeps the stories a house tells of itself - the saint's own life told by a disciple who mourned him; the elders' words carried from Egypt; the island's remembered founder; the faith believed everywhere, always, by all. What it does not keep is an account told by someone we failed, in their own words, naming what we did to them and how we answered for it.
uses.record_text:
Authority to teach or narrate rests on having seen and heard a named master, and formation happens by imitation of a named exemplar. Sulpitius writes 'the life of a most holy man, which shall serve in future as an example to others' (Vita I), and Marmoutier's disciples are 'disciplined after the example of the saintly master' (Vita X), and Martin's last saying is 'I have sinned if I leave you a different example' (Ep. III), and Gallus can say 'I myself am a witness' (Dial. II.4). Cassian writes that 'these things cannot be taught save by one who has had experience of them' (Inst. Pref.). The Conferences are reported speech of named elders whom God 'has deemed us worthy both to see ... and to dwell with'. The novice takes his examples 'from a very few or indeed from one or two only' (Inst. IV.40). At Lérins the value is present as writings collated (Comm. ch. 3, ch. 28). It is also present as a disciple's Life of his master (Hilary's Life of Honoratus, Gennadius ch. LXX).
The texts raise no concern about attestation, but they do raise one about convention: a shared late-antique literary convention, which weakens what convergence proves. The value passes every test applied to it. It repeats across the kinds of evidence tested, one of them by existence alone. The form of both nodes' literature depends on it. The Dialogues are built as eyewitness testimony, and the Conferences are built as heard conferences, and each corpus defends its authority on that ground, while imitation of a named exemplar is the stated way that formation works at both nodes. It explains why Sulpitius writes a Life and why Hilary writes a Life, why Cassian writes reported speech, and why this world's stories are almost entirely first-person-attested. The value persists across nodes, 'with Vincent transforming the value from heard to read.' In the interaction test it passes with one negative cell.
Is this one value? As far as the evidence allows, in the sense the tests measure, yes. It is also a convention shared far beyond this world: 'two unconnected Latin monastic communities in 400 could each have inherited it separately.' The link across nodes is confirmed, but it is discounted as evidence of unity. The value is supporting, not primary. It organizes the literature's form and the formation mechanism, but it works within the context that the monk-bishop and Egypt-as-measure gravities establish, since the exemplar is a monk-bishop or an Egyptian father. A convention that the world shares with its neighbours does not meet the primary bar. The record's confidence and its gravity standing agree.
It held, but it fractured at the edge through transmission. In the grace controversy it becomes a weapon. Cassian's authority is that he heard Chaeremon. Prosper attacks 'a man of priestly rank' without naming him. The eyewitness-teacher's standing survives the attack. The fracture came in transmission, since the excision of Conferences XII and XXII removed two eyewitness conferences from this world's own English text. Gennadius gives 'two divisions' against the three Dialogues in this world's text. This shows that copying split the eyewitness frame itself again.

uses.sentence: What the brethren at Tours sang, and at what hours, our own record does not dwell on; it dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap.
uses.paragraph: The limits matter as much as the claims. What the brethren at Tours sang, and at what hours, our own record does not dwell on; it dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap. Cassian wrote the received Egyptian system for the south - twelve psalms, lessons from the old books and the new, unceasing prayer as the aim they served - but what a house in Gaul did with them he never wrote, beyond saying that no one in our monasteries kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even for a year. And of the island's own day - what Lerins kept, how it kept it, an order sung - nothing at all. We carry the founder's coming across the serpents and his going off to a see, and Vincent's own rule against forgetting; we do not carry what a day on the island held.

uses.sentence: The hiddenness we valued was the monk's own cell, where a man kept himself from the world he had left.
uses.paragraph: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was - not underground, but in the courts, among bishops who had given way with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue. The violence we knew was heretics driving a bishop into exile, and later bishops handing heretics to the sword. Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt men in the Spains, where a man could be counted a heretic for the clothes he wore. But that was the sword drawn in the Church's cause by bishops, not a persecution that drove believers into hiding. What some of us did hide was different. Martin kept one thing hidden because of the times: that he had gone to the court and yielded once to a communion he abhorred, to save men from being killed. He hid that out of grief, not fear. The hiddenness we valued was the monk's own cell, where a man kept himself from the world he had left. Not catacombs. Wooden cells and caves.
uses.record_text: The monk's own dwelling, and the place where everything happens to him. There Martin prays, receives saints, and is tempted by a purple-robed devil behind a closed door. There Cassian's junior may not go out without leave, stays all day at his work, and is assailed at noon by the disease that makes him hate the cell itself.

uses.sentence: After that he was handed to a dean over ten, and taught the alphabet, as it were, in the direction of perfection.
uses.paragraph: The process among the brethren at Marseilles is Egypt's, and Cassian set it down as the fathers' own. A man came to the door. He was put off and scorned there ten days or more, of set purpose, to prove he meant it. When he was let in, he was searched for even a single hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the garments of the house. Then he was lodged a year under the guest-elder. After that he was handed to a dean over ten, and taught the alphabet, as it were, in the direction of perfection. His old clothes were not thrown away. The steward kept them in his cupboard, and if the man was seen once to cool toward the rule he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the newly received monk as Egypt receives him. uses.sentence: What we said of ourselves is that we received it from the fathers and kept it where Gaul's cold allowed.
uses.paragraph: We held what Egypt handed us and never claimed it went back unbroken to the first days. The psalms and the hours had a story. Among the fathers of Egypt only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. They argued whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupted them. One father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel. That is the rule Cassian brought to Gaul as the fathers' own, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. It is a beginning claimed in Egypt, not in Jerusalem. We never said we had it from the apostles. What we said of ourselves is that we received it from the fathers and kept it where Gaul's cold allowed. Egypt was our measure, in the south. At Tours the highest word spoken was different. Martin had the apostles' own power - over death, over demons, over emperors. That named the kind of power the saint showed, not a line of customs kept. And the test of what was legitimate ran through everything we held. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever has been handed down from antiquity is to be held fast. We did not invent a proof that our hours went back to the first believers. We said Egypt gave them to us, and that an angel gave them to Egypt. The authority was in whose they were, not in how old.
uses.record_text: What Cassian carried from Egypt and Palestine to a Gallic bishop's "new monastery." Not a written Rule of his own. Rather, "the customs of the monasteries which we have seen observed" there, "as they were there delivered to us by the Fathers." We keep them where Gaul's cold and our weak bodies allow. Where they do not, we balance them from Pontus and Mesopotamia.

use_note.means: The customs of the monasteries meant what Cassian carried from Egypt to Gaul, received from the fathers and not written as a Rule, kept as far as the cold allowed.

uses.sentence: His grace always works together with our will, going before it and following it, inspiring the first desire and crowning the last perseverance.
uses.paragraph: God as we held him is the Lord who never lets go of the tiller and whose hand is on everything. In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person - that was Vincent's word on the island, and it was not debated among us but confessed as what the Church believes. The Word of God does not change into flesh, and we do not worship a Quaternity. What we called him in our prayers was this: not only Protector and Saviour but Helper and Sponsor - Saviour, because he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. He wills all men to be saved, and to think otherwise was for us grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. He does not will only some instead of all. His grace always works together with our will, going before it and following it, inspiring the first desire and crowning the last perseverance. And at the same time the will always remains free in man, to neglect or delight in that grace, so that a monk's fasting and watching are truly his and truly required. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself; and God does not send rich crops to the idle. Both are held. How he works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. He is the God who judges now, not only at the end - a teaching one of us held, not all. And he is the one met in the beggar at the gate, wearing the half of a cloak.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. Grace "always co-operates with our will"; it goes before the will and follows it; it inspires the first desire and crowns the last perseverance. We hold it together, on purpose, with a will that stays free - in a relation "that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man."

use_note.means: Grace meant, for Cassian's Marseilles, God's help without which no effort reaches its goal, going before the will and crowning it, held on purpose with a will that stays free.

uses.sentence: Martin, alone in his cell, saw a Christ in purple and told him he would believe only in one who showed the wounds.
uses.paragraph: And one private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, saw a Christ in purple and told him he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.sentence: The condemned man was put to death.
uses.paragraph: The power claimed by bishops when they made common cause with an emperor's court, and the man we remember is the one who said it was a foul thing. Here is what our record holds. At Treves the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, and in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics by bishops in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court. The accuser there was himself a bishop. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. He held that it was punishment enough for the bishops to declare men heretics and put them out of the churches, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went, our record says, to protect even heretics themselves. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin pledged that night that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: Meanwhile, the bishops Martin would not share communion with went to the king in terror. They complained that they had been condemned in advance. It was all over for the standing of every one of them, they said, if Martin's authority now backed the stubbornness of Theognitus. He alone had so far condemned them by a sentence given in public. They said the man should never have been let inside the walls. He was now not just the heretics' defender but their champion. And nothing had really been gained by Priscillian's death if Martin was going to play the part of his avenger. At last they threw themselves down, weeping and wailing, and begged the emperor to use his power against this one man. The emperor came close to being forced to give Martin, too, the fate of heretics. Still, although he was inclined to favor the bishops too much, he knew Martin surpassed all others in faith, holiness, and excellence. So he tried another way to get the better of the holy man. First he sent for him in private and spoke to him very kindly. He assured Martin that the heretics had been condemned by regular public trials, not by the priests' persecution. He said there was no reason for Martin to think communion with Ithacius and the rest of that party was something to condemn. He added that Theognitus had caused division out of personal hatred rather than for the cause he stood for. In fact, he said, Theognitus was the only one who had so far cut himself off from communion. The rest had changed nothing. He also pointed out that a synod held a few days before had ruled that Ithacius could not be charged with any fault. When these arguments hardly moved Martin, the king grew furious and hurried out of his presence. Without delay, executioners were appointed for the people Martin had pleaded for. When Martin learned of this, he rushed to the palace, though it was already night. He promised that if these people were spared, he would take communion. He asked only that the tribunes already sent to the Spanish provinces to destroy the churches be called back. There was no delay: Maximus granted everything he asked. The next day, the ordination of Felix as bishop was being arranged. Felix was without doubt a man of great holiness, truly worthy of being made a priest in happier times. Martin took part in the communion that day. He judged it better to give way for the moment than to ignore the safety of those with a sword hanging over their heads. Even so, he would not confirm his communion by signing his name, though the bishops tried their very hardest to make him. The next day he hurried away from that place. On the way back he was filled with grief and mourning that he had been mixed up, even for an hour, in the evil communion. Not far from a village named Andethanna, remote woods stretch far and wide in deep solitude. There he sat down, while his companions went on a little way ahead of him. He sank into deep thought, by turns accusing and defending the cause of his grief and what he had done. Suddenly an angel stood beside him and said, "Martin, you are right to feel remorse, but you had no other way out of your difficulty. Renew your strength and take up your courage again. Otherwise you will put at risk not only your good name now, but your very salvation." So from then on he took great care never to be mixed up in communion with the party of Ithacius. But once he cured some of the possessed more slowly than usual, and with less of the grace he usually had. At once he confessed to us in tears that he felt his power had lessened. He said it was because of the evil of that communion. He had taken part in it for a moment out of necessity, not with his whole heart. He lived sixteen years after this. But he never again attended a synod, and he kept well away from all gatherings of bishops.

use_note.means: Gallus narrates how Martin, to stop the tribunes, took communion with the Ithacian bishops, was answered by an angel, and afterwards felt his healing power diminished.

One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.sentence: He left in grief, felt his power lessened, and never went to a synod again.
uses.paragraph: And when the sword was drawn? Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics in the Spains. He held that bishops declaring men heretics and casting them out was enough, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a Church cause was a foul and unheard-of thing. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and others would follow, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When anger failed, the emperor named executioners. Martin pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared. It was granted. He left in grief, felt his power lessened, and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: Meanwhile, the bishops Martin would not share communion with went to the king in terror. They complained that they had been condemned in advance. It was all over for the standing of every one of them, they said, if Martin's authority now backed the stubbornness of Theognitus. He alone had so far condemned them by a sentence given in public. They said the man should never have been let inside the walls. He was now not just the heretics' defender but their champion. And nothing had really been gained by Priscillian's death if Martin was going to play the part of his avenger. At last they threw themselves down, weeping and wailing, and begged the emperor to use his power against this one man. The emperor came close to being forced to give Martin, too, the fate of heretics. Still, although he was inclined to favor the bishops too much, he knew Martin surpassed all others in faith, holiness, and excellence. So he tried another way to get the better of the holy man. First he sent for him in private and spoke to him very kindly. He assured Martin that the heretics had been condemned by regular public trials, not by the priests' persecution. He said there was no reason for Martin to think communion with Ithacius and the rest of that party was something to condemn. He added that Theognitus had caused division out of personal hatred rather than for the cause he stood for. In fact, he said, Theognitus was the only one who had so far cut himself off from communion. The rest had changed nothing. He also pointed out that a synod held a few days before had ruled that Ithacius could not be charged with any fault. When these arguments hardly moved Martin, the king grew furious and hurried out of his presence. Without delay, executioners were appointed for the people Martin had pleaded for. When Martin learned of this, he rushed to the palace, though it was already night. He promised that if these people were spared, he would take communion. He asked only that the tribunes already sent to the Spanish provinces to destroy the churches be called back. There was no delay: Maximus granted everything he asked. The next day, the ordination of Felix as bishop was being arranged. Felix was without doubt a man of great holiness, truly worthy of being made a priest in happier times. Martin took part in the communion that day. He judged it better to give way for the moment than to ignore the safety of those with a sword hanging over their heads. Even so, he would not confirm his communion by signing his name, though the bishops tried their very hardest to make him. The next day he hurried away from that place. On the way back he was filled with grief and mourning that he had been mixed up, even for an hour, in the evil communion. Not far from a village named Andethanna, remote woods stretch far and wide in deep solitude. There he sat down, while his companions went on a little way ahead of him. He sank into deep thought, by turns accusing and defending the cause of his grief and what he had done. Suddenly an angel stood beside him and said, "Martin, you are right to feel remorse, but you had no other way out of your difficulty. Renew your strength and take up your courage again. Otherwise you will put at risk not only your good name now, but your very salvation." So from then on he took great care never to be mixed up in communion with the party of Ithacius. But once he cured some of the possessed more slowly than usual, and with less of the grace he usually had. At once he confessed to us in tears that he felt his power had lessened. He said it was because of the evil of that communion. He had taken part in it for a moment out of necessity, not with his whole heart. He lived sixteen years after this. But he never again attended a synod, and he kept well away from all gatherings of bishops.

uses.sentence: Discretion was the virtue that kept every other virtue from destroying itself, the royal road between excess and slackness, gained only by humility and by showing one's thoughts to the elders.
uses.paragraph: The shape of the discretion was this. Two old men who had lived apart forty years met again; one said the sun had never seen him eating, the other said nor me angry. Discretion was the virtue that kept every other virtue from destroying itself, the royal road between excess and slackness, gained only by humility and by showing one's thoughts to the elders. It judged the thought, not the man who brought it. A brother who spilled three lentils during his week as cook was suspended from prayer until he did penance, because everything in the house belonged to the Lord. That severity sat beside a patience for the thought laid bare.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, discretion is the virtue by which every other is kept from destroying itself. It is "the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator," the "eye and light of the body," the "royal road" between excess and slackness. It is gained "only ... by true humility." That means testing every thought, like a good money-changer testing coin, against the judgment of the elders.

use_note.means: Discretion meant, for Cassian, the virtue that regulates all others, the royal road between excess and slackness, gained only by humility and by showing thoughts to the elders.

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught, and Cassian set it down, that God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation.
uses.paragraph: What we held about how a man comes to faith is this: the beginning of it is not ours. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught, and Cassian set it down, that God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. The initiative, before a good will even rises, comes from God. That is not the whole of it, but it is the first thing: the drawing comes before the turning.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? uses.sentence: Twelve psalms at evening, learned by heart, and twelve at night - the number an angel fixed when the fathers of Egypt could not settle it themselves.
uses.paragraph: A mill-wheel fed and a body held still - that is the shape of a day among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set it down from Egypt. The whole was built to serve one aim: prayer that never stops, the way a blacksmith beats his anvil between strokes. Twelve psalms at evening, learned by heart, and twelve at night - the number an angel fixed when the fathers of Egypt could not settle it themselves. Between those hours, labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. The psalms at the work, too. A man rarely went out except for prayer. The work itself was held sacred: a cook who left three lentils on the floor during his week of duty was judged a pilferer of the Lord's property and suspended from prayer until he did penance, because everything in the house is consecrated to God. That whole order was Egypt's, received from the fathers, not ours. Cassian wrote it out for a bishop's new house and said plainly that no one who joined our monasteries had kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even for a year. What a house in Gaul did instead, day by day, he never wrote.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk at Tours and Marseilles, served at Marseilles by a received Egyptian system of psalms at fixed hours said to be an angel's.

The power was shown for the rustics who had not yet heard the name of Christ, and a catechumen not yet baptized saw Christ in a dream.

uses.sentence: No one in our record claims it.
uses.paragraph: Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the books, read at the hours. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.
uses.record_text: What did we have of Jesus? The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

use_note.means: The record attests that this world's books never claim a witness to the Lord and never argue the resurrection to a doubter, and it cannot supply either.
not_for: a proof of the resurrection written by this world for a doubter, which the record says is absent

uses.sentence: He does not will only some instead of all.
uses.paragraph: God as we held him is the Lord who never lets go of the tiller and whose hand is on everything. In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person - that was Vincent's word on the island, and it was not debated among us but confessed as what the Church believes. The Word of God does not change into flesh, and we do not worship a Quaternity. What we called him in our prayers was this: not only Protector and Saviour but Helper and Sponsor - Saviour, because he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. He wills all men to be saved, and to think otherwise was for us grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. He does not will only some instead of all. His grace always works together with our will, going before it and following it, inspiring the first desire and crowning the last perseverance. And at the same time the will always remains free in man, to neglect or delight in that grace, so that a monk's fasting and watching are truly his and truly required. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself; and God does not send rich crops to the idle. Both are held. How he works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. He is the God who judges now, not only at the end - a teaching one of us held, not all. And he is the one met in the beggar at the gate, wearing the half of a cloak.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

uses.sentence: What we can say is this: the monk's girdle of dead skin signified that he bore about the mortification of those members in which are contained the seeds of lust.
uses.paragraph: Here is where our record thins. Three whole texts on the sexual body and its discipline - Conferences XII and XXII, and the Institutes' sixth book - were removed by a nineteenth-century translator from the one edition this build can read. That is an edition's absence, not our own silence, and the two must not be blurred. We speak only as far as the surviving edge lets us, and no further. What we can say is this: the monk's girdle of dead skin signified that he bore about the mortification of those members in which are contained the seeds of lust. And we held the good as a meadow - the grazed part marriage, the ruined part fornication, the flowered part virginity. Marriage was the ground, and virginity the height. But for the body's own struggle, and how it was met, we cannot speak past what those removed books held. The honest limit is this: we marked the leaving of marriage, not marriage itself; and on the body's discipline our surviving record is incomplete.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, mortification is the state of being dead to the world and its desires, figured as crucifixion. "As then one who is crucified no longer has the power of moving or turning his limbs in any direction as he pleases, so we also ought to affix our wishes and desires." It is read into the monk's very clothes. The girdle of dead skin "signifies that he bears about the mortification of those members in which are contained the seeds of lust."

use_note.means: Mortification meant being already dead to the world as a crucified man cannot move his limbs, the state every practice assumes, worn in the girdle and the tunic.

uses.paragraph: So what we hold is Egypt's order, written for Gaul, and Cassian's own admission that we did not keep it. Where they do not, we balance them from Pontus and Mesopotamia.

uses.sentence: The countryside people the saint's power was shown for never speak.
uses.paragraph: Where the account of someone we failed, or turned away, or harmed would be - a novice scorned too long, a woman's word unheard, a crowd met with curses - our record is silent. The countryside people the saint's power was shown for never speak. The women of both houses left no word. The bishops who objected to Martin at the election are heard only through the man who called them ridiculous. So the honest answer is this. A failure named and answered, in the voice of the one we failed, is not in our record to give.
