uses.sentence: When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for.
uses.paragraph: Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent into the Spains, and found the bishops there in daily fellowship with the accuser, a bishop himself. He held that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing, and went to protect even heretics. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and others would follow, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin yielded once - pledged he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled - and it was granted. Afterward an angel told him his compunction was just, he felt his power lessened, and he never sat with bishops again. That unsettled us because the saint himself never called it right, and because it showed how the bishops could act when power was near.
uses.record_text: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

uses.sentence: After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new.
uses.paragraph: The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough. And it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way.
uses.record_text: What did we have of Jesus? The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

use_note.means: The record attests that this world's books never claim a witness to the Lord and never argue the resurrection to a doubter, and it cannot supply either.

uses.sentence: Thoughts will come - a man cannot keep them from rising.
uses.paragraph: Your mind is a mill turned by a stream, and the wheel cannot stop turning. That is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of it. Thoughts will come - a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. The miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into the wheel.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, thoughts are the raw material of the interior struggle. "It is impossible for the mind not to be approached by thoughts, but it is in the power of every earnest man either to admit them or to reject them." They come "from God, from the devil, and from ourselves." The mind is a mill-wheel that must grind something; the miller decides "whether he will have wheat or barley or darnel ground by it."

uses.sentence: Martin pledged that night that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled.
uses.paragraph: The power claimed by bishops when they made common cause with an emperor's court, and the man we remember is the one who said it was a foul thing. Here is what our record holds. At Treves the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, and in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics by bishops in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court. The accuser there was himself a bishop. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. He held that it was punishment enough for the bishops to declare men heretics and put them out of the churches, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went, our record says, to protect even heretics themselves. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin pledged that night that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: Meanwhile, the bishops Martin would not share communion with went to the king in terror. They complained that they had been condemned in advance. It was all over for the standing of every one of them, they said, if Martin's authority now backed the stubbornness of Theognitus. He alone had so far condemned them by a sentence given in public. They said the man should never have been let inside the walls. He was now not just the heretics' defender but their champion. And nothing had really been gained by Priscillian's death if Martin was going to play the part of his avenger. At last they threw themselves down, weeping and wailing, and begged the emperor to use his power against this one man. The emperor came close to being forced to give Martin, too, the fate of heretics. Still, although he was inclined to favor the bishops too much, he knew Martin surpassed all others in faith, holiness, and excellence. So he tried another way to get the better of the holy man. First he sent for him in private and spoke to him very kindly. He assured Martin that the heretics had been condemned by regular public trials, not by the priests' persecution. He said there was no reason for Martin to think communion with Ithacius and the rest of that party was something to condemn. He added that Theognitus had caused division out of personal hatred rather than for the cause he stood for. In fact, he said, Theognitus was the only one who had so far cut himself off from communion. The rest had changed nothing. He also pointed out that a synod held a few days before had ruled that Ithacius could not be charged with any fault. When these arguments hardly moved Martin, the king grew furious and hurried out of his presence. Without delay, executioners were appointed for the people Martin had pleaded for. When Martin learned of this, he rushed to the palace, though it was already night. He promised that if these people were spared, he would take communion. He asked only that the tribunes already sent to the Spanish provinces to destroy the churches be called back. There was no delay: Maximus granted everything he asked. The next day, the ordination of Felix as bishop was being arranged. Felix was without doubt a man of great holiness, truly worthy of being made a priest in happier times. Martin took part in the communion that day. He judged it better to give way for the moment than to ignore the safety of those with a sword hanging over their heads. Even so, he would not confirm his communion by signing his name, though the bishops tried their very hardest to make him. The next day he hurried away from that place. On the way back he was filled with grief and mourning that he had been mixed up, even for an hour, in the evil communion. Not far from a village named Andethanna, remote woods stretch far and wide in deep solitude. There he sat down, while his companions went on a little way ahead of him. He sank into deep thought, by turns accusing and defending the cause of his grief and what he had done. Suddenly an angel stood beside him and said, "Martin, you are right to feel remorse, but you had no other way out of your difficulty. Renew your strength and take up your courage again. Otherwise you will put at risk not only your good name now, but your very salvation." So from then on he took great care never to be mixed up in communion with the party of Ithacius. But once he cured some of the possessed more slowly than usual, and with less of the grace he usually had. At once he confessed to us in tears that he felt his power had lessened. He said it was because of the evil of that communion. He had taken part in it for a moment out of necessity, not with his whole heart. He lived sixteen years after this. But he never again attended a synod, and he kept well away from all gatherings of bishops.

use_note.means: Gallus narrates how Martin, to stop the tribunes, took communion with the Ithacian bishops, was answered by an angel, and afterwards felt his healing power diminished.
not_for: the angel's speech and the lessened power as established fact, when they rest on Martin's tearful report through Gallus

uses.sentence: Where the brethren stood to sing the twelve psalms that an angel fixed for the fathers, what covered them or what they stood on - that is not in our record.
uses.paragraph: I cannot say. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Where we gathered is named by place, never described as a building. At Tours, a wooden cell for the saint and caves for the brethren. The island where Honoratus went and Vincent dwelt is a harbour, a camp of God, and a place no one would live before he came - never floor, wall, or roof. Cassian wrote for a bishop founding a new monastery in a province that did not have one, and he wrote of Egypt's customs, not of Gaul's construction. Where the brethren stood to sing the twelve psalms that an angel fixed for the fathers, what covered them or what they stood on - that is not in our record. The one procession we are told of moved on the road, between Tours and the monastery, with two thousand monks and a choir of virgins following the body. If you dug, we could not tell you what you would find.
uses.record_text: The fathers of Egypt argue whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupts them. One father rises to sing, finishes the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanishes. The number is fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel.

use_note.means: Cassian relays the Egyptian fathers' tale that an angel fixed the daily psalms at twelve by singing the twelfth with Alleluia and vanishing.
not_for: Martin's angels, which sit in gallic.term.angels
Egypt's founding story presented as Gaul's own
the Divine Office as later codified

uses.sentence: The faith was what had been believed everywhere, always, by all.
uses.paragraph: What we held was received, not invented. The customs of the monasteries were the fathers' own, brought from Egypt, not ours. The faith was what had been believed everywhere, always, by all. We were keepers, not authors - disciples, not teachers - followers, not leaders. That grammar of reception runs through everything: the psalter's number came from an angel the fathers received it from, not from us; the office was not sought but seized; and at the moment a man felt his labour had accomplished something, our discipline taught him to say Not I, but the grace of God with me.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

use_note.means: The rule meant Vincent's test of the faith, what has been believed everywhere, always, by all, preferring the whole, the old and consent to the part, the new and few.
not_for: the Vincentian canon as a slogan in later polemic over which communion holds the faith
a monastic Rule, whether Cassian's customs or Benedict's
a formula consistently applied, when its use in the live grace dispute is contested in gallic.contested.who-holds-antiquity

uses.sentence: Our age had no persecutor.
uses.paragraph: If the question is whether any of our own people wrote under threat, the answer is no - not in what reaches us. Our age had no persecutor. What we feared was not the rack but the cooling, the desertion, and the noon assault on a monk alone in his cell.
uses.record_text: Hiding in the catacombs? No. Our age had no persecutor. Sulpitius says of Martin that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack; without them, he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding his blood - in hunger, in watchings, in nakedness, in fasting. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was. Did it change what we were? Martin's road began by leaving Caesar's service at a donative: I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. Before he gathered his first brethren, the violence of heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder. And at Treves, where the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place; he held it a foul and unheard-of thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church. He yielded there once, to save lives, and never sat with bishops again. What would an outsider have found strangest? We can only tell you what they laughed at. Some bystanders at a city gate laughed at a soldier walking in half a cloak. Bishops at the election said Martin's person was despicable, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting. Cassian says the Egyptians' sheepskin and little hoods would be a subject for derision in Gaul, so we did not wear them. Our own presbyter, raging in the courtyard, called the saint's visions ridiculous fancies. And what were we accused of? Sulpitius says that some of Martin's calumniators, though very few, were reported to be bishops. Others reported the brethren at Marseilles to Africa and to Rome for what they held about grace. A man of Marseilles wrote that at Carthage a monk, pale, with his hair shaved to the skin, could hardly be looked at without curses, and that servants of God from Egypt were met in the street with hissing. That was Africa, not Gaul. But it is the nearest our record comes to a crowd's own voice.

use_note.means: This witness says the Gallic monks met no persecution but faced derision at dress, hair and visions, and accusation by bishops and reporters to Africa.
not_for: the Carthage crowd's derision as a Gallic town's reaction, when it is Salvian's report of Africa
the objecting bishops as fairly heard, when only Sulpitius speaks for them
persecution or hiding in their own time, which the witness denies

uses.sentence: At the funeral there were two thousand monks, old men and young soldiers of Christ, and a choir of virgins — sung psalms, hymns beginning then to be written — but where they stood to sing it, the book does not say.
uses.paragraph: At Tours, wooden cells and caves. The saint's own cell was wood, and the brethren dwelt in caves hollowed from the rock around it. A rude little stool, such as those in use by the lowest of servants. No church is described there in our record. At the funeral there were two thousand monks, old men and young soldiers of Christ, and a choir of virgins — sung psalms, hymns beginning then to be written — but where they stood to sing it, the book does not say.
uses.record_text: Foreknowing his death, Martin goes to make peace among quarrelling clerics. He sickens, and refuses straw for his bed of sackcloth and ashes rather than set his disciples a softer example. He is carried to burial by two thousand monks, old men and young soldiers of Christ, and a choir of virgins.

use_note.means: Sulpitius tells Bassula that Martin, foreknowing his death, went to make peace at Condate, died refusing straw, and was buried by two thousand monks and a choir of virgins.

uses.sentence: Our own teacher Chaeremon had answered on both sides with Scripture's own cases and said that how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, men held that grace and effort work together. The will stays free; grace goes before it, works with it, and crowns it; and still God asks real labour of us. Others reported that teaching to Africa and to Rome. Vincent read the Apostolic See's own letter as written for his own side, for antiquity. But he never said the question was closed. Our own teacher Chaeremon had answered on both sides with Scripture's own cases and said that how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.record_text:
Human effort and free choice are real, and they matter. This world argues that point under pressure from Augustine's own later teaching on grace.
Cassian's own text states the position directly. He gives it through the teaching he attributes to Abbot Chaeremon. God's grace always works together with a person's own will, for that will's own good. But it sometimes waits on some real effort from the person before it is given (Conf. XIII.13). To deny that God wants everyone saved, and not just some, Chaeremon says, would be a grave blasphemy (Conf. XIII.7). Neither side of the argument should be pushed too far, Chaeremon warns. Exactly how grace and free will fit together, in the end, is a question human reason cannot fully answer (Conf. XIII.11, XIII.18). Elsewhere, Cassian's own manual for monks, in its climactic book, gives plain advice. A monk who feels he is making progress should credit it all to God's grace, and not to himself (Inst. XII.9).
What the wider Church heard about this teaching came mostly at second hand. Augustine himself reports that the Gallic monks he is answering already grant one point: that God's grace goes ahead of the human will. But they remain unsettled on the question of predestination. That is a report from the other side, not this world's own voice. What is known of Rome's own reply survives only at a distance - Prosper's appeal to the Pope, Celestine's letter to the Gallic bishops, a Roman critique of Cassian's own thirteenth Conference. None of it comes from a text this world wrote itself; it comes through a modern editor's own account of that history. Gennadius, writing on his own, confirms only that a dispute between Cassian and Prosper existed at all. At Tours, there is simply nothing on this question. The corpus there closed before it was ever raised.
At Lérins, the current runs the other way, though how far Vincent himself took part is genuinely disputed. He quotes Pope Celestine's own words, that novelty must give way to old and settled teaching. He reads those words as backing his own side. But nothing in his surviving text names Augustine, or the fight itself, outright.
This argument is Cassian's own, within this world's own voices. No other Native voice in this world independently holds it. Yet it matters enormously wherever it appears. Several other parts of this world's own literature depend on it. It turned one whole Conference, out of twenty-four, into a direct answer to a crisis in formation. And it explains a great deal of what survives about Prosper, Celestine, and a Roman critique of Cassian himself. But it does not appear evenly across this world's whole span. Tours has nothing to say about it, for reasons of plain timing, not disagreement. For that reason, this record calls it a supporting idea at the level of the whole world. Within the southern house alone, though, it is treated as the leading concern. The evidence for the position is strong. Yet its reach across the whole world stays narrow. That gap is itself a real and disclosed tension in how this record is classified. A reader should not mistake the modest classification for any doubt about what Cassian and Chaeremon actually taught.
Under pressure from Rome, the argument grew stronger, and who carried it changed too. It began as monks writing for other monks. It ended, a generation later, with a bishop, trained at Lérins, writing at the order of a church council. Inside this world's own literature, though, it began as something much simpler. It was a remedy for the pride of a monk who feels, at last, that he is making progress - offered long before anyone outside gave it any name at all.

use_note.means: Human effort and free choice are held real and to matter while grace goes before and crowns them, argued under Augustine's pressure in a relation Cassian says reason cannot grasp.

uses.sentence: He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the garments of the house.
uses.paragraph: The process among the brethren at Marseilles is Egypt's, and Cassian set it down as the fathers' own. A man came to the door. He was put off and scorned there ten days or more, of set purpose, to prove he meant it. When he was let in, he was searched for even a single hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the garments of the house. Then he was lodged a year under the guest-elder. After that he was handed to a dean over ten, and taught the alphabet, as it were, in the direction of perfection. His old clothes were not thrown away. The steward kept them in his cupboard, and if the man was seen once to cool toward the rule he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the newly received monk as Egypt receives him. Ten days or more at the door "of set purpose repelled and scorned," searched for a hidden coin, stripped and reclothed "by the Abbot's hands," lodged a year under the guest-Elder, then handed to a dean over ten and taught "the alphabet ... in the direction of perfection." And Cassian's own admission: no one in our monasteries has kept it up "unbroken even for a year."

use_note.means: The junior meant the monk newly received as Egypt receives him, scorned at the door and taught to conquer his wishes, a standard Cassian says Gallic houses did not keep.
not_for: a Benedictine novitiate with a defined year and vows
novice as simply any beginner

uses.sentence: One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity.
uses.paragraph: In substance and person we confessed what the island taught: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. That was not a thing we debated; it was what we already believed, what the bishops at Ephesus had guarded by refusing novelty.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? uses.sentence: A thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to tell it, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered.
uses.paragraph: There was a place inside the fence for someone who had not yet believed, and a patience kept for the one who lost heart. At Tours a boy named Martin went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. The catechumen who belonged to the Church but had not yet been baptized was not outside; he was still learning. And among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, knew the monk's own trouble. A man's bright early days cool. He comes to hate his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a pious reason to leave. That cooling was the professed man's own fear, not a beginner's stumble - a disease of temperature that damns. The remedy was not argument but staying. The senior held him in his cell as in a secure harbour, and taught him to lay bare every thought. A thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to tell it, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. What was shown was not belief as an achieved state but labour and patience. Two old men met after forty years apart; the abbot of many said the sun had never seen him eating, and the hermit answered, "nor me angry". They proved perseverance, not perfection. uses.paragraph: Everything, we said - and proved the claim by the life the brethren kept. Among the brethren at Marseilles a man was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the clothing of the house. That is the sign, not the whole list. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, named three renunciations, and giving up one's goods was only the first. Leaving behind bodily wealth and riches - possessions, kin, the life one had in the world - is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the man who has renounced. The second renunciation is of habits, vices, and the mind's former affections - the whole interior road of the faults. The third is drawing the mind away from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come. So the claim was this: marriage, property, honours, secular business, kin. Martin was a soldier in Caesar's service who left it at a donative, saying he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight. The fathers remembered a man who fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that compelled turning into a willing one. And Salvian, who wrote from one of the houses at Marseilles, named those who had taken our way of life as the ones who chose to be lowly, poor, and unesteemed.

uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

Yet bishops were the ones who ordained, judged doctrine, and held councils - and Martin would not sit with them after Trier.
uses.record_text:
Bishops and synods guard the truth, yet the saint keeps fleeing them. The state, in this world's own view, has no right to judge the Church's own causes.
At Tours, the office is the thing fled. Bishops resist Martin's election (Vita IX). Some of Martin's slanderers, Sulpitius says, turned out to be bishops themselves, though very few (Vita XXVII). Before Maximus, Sulpitius writes, apostolic authority held its ground in Martin alone, while the priestly dignity around him bowed to the emperor's court (Vita XX). After the forced communion at Trier, Martin never again attended a synod, and stayed carefully away from every assembly of bishops for the rest of his life (Dial. III.13). Sulpitius calls it a foul, unheard-of wrong for a secular ruler to sit in judgment on a matter belonging to the Church (Sacred History II.50).
At Marseilles, the office is both temptation and a defiance of the Pope. Cassian's Abbot Moses teaches that the devil can push a man to want holy orders under the pretext of doing good for many people (Conf. I.20). Vainglory brings a 'desire for the priesthood or diaconate' (Inst. XI.14). Archebius was 'expelled.' And, as the editor tells it, the Massilians held to their own views even against the authority of the Pope brought to bear on them.
At Lérins, the counter-current runs the other way. Vincent rules that an ancient General Council's decrees should be preferred over the rashness and ignorance of a few (Comm. ch. 3), and names 'the twofold authority of the Apostolic See' (ch. 32). Yet in the same voice, he holds that no rank exempts a lone dissenter: whether a teacher is holy and learned, a bishop, a Confessor, or a martyr, a view held against the consent of all is only his own private fancy (ch. 28).
This tension never resolves evenly. Guarding antiquity by councils while fleeing synods, and producing bishops while distrusting the office, keeps this world from being reducible to a seminary that looked like a monastery. Over time it tips one way: the Lérins network becomes the very episcopate it once fled, and the argument over grace comes to be carried forward by a synodal commission - a shift that marks this world's own ending.

use_note.means: Bishops, synods and emperors are held to guard the truth yet the saint keeps fleeing them, so authority is honoured and refused within the same stories.

uses.sentence: The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself; and God does not send rich crops to the idle.
uses.paragraph: God as we held him is the Lord who never lets go of the tiller and whose hand is on everything. In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person - that was Vincent's word on the island, and it was not debated among us but confessed as what the Church believes. The Word of God does not change into flesh, and we do not worship a Quaternity. What we called him in our prayers was this: not only Protector and Saviour but Helper and Sponsor - Saviour, because he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. He wills all men to be saved, and to think otherwise was for us grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. He does not will only some instead of all. His grace always works together with our will, going before it and following it, inspiring the first desire and crowning the last perseverance. And at the same time the will always remains free in man, to neglect or delight in that grace, so that a monk's fasting and watching are truly his and truly required. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself; and God does not send rich crops to the idle. Both are held. How he works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. He is the God who judges now, not only at the end - a teaching one of us held, not all. And he is the one met in the beggar at the gate, wearing the half of a cloak.
uses.record_text:
Then Germanus said: "The reward of our efforts is perfect chastity. It is gained by the earnestness of one's own toil. It seems absurd to us not to credit it mainly to the labor of the man who makes the effort. For suppose, for example, that we see a farmer taking the greatest pains to work the ground. It is foolish not to credit the fruits to his labor."
Chaeremon said: "The farmer may take the greatest pains to work the ground. Even so, he cannot at once credit his crops and their rich fruits to his own labor. He finds that his efforts often come to nothing unless timely rains and a quiet, calm winter help them. God's goodness, then, does not grant these rich crops to lazy farmers who do not work their fields by ploughing them often. For a man should think this over and weigh it with the greatest care. By his own strength he could not have made the very efforts he put in so earnestly out of his desire for wealth. He could have made them only if the Lord's protection and mercy had given him strength for all the work of farming. From this we clearly conclude that the first step comes from God. This is true not only of our actions but also of good thoughts. God puts a good will in us to begin with. He gives us the chance to carry out what we rightly desire. But our part is to follow humbly, day by day, the grace of God that is drawing us."

use_note.means: Cassian records Germanus arguing that effort earns its fruit and Chaeremon answering that a husbandman's labour still needs rain and calm weather from God.

uses.sentence: And the mark it all serves: purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity.
uses.paragraph: And the mark it all serves: purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, and the archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the immediate goal of the whole monastic life, as distinct from its end, the kingdom of heaven. It is the "definite mark" at which every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation is aimed, "which is charity." By it all of these are ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself.

uses.sentence: How God works all things in us and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man.
uses.paragraph: His grace goes before our will, helps it, and crowns it. The beginning even of our good thoughts comes from God, who inspires a good will to begin with. We call him not only Saviour but Helper - Saviour because he calls us when we are still unwilling, Helper because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Grace kindles the desire, enables the virtue, and preserves it to the end. A husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; the crop cannot be ascribed to the man's labour alone, and God does not send rich crops to the idle. How God works all things in us and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.record_text: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.

use_note.means: Cassian reports Chaeremon teaching that grace kindles desire, enables virtue and preserves it without destroying free will, and that their union exceeds human reason.
not_for: a settled verdict that the teaching is semi-Pelagian, when that label is contested

uses.sentence: The Lord we knew was the crucified one.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the books served the hours of prayer. What we keep of Martin's own reading is one story: the devil came to his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time, then said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. Beside the cloak story Sulpitius set the sentence: what is done to the least of these is done to him.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

uses.sentence: When anger failed, the emperor named executioners.
uses.paragraph: And when the sword was drawn? Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics in the Spains. He held that bishops declaring men heretics and casting them out was enough, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a Church cause was a foul and unheard-of thing. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and others would follow, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When anger failed, the emperor named executioners. Martin pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared. It was granted. He left in grief, felt his power lessened, and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: Meanwhile, the bishops Martin would not share communion with went to the king in terror. They complained that they had been condemned in advance. It was all over for the standing of every one of them, they said, if Martin's authority now backed the stubbornness of Theognitus. He alone had so far condemned them by a sentence given in public. They said the man should never have been let inside the walls. He was now not just the heretics' defender but their champion. And nothing had really been gained by Priscillian's death if Martin was going to play the part of his avenger. At last they threw themselves down, weeping and wailing, and begged the emperor to use his power against this one man. The emperor came close to being forced to give Martin, too, the fate of heretics. Still, although he was inclined to favor the bishops too much, he knew Martin surpassed all others in faith, holiness, and excellence. So he tried another way to get the better of the holy man. First he sent for him in private and spoke to him very kindly. He assured Martin that the heretics had been condemned by regular public trials, not by the priests' persecution. He said there was no reason for Martin to think communion with Ithacius and the rest of that party was something to condemn. He added that Theognitus had caused division out of personal hatred rather than for the cause he stood for. In fact, he said, Theognitus was the only one who had so far cut himself off from communion. The rest had changed nothing. He also pointed out that a synod held a few days before had ruled that Ithacius could not be charged with any fault. When these arguments hardly moved Martin, the king grew furious and hurried out of his presence. Without delay, executioners were appointed for the people Martin had pleaded for. When Martin learned of this, he rushed to the palace, though it was already night. He promised that if these people were spared, he would take communion. He asked only that the tribunes already sent to the Spanish provinces to destroy the churches be called back. There was no delay: Maximus granted everything he asked. The next day, the ordination of Felix as bishop was being arranged. Felix was without doubt a man of great holiness, truly worthy of being made a priest in happier times. Martin took part in the communion that day. He judged it better to give way for the moment than to ignore the safety of those with a sword hanging over their heads. Even so, he would not confirm his communion by signing his name, though the bishops tried their very hardest to make him. The next day he hurried away from that place. On the way back he was filled with grief and mourning that he had been mixed up, even for an hour, in the evil communion. Not far from a village named Andethanna, remote woods stretch far and wide in deep solitude. There he sat down, while his companions went on a little way ahead of him. He sank into deep thought, by turns accusing and defending the cause of his grief and what he had done. Suddenly an angel stood beside him and said, "Martin, you are right to feel remorse, but you had no other way out of your difficulty. Renew your strength and take up your courage again. Otherwise you will put at risk not only your good name now, but your very salvation." So from then on he took great care never to be mixed up in communion with the party of Ithacius. But once he cured some of the possessed more slowly than usual, and with less of the grace he usually had. At once he confessed to us in tears that he felt his power had lessened. He said it was because of the evil of that communion. He had taken part in it for a moment out of necessity, not with his whole heart. He lived sixteen years after this. But he never again attended a synod, and he kept well away from all gatherings of bishops.

use_note.means: Gallus narrates how Martin, to stop the tribunes, took communion with the Ithacian bishops, was answered by an angel, and afterwards felt his healing power diminished.

uses.sentence: The mind is a wheel turned by a stream, and the miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it.
uses.paragraph: Yes. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of the mind as a mill that cannot stop turning. Thoughts will come - from God, from the devil, from ourselves - and a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. The mind is a wheel turned by a stream, and the miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, thoughts are the raw material of the interior struggle. "It is impossible for the mind not to be approached by thoughts, but it is in the power of every earnest man either to admit them or to reject them." They come "from God, from the devil, and from ourselves." The mind is a mill-wheel that must grind something; the miller decides "whether he will have wheat or barley or darnel ground by it."

uses.sentence: Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen; he stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized.
uses.paragraph: We kept one story of how it began, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen; he stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. At a donative before battle he told Caesar he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight, offered to stand unarmed before the enemy line, and the enemy surrendered before morning. That was his road. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness says Jesus sought the unpitied, citing Martin's cloak, the guest received as Christ and grace calling the unwilling, while naming its thin personal testimony.

uses.sentence: Every claim of ours that names its record and stays inside it - the cloak, the forced communion, the husbandman, the twelve psalms as Egypt's founding tale, the angel who answered Paphnutius - would stand as what that text says, not as what happened.
uses.paragraph: What would survive is this. We had two nodes that never wrote of each other. At Tours, one man told one saint's story, and said himself he was not present. In the south, Cassian set down Egypt's order for a new house and admitted no one in Gaul kept it a year. Vincent wrote a rule for the faith and never told the island's day. A presbyter saw a ruined city's notables ask for games. Every claim of ours that names its record and stays inside it - the cloak, the forced communion, the husbandman, the twelve psalms as Egypt's founding tale, the angel who answered Paphnutius - would stand as what that text says, not as what happened.
uses.record_text: A jealous brother hides his own book in young Paphnutius's cell and accuses him of theft before the whole desert; Paphnutius says nothing, does penance for a crime he did not commit, and is vindicated only when the accuser, possessed, confesses - and can be healed by no one but the man he wronged.

He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.sentence: The fathers of Egypt argued whether it should be fifty or sixty, and the Vesper hour interrupted them; one father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished, and the number was fixed forever by an angel, not by any monk.
uses.paragraph: And the last thing is Egypt. The customs, the twelve psalms, the teaching on purity of heart - all of it came to us from the fathers, not from us. Even the number of psalms was not ours to choose. The fathers of Egypt argued whether it should be fifty or sixty, and the Vesper hour interrupted them; one father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished, and the number was fixed forever by an angel, not by any monk. That is the grammar we stood in. Scripture was not a problem we solved; it was the word we received, read at the hours, learned by heart, and heard through the fathers who had received it before us.

uses.sentence: Martin was lured out of his monastery by a man pretending his wife was ill, escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and taken into an office he had not sought.
uses.paragraph: What belongs with that is the shape of what happened next. The churches came for the men who had left them. A bishop's see was capture, not achievement. Martin was lured out of his monastery by a man pretending his wife was ill, escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and taken into an office he had not sought. The Egyptian bishop Archebius told two Gallic travellers that he had been carried off to a town after thirty-seven years among the anchorites, and that he counted it as being expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it. On the island the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive and took him off to a see. So what a man gave up to join us did not mean he was done with the world's claims on him.

uses.sentence: Martin went to the court to stop it.
uses.paragraph: The power claimed by bishops when they made common cause with an emperor's court, and the man we remember is the one who said it was a foul thing. Here is what our record holds. At Treves the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, and in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics by bishops in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court. The accuser there was himself a bishop. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. He held that it was punishment enough for the bishops to declare men heretics and put them out of the churches, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went, our record says, to protect even heretics themselves. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin pledged that night that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

uses.sentence: The end of our life was the kingdom; the nearer goal was purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity.
uses.paragraph: The third is the shape of what we looked for. The end of our life was the kingdom; the nearer goal was purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. Every fast and vigil was ranked by whether it cleared the heart - an aid, never the point. When Scripture was read, it was read for that mark. At Tours the reader for the day was blocked by the crowd at the election, so a bystander seized the psalter and opened it where it fell - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict. We do not tell you that was right. We tell you it is how Scripture was heard: as a voice speaking now, to this hour, for this need.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the immediate goal of the whole monastic life, as distinct from its end, the kingdom of heaven. uses.paragraph: So our record does not argue belief into anyone. It says the Lord sought the unpitied, that he draws the unwilling, and that a man came to faith by seeing Christ in the half of a soldier's cloak. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. uses.sentence: The will stays free; grace goes before it, works with it, and crowns it; and still God asks real labour of us.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, men held that grace and effort work together. The will stays free; grace goes before it, works with it, and crowns it; and still God asks real labour of us. Others reported that teaching to Africa and to Rome. Vincent read the Apostolic See's own letter as written for his own side, for antiquity. But he never said the question was closed. Our own teacher Chaeremon had answered on both sides with Scripture's own cases and said that how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.record_text:
Human effort and free choice are real, and they matter. This world argues that point under pressure from Augustine's own later teaching on grace.
Cassian's own text states the position directly. He gives it through the teaching he attributes to Abbot Chaeremon. God's grace always works together with a person's own will, for that will's own good. But it sometimes waits on some real effort from the person before it is given (Conf. XIII.13). To deny that God wants everyone saved, and not just some, Chaeremon says, would be a grave blasphemy (Conf. XIII.7). Neither side of the argument should be pushed too far, Chaeremon warns. Exactly how grace and free will fit together, in the end, is a question human reason cannot fully answer (Conf. XIII.11, XIII.18). Elsewhere, Cassian's own manual for monks, in its climactic book, gives plain advice. A monk who feels he is making progress should credit it all to God's grace, and not to himself (Inst. XII.9).
What the wider Church heard about this teaching came mostly at second hand. Augustine himself reports that the Gallic monks he is answering already grant one point: that God's grace goes ahead of the human will. But they remain unsettled on the question of predestination. That is a report from the other side, not this world's own voice. What is known of Rome's own reply survives only at a distance - Prosper's appeal to the Pope, Celestine's letter to the Gallic bishops, a Roman critique of Cassian's own thirteenth Conference. None of it comes from a text this world wrote itself; it comes through a modern editor's own account of that history. Gennadius, writing on his own, confirms only that a dispute between Cassian and Prosper existed at all. At Tours, there is simply nothing on this question. The corpus there closed before it was ever raised.
At Lérins, the current runs the other way, though how far Vincent himself took part is genuinely disputed. He quotes Pope Celestine's own words, that novelty must give way to old and settled teaching. He reads those words as backing his own side. But nothing in his surviving text names Augustine, or the fight itself, outright.
This argument is Cassian's own, within this world's own voices. No other Native voice in this world independently holds it. Yet it matters enormously wherever it appears. Several other parts of this world's own literature depend on it. It turned one whole Conference, out of twenty-four, into a direct answer to a crisis in formation. And it explains a great deal of what survives about Prosper, Celestine, and a Roman critique of Cassian himself. But it does not appear evenly across this world's whole span. Tours has nothing to say about it, for reasons of plain timing, not disagreement. For that reason, this record calls it a supporting idea at the level of the whole world. Within the southern house alone, though, it is treated as the leading concern. The evidence for the position is strong. Yet its reach across the whole world stays narrow. That gap is itself a real and disclosed tension in how this record is classified. A reader should not mistake the modest classification for any doubt about what Cassian and Chaeremon actually taught.
Under pressure from Rome, the argument grew stronger, and who carried it changed too. It began as monks writing for other monks. It ended, a generation later, with a bishop, trained at Lérins, writing at the order of a church council. Inside this world's own literature, though, it began as something much simpler. It was a remedy for the pride of a monk who feels, at last, that he is making progress - offered long before anyone outside gave it any name at all.

use_note.means: Human effort and free choice are held real and to matter while grace goes before and crowns them, argued under Augustine's pressure in a relation Cassian says reason cannot grasp.

uses.sentence: At Tours the answer is a story.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. That is one man's own confession, made alone.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

uses.sentence: The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, named three renunciations, and giving up one's goods was only the first.
uses.paragraph: Everything, we said - and proved the claim by the life the brethren kept. Among the brethren at Marseilles a man was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the clothing of the house. That is the sign, not the whole list. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, named three renunciations, and giving up one's goods was only the first. Leaving behind bodily wealth and riches - possessions, kin, the life one had in the world - is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the man who has renounced. The second renunciation is of habits, vices, and the mind's former affections - the whole interior road of the faults. The third is drawing the mind away from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come. So the claim was this: marriage, property, honours, secular business, kin. Martin was a soldier in Caesar's service who left it at a donative, saying he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight. The fathers remembered a man who fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that compelled turning into a willing one. And Salvian, who wrote from one of the houses at Marseilles, named those who had taken our way of life as the ones who chose to be lowly, poor, and unesteemed.
uses.record_text: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."

use_note.means: Renunciation meant the act that makes a monk, a death to the world of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest of three stages.
not_for: giving things up as the whole monastic act

uses.sentence: On the island Vincent wrote what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person.
uses.paragraph: On the island Vincent wrote what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.
not_for: a penal substitution doctrine, when the sixth-hour sentence is near it but not the same

uses.sentence: Renunciation has three stages.
uses.paragraph: Here is what the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, said about it. Renunciation has three stages. The first is giving up one's goods - "of what is not our own," they said, because all things are God's. But that stage alone is not enough to make a man perfect. The second is giving up one's former way of life, its vices and passions of soul and flesh. The third is withdrawing the mind from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come. A professed man had cut himself off from marriage, kin, property, and the life of the world for a stricter life in Christ's service. That cut showed in his body and his dwelling.
