uses.sentence: At Tours the record is one named man - Martin, master and bishop both, who kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the record is one named man - Martin, master and bishop both, who kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office. Authority rested where the power was felt. He needed no title. Sulpitius calls him "our master" and says it was unlawful to do anything but acquiesce to him. His disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Yet Martin himself, on a question touching whether a tradition had come down from antiquity, consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics, and would not honour a tomb where no steady tradition supported it. One of those presbyters was Brictio, whom Martin had raised from boyhood and who stormed into the courtyard in a fury. The man had sat down on his wooden seat one day, and Brictio came raging that he was holier than the master who brought him up, calling his visions ridiculous fancies and dreaming that he himself deserved the episcopate. Martin held that demons were driving him, but said he would bear with Brictio the way Christ bore with Judas. He would not remove him. That presbyter's rank came from somewhere, not from Martin alone, but where and how the record does not say.
uses.record_text:
Renunciation kept producing bishops. Men renounced the world to become monks, and then the office of bishop overtook them.

Martin shows the pattern. He kept up the position of a bishop properly, yet he did not lay aside the aims and virtues of a monk.

Of the eighty disciples at Marmoutier, numbers were afterwards made bishops (Vita, ch. X). The disciples were trained after their master's example.

Everything Cassian wrote was addressed to bishops, or to men who became bishops. His formation writing was for a bishop's new monastery. Honoratus moves from monk to bishop between two of his dedications (Conferences, prefaces II and III).

Archebius is the Egyptian counter-case. He counted his appointment as expulsion from the monastic system, as unworthy of it. Cassian carried his story west (Conferences XI.2).

Hilary of Arles preached on Honoratus in the south's own Latin. He tells how the priest's headband fastened on a man who fled from it, and how the honor came to him. The Latin is there in the source, but this English wording of it is rated Inferential/Thin.

What sets this world apart is a seminary that looked like a monastery. Every primary voice attests this pattern, and Gennadius confirms it independently. It holds in both north and south, more strongly than any other pattern in this world. It is the only one that a Latin insider in the south, Hilary, attests apart from Cassian.

It explains three things. The withdrawal stayed close to the city. The grace argument reached Rome. The ending was a change in how the institution spoke, not a collapse.

The controversy over grace did not break the pattern. It strengthened it into the Lérins network of bishops. Celestine's letter named Venerius, Cassian's own bishop, first (Gibson's editorial introduction). It warned that priests ought not to teach so as to invade the bishops' rights.

By the 470s a bishop formed at Lérins, Faustus, carried the argument at the commission of synods. Under barbarian pressure this was the institution left standing. Gennadius, writing from the same city about 495, reports two monasteries still standing.

These pressures did not change the pattern. They made it the way the world ended.

use_note.means: Renunciation kept producing bishops, so this world's monks were repeatedly seized into the office they were taught to flee and kept a monk's virtues inside the see.

uses.sentence: And he taught plainly that a newborn has no merits before him - he spoke of "the case even of infants, who have as yet done nothing either good or bad".
uses.paragraph: We never argued it as a formula, and where Cassian touched it he touched it as Egypt's fathers touched it - as a thing held, not debated. Here is what our record keeps. Among the brethren at Marseilles, Abbot Chaeremon named three stages of the grace by which we are saved: the first kindles our desire toward salvation, the second enables us in the good we wish for, the third preserves us to the end in the virtues. All three are God's gift. And he taught plainly that a newborn has no merits before him - he spoke of "the case even of infants, who have as yet done nothing either good or bad". That is the nearest our record comes to your question's shape: infants with no works of their own, and grace going before every stage. But whether they bear guilt from birth, by what they are rather than what they have done, Cassian does not say. What he does say is this: the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; he does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and it is grievous blasphemy to think otherwise. Free will always remains in a man, and it is weak, and the help of God is necessary to it every day and hour. How both are true - how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. The inherited guilt as a thing confessed apart from the grace that answers it is not in our record to give you.
uses.record_text: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.

use_note.means: Cassian reports Chaeremon teaching that grace kindles desire, enables virtue and preserves it without destroying free will, and that their union exceeds human reason.
not_for: a settled verdict that the teaching is semi-Pelagian, when that label is contested
the claim that grace looks for human effort, which sits in gallic.quote.chaeremon-grace-requires-our-effort

uses.sentence: A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics by bishops in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court.
uses.paragraph: The power claimed by bishops when they made common cause with an emperor's court, and the man we remember is the one who said it was a foul thing. Here is what our record holds. At Treves the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, and in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics by bishops in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court. The accuser there was himself a bishop. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. He held that it was punishment enough for the bishops to declare men heretics and put them out of the churches, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went, our record says, to protect even heretics themselves. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin pledged that night that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: Meanwhile, the bishops Martin would not share communion with went to the king in terror. They complained that they had been condemned in advance. It was all over for the standing of every one of them, they said, if Martin's authority now backed the stubbornness of Theognitus. He alone had so far condemned them by a sentence given in public. They said the man should never have been let inside the walls. He was now not just the heretics' defender but their champion. And nothing had really been gained by Priscillian's death if Martin was going to play the part of his avenger. At last they threw themselves down, weeping and wailing, and begged the emperor to use his power against this one man. The emperor came close to being forced to give Martin, too, the fate of heretics. Still, although he was inclined to favor the bishops too much, he knew Martin surpassed all others in faith, holiness, and excellence. So he tried another way to get the better of the holy man. First he sent for him in private and spoke to him very kindly. He assured Martin that the heretics had been condemned by regular public trials, not by the priests' persecution. He said there was no reason for Martin to think communion with Ithacius and the rest of that party was something to condemn. He added that Theognitus had caused division out of personal hatred rather than for the cause he stood for. In fact, he said, Theognitus was the only one who had so far cut himself off from communion. The rest had changed nothing. He also pointed out that a synod held a few days before had ruled that Ithacius could not be charged with any fault. When these arguments hardly moved Martin, the king grew furious and hurried out of his presence. Without delay, executioners were appointed for the people Martin had pleaded for. When Martin learned of this, he rushed to the palace, though it was already night. He promised that if these people were spared, he would take communion. He asked only that the tribunes already sent to the Spanish provinces to destroy the churches be called back. There was no delay: Maximus granted everything he asked. The next day, the ordination of Felix as bishop was being arranged. Felix was without doubt a man of great holiness, truly worthy of being made a priest in happier times. Martin took part in the communion that day. He judged it better to give way for the moment than to ignore the safety of those with a sword hanging over their heads. Even so, he would not confirm his communion by signing his name, though the bishops tried their very hardest to make him. The next day he hurried away from that place. On the way back he was filled with grief and mourning that he had been mixed up, even for an hour, in the evil communion. Not far from a village named Andethanna, remote woods stretch far and wide in deep solitude. There he sat down, while his companions went on a little way ahead of him. He sank into deep thought, by turns accusing and defending the cause of his grief and what he had done. Suddenly an angel stood beside him and said, "Martin, you are right to feel remorse, but you had no other way out of your difficulty. Renew your strength and take up your courage again. Otherwise you will put at risk not only your good name now, but your very salvation." So from then on he took great care never to be mixed up in communion with the party of Ithacius. But once he cured some of the possessed more slowly than usual, and with less of the grace he usually had. At once he confessed to us in tears that he felt his power had lessened. He said it was because of the evil of that communion. He had taken part in it for a moment out of necessity, not with his whole heart. He lived sixteen years after this. But he never again attended a synod, and he kept well away from all gatherings of bishops.

use_note.means: Gallus narrates how Martin, to stop the tribunes, took communion with the Ithacian bishops, was answered by an angel, and afterwards felt his healing power diminished.
not_for: the angel's speech and the lessened power as established fact, when they rest on Martin's tearful report through Gallus

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles the reading was built into the day.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles the reading was built into the day. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. And beside every virtue a monk felt he had gained, Cassian set the Apostle's sentence: not I, but the grace of God with me.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk at Tours and Marseilles, served at Marseilles by a received Egyptian system of psalms at fixed hours said to be an angel's.

uses.paragraph: Marriage was a thing left behind, and its leaving was the renunciation. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that the first stage of a monk's turning was giving up goods, family, and the world's honours - and that this, though it is called leaving all things, was only the first and easiest stage. The act that made a monk was figured as death, and the monk was dead to the world and its deeds and desires. At Tours Martin left Caesar's service at a donative and never married; he gathered brethren, and the bishops who objected to his election said his clothes were mean and his hair disgusting, not that he had taken a wife. The whole of what we marked was the cut, not the bond. For a woman the cut had its own form. A girl was devoted by her father to perpetual virginity, and the bishop placed on her the dress characteristic of that state. At Martin's funeral the consecrated virgins walked as a choir. Cassian taught that marriage may be excused; virginity points to glory. The completed victory is not to be seen.

uses.sentence: It was bishops bowing to the royal court, and a secular ruler made judge in a cause of the Church.
uses.paragraph: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. Martin's road began by leaving Caesar's service at a donative: I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. Before he gathered his first brethren, the violence of heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder. The trouble was not soldiers hunting believers. It was bishops bowing to the royal court, and a secular ruler made judge in a cause of the Church.
uses.record_text: The bishops had given way weakly. They let the royal court outrank the priesthood's own dignity. But Martin alone still held the authority handed down from the apostles.

uses.sentence: No, never that phrase.
uses.paragraph: No, never that phrase. What we kept for conversion is one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.paragraph: So leadership among us was not established. It was capture, and then it was patience. A presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood stormed into the courtyard, called the master's visions ridiculous fancies, and Martin bore with him afterward the way Christ bore with Judas. That is the shape of authority in our record: fled, overtaken, and keeping a monk's humility inside the office it could not refuse.
uses.record_text: Then the holy man explained, both to him and to all of us, how he had seen demons driving him on. He declared that the insults heaped on him did not move him. In fact, they had hurt the man who spoke them instead. Later, this same Brictio was often accused before Martin of many serious crimes. Yet Martin could not be persuaded to remove him from the priesthood. He did not want to be suspected of taking revenge for the wrong done to himself. And he often repeated this saying: ‘If Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio?’

use_note.means: Gallus, in Sulpitius's Dialogues, reports that Martin refused to remove the accused presbyter Brictio, often saying that if Christ bore with Judas he should bear with Brictio.

uses.sentence: At Tours a boy named Martin went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen.
uses.paragraph: There was a place inside the fence for someone who had not yet believed, and a patience kept for the one who lost heart. At Tours a boy named Martin went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. The catechumen who belonged to the Church but had not yet been baptized was not outside; he was still learning. And among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, knew the monk's own trouble. A man's bright early days cool. He comes to hate his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a pious reason to leave. That cooling was the professed man's own fear, not a beginner's stumble - a disease of temperature that damns. The remedy was not argument but staying. The senior held him in his cell as in a secure harbour, and taught him to lay bare every thought. A thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to tell it, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. What was shown was not belief as an achieved state but labour and patience. Two old men met after forty years apart; the abbot of many said the sun had never seen him eating, and the hermit answered, "nor me angry". They proved perseverance, not perfection. At Tours the presbyter who stormed into the courtyard, called his master's visions ridiculous fancies, and repented within the hour was not removed. Martin bore with him afterward, asking why he should not bear with the man if Christ bore with Judas.

It is "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection." The elders' rule: "a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it." So "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered."

uses.sentence: From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year.
uses.paragraph: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like — only as far as those pages say, and no further.
uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

use_note.means: The record attests that everything it holds about this world's places and daily life comes from texts, and cannot supply any excavation, material find or account of the island's days.

uses.sentence: Martin took one communion he abhors, to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics, and afterward he confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by it.
uses.paragraph: And one elder is kept who confessed a power lessened. Martin took one communion he abhors, to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics, and afterward he confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by it. But that is not the house answering to someone it failed; it is the saint's own judgment on himself.
uses.record_text: Meanwhile, the bishops Martin would not share communion with went to the king in terror. They complained that they had been condemned in advance. It was all over for the standing of every one of them, they said, if Martin's authority now backed the stubbornness of Theognitus. He alone had so far condemned them by a sentence given in public. They said the man should never have been let inside the walls. He was now not just the heretics' defender but their champion. And nothing had really been gained by Priscillian's death if Martin was going to play the part of his avenger. At last they threw themselves down, weeping and wailing, and begged the emperor to use his power against this one man. The emperor came close to being forced to give Martin, too, the fate of heretics. Still, although he was inclined to favor the bishops too much, he knew Martin surpassed all others in faith, holiness, and excellence. So he tried another way to get the better of the holy man. First he sent for him in private and spoke to him very kindly. He assured Martin that the heretics had been condemned by regular public trials, not by the priests' persecution. He said there was no reason for Martin to think communion with Ithacius and the rest of that party was something to condemn. He added that Theognitus had caused division out of personal hatred rather than for the cause he stood for. In fact, he said, Theognitus was the only one who had so far cut himself off from communion. The rest had changed nothing. He also pointed out that a synod held a few days before had ruled that Ithacius could not be charged with any fault. When these arguments hardly moved Martin, the king grew furious and hurried out of his presence. Without delay, executioners were appointed for the people Martin had pleaded for. When Martin learned of this, he rushed to the palace, though it was already night. He promised that if these people were spared, he would take communion. He asked only that the tribunes already sent to the Spanish provinces to destroy the churches be called back. There was no delay: Maximus granted everything he asked. The next day, the ordination of Felix as bishop was being arranged. Felix was without doubt a man of great holiness, truly worthy of being made a priest in happier times. Martin took part in the communion that day. He judged it better to give way for the moment than to ignore the safety of those with a sword hanging over their heads. Even so, he would not confirm his communion by signing his name, though the bishops tried their very hardest to make him. The next day he hurried away from that place. On the way back he was filled with grief and mourning that he had been mixed up, even for an hour, in the evil communion. Not far from a village named Andethanna, remote woods stretch far and wide in deep solitude. There he sat down, while his companions went on a little way ahead of him. He sank into deep thought, by turns accusing and defending the cause of his grief and what he had done. Suddenly an angel stood beside him and said, "Martin, you are right to feel remorse, but you had no other way out of your difficulty. Renew your strength and take up your courage again. Otherwise you will put at risk not only your good name now, but your very salvation." So from then on he took great care never to be mixed up in communion with the party of Ithacius. But once he cured some of the possessed more slowly than usual, and with less of the grace he usually had. At once he confessed to us in tears that he felt his power had lessened. He said it was because of the evil of that communion. He had taken part in it for a moment out of necessity, not with his whole heart. He lived sixteen years after this. But he never again attended a synod, and he kept well away from all gatherings of bishops.

use_note.means: Gallus narrates how Martin, to stop the tribunes, took communion with the Ithacian bishops, was answered by an angel, and afterwards felt his healing power diminished.
not_for: the angel's speech and the lessened power as established fact, when they rest on Martin's tearful report through Gallus
the earlier petition at the palace over the tribunes, which sits in gallic.quote.gallus-on-the-tribunes-for-the-spains

uses.sentence: At Tours the reader for the day was blocked by the crowd at the election, so a bystander seized the psalter and opened it where it fell - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict.
uses.paragraph: The third is the shape of what we looked for. The end of our life was the kingdom; the nearer goal was purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. Every fast and vigil was ranked by whether it cleared the heart - an aid, never the point. When Scripture was read, it was read for that mark. At Tours the reader for the day was blocked by the crowd at the election, so a bystander seized the psalter and opened it where it fell - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict. We do not tell you that was right. We tell you it is how Scripture was heard: as a voice speaking now, to this hour, for this need.

uses.sentence: At Tours the saint prayed without a gap, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes.
uses.paragraph: What we carry of our worship is this. At Tours the saint prayed without a gap, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. At Marseilles Cassian handed us the hours from Egypt - twelve psalms at evening, twelve at night, the number fixed by an angel who sang the twelfth with Alleluia and vanished. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. The hours kept the Lord's death and rising: at the third hour the Spirit came down; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. That is what our own books say of it.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk at Tours and Marseilles, served at Marseilles by a received Egyptian system of psalms at fixed hours said to be an angel's.
not_for: the Divine Office as one settled book that all monks everywhere recited
prayer as private devotion and feeling
the eucharist as a rite, which sits in gallic.term.communion

uses.sentence: Our approach and purpose in reading the Scriptures is what Cassian set down for the hours and what Vincent held as the rule of understanding.
uses.paragraph: Our approach and purpose in reading the Scriptures is what Cassian set down for the hours and what Vincent held as the rule of understanding. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, and after the psalms came two lessons - one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body. The hours themselves were received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to them by an angel's ministry. Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than sufficient for all things. Yet it needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way and almost as many senses are extracted from it as there are readers. So what we held was this: the Scriptures are read at the hours, daily, by heart, as prayer - not first as a text to be studied but as the voice we speak back to God. And where doctrine is contested, the rule is universality, antiquity, and consent - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, the old, and the consent of the Fathers collated. The Apostle's words were on a monk's lips at the moment he felt his labour had done something: not I, but the grace of God with me. That is purpose: to be turned into prayer, held as one body, and read by the Fathers' consent, never by a man inventing his own sense alone.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

use_note.means: The rule meant Vincent's test of the faith, what has been believed everywhere, always, by all, preferring the whole, the old and consent to the part, the new and few.
not_for: the Vincentian canon as a slogan in later polemic over which communion holds the faith
a monastic Rule, whether Cassian's customs or Benedict's
a formula consistently applied, when its use in the live grace dispute is contested in gallic.contested.who-holds-antiquity
novelty as a value in itself, which sits in gallic.term.novelty-antiquity

uses.sentence: A girl was devoted by her father to perpetual virginity, and the bishop placed on her the dress characteristic of that state.
uses.paragraph: Marriage was a thing left behind, and its leaving was the renunciation. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that the first stage of a monk's turning was giving up goods, family, and the world's honours - and that this, though it is called leaving all things, was only the first and easiest stage. The act that made a monk was figured as death, and the monk was dead to the world and its deeds and desires. At Tours Martin left Caesar's service at a donative and never married; he gathered brethren, and the bishops who objected to his election said his clothes were mean and his hair disgusting, not that he had taken a wife. The whole of what we marked was the cut, not the bond. For a woman the cut had its own form. A girl was devoted by her father to perpetual virginity, and the bishop placed on her the dress characteristic of that state. At Martin's funeral the consecrated virgins walked as a choir. Cassian taught that marriage may be excused; virginity points to glory. The completed victory is not to be seen.
uses.record_text: A consecrated state with its own dress and its own "glory." Marriage may be excused; virginity points to glory. Its completed victory is not to be seen.

use_note.means: Virginity meant a consecrated state given by the bishop's hands, with its own dress, where marriage is excused and virginity points to glory, seen mostly through Tours.
not_for: virginity as sexual abstinence merely, or as repression
nuns under a later rule
the south's own teaching on chastity, which was cut from the vendored English edition

uses.sentence: Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again.
uses.paragraph: What the reading was for is held at the hours. At the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles. At the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid. At the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. That is what we confessed, at the hours, together.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

use_note.means: This witness says this world knew Jesus as the crucified one met in the poor, kept his death and rising at the hours, and preached grace drawing the unwilling.
not_for: a Gallic treatise on the atonement, which no one in this world wrote
the Christ with wounds as independently witnessed, when one author reports Martin's word
the resurrection as argued rather than confessed at the hours

uses.sentence: Vincent on the island wrote a remembrancer against forgetting, not a charter for successors.
uses.paragraph: No line runs straight from our houses to any church you know. The monasteries of Gaul, in the span we speak from, had no single rule written and kept across all of them. What Cassian set down for a bishop's new house were the customs of Egypt, received from the fathers, not a Rule of his own making. Vincent on the island wrote a remembrancer against forgetting, not a charter for successors. And of the island's own day - what rule it kept, what a novice was taught, how the hours were sung - our record holds nothing at all.
uses.record_text: Vincent's book. By its own name it is an aid to memory, against his own forgetting. He signs it "Peregrinus, the least of all the servants of God" - a teller, not an author.

use_note.means: Commonitory was Vincent's own name for his book, an aid to memory against forgetting, and Peregrinus the pilgrim name under which he wrote it.
not_for: Commonitory as the name of a doctrinal treatise

uses.sentence: And at the election a bystander seized the psalter, read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors.
uses.paragraph: We did not read them the way you are reading them now. The difference is not what we saw in them but what we did with them. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer was held to it by a rule. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The words were not read once and set aside. They were the grain the mill turned. A man kept praying even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The Apostle's word not I, but the grace of God with me was taught to a monk at the moment he felt his own fasting had done something. At Tours the saint took the Apostle's least of these as the beggar at the gate. And at the election a bystander seized the psalter, read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. So what you are missing is not a key to the text. It is the use the text was put to. You read it to understand it. We said it to feed the wheel that cannot stop turning, and heard it speak into the hour we were standing in.

uses.sentence: The power was shown for the rustics who had not yet heard the name of Christ, and a catechumen not yet baptized saw Christ in a dream.
uses.paragraph: Who counts as outside? A man who has left the consent of the universal and ancient Church under his own name is to be cut off by bishops' sentence, lest one sick sheep infect the flock. But Martin went to Trier to protect even heretics from the sword, and the Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. The power was shown for the rustics who had not yet heard the name of Christ, and a catechumen not yet baptized saw Christ in a dream.
uses.record_text: A catechumen soldier has nothing left but his cloak. He cuts it in two for a naked beggar at a city gate. That night he sees Christ wearing the half he gave away.

use_note.means: Sulpitius tells that Martin, a catechumen soldier, cut his cloak in two for a beggar at a city gate and that night saw Christ wearing the half he gave.

uses.sentence: Those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.paragraph: First, the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, taught that God does not will only some to be saved instead of all. He does not want even one of his little ones to perish, and to think otherwise is grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. That is Abbot Chaeremon's own word, and we held it.
uses.record_text: For if He wills none of His little ones to perish, how can we, without grievous blasphemy, imagine He does not will all people's salvation? That He wills only some to be saved, instead of all people in general?

use_note.means: Chaeremon, in Cassian's Conference XIII, argues it would be grievous blasphemy to imagine God wills only some, rather than all, to be saved.

uses.sentence: He stayed enrolled but not yet baptized for years, into his soldiering.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the saint himself began as a soldier under oath, a catechumen not yet baptized, who cut his one cloak in two at a city gate for a beggar while some of the bystanders laughed. He stayed enrolled but not yet baptized for years, into his soldiering. And a soldier could be regarded as a monk even while still in Caesar's service.
uses.record_text: At a donative on the eve of battle a soldier tells Caesar he is now the soldier of Christ and may not fight, offers to stand unarmed before the enemy line - and the enemy surrenders before morning.

use_note.means: Sulpitius records Martin, at a donative before battle, telling Julian Caesar that he is now Christ's soldier and offering to stand unarmed, whereupon the enemy surrenders.

uses.sentence: And at Marseilles we had no Martin to go to court; whether any voice there spoke against what happened at Treves, no one kept.
uses.paragraph: That unsettled me - that bishops could make such common cause with a court, that a secular ruler could sit as judge in an ecclesiastical cause, and that the man who went to stop it paid for it with diminished power and never sat with bishops again. Two limits belong with this. The accuser is heard only through the man who called him worthless. And at Marseilles we had no Martin to go to court; whether any voice there spoke against what happened at Treves, no one kept.
uses.record_text: The office our monks keep being taken into. A monk "carried off," "escorted under guard," "bound to the long-avoided office," who then keeps "the objects and virtues of a monk" in a see. And at the same time our own formation teaching names the desire for that office as vainglory's suggestion and the devil's pretext.

use_note.means: The monk-bishop meant the office into which monks keep being seized and must never seek, kept with a monk's humility though formation teaching names the wish for it vainglory.

uses.sentence: He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.
uses.paragraph: The power claimed by bishops when they made common cause with an emperor's court, and the man we remember is the one who said it was a foul thing. Here is what our record holds. At Treves the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, and in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics by bishops in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court. The accuser there was himself a bishop. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. He held that it was punishment enough for the bishops to declare men heretics and put them out of the churches, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went, our record says, to protect even heretics themselves. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin pledged that night that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: He lived sixteen years after this. But he never again went to a synod, and he carefully kept away from every gathering of bishops.

use_note.means: Gallus says in the Dialogues that Martin lived sixteen years after the coerced communion and never again attended a synod or assembly of bishops.
not_for: the coerced communion and the angel's rebuke themselves, which sit in gallic.quote.gallus-on-the-forced-communion-and-the-angel
a claim that Martin rejected bishops or the episcopate as such
a date for the Treves affair computed from Gallus's sixteen years

uses.sentence: He is the God who judges now, not only at the end - a teaching one of us held, not all.
uses.paragraph: God as we held him is the Lord who never lets go of the tiller and whose hand is on everything. In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person - that was Vincent's word on the island, and it was not debated among us but confessed as what the Church believes. The Word of God does not change into flesh, and we do not worship a Quaternity. What we called him in our prayers was this: not only Protector and Saviour but Helper and Sponsor - Saviour, because he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. He wills all men to be saved, and to think otherwise was for us grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. He does not will only some instead of all. His grace always works together with our will, going before it and following it, inspiring the first desire and crowning the last perseverance. And at the same time the will always remains free in man, to neglect or delight in that grace, so that a monk's fasting and watching are truly his and truly required. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself; and God does not send rich crops to the idle. Both are held. How he works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. He is the God who judges now, not only at the end - a teaching one of us held, not all. And he is the one met in the beggar at the gate, wearing the half of a cloak.
uses.record_text:
Antichrist is close at hand, in Sulpitius's own telling. A solemn expectation of judgment presses in, in Vincent's. God's judgment is already happening, in the ruin of Gaul, in Salvian's. These are the ecology's own three distinct ways of holding the same idea - that time is running out.
At Tours, the mood is imminent and apocalyptic. From a run of false Christs, Sulpitius reasons that Antichrist himself must be near, already at work in these very impostors (Vita XXIV). Gallus recounts that Martin told him and his companions that Antichrist had already been born and had, by the time Martin spoke of it, grown into boyhood, waiting only to come of age (Dial. II.14). In one of his own letters, Sulpitius describes sitting alone with a mind full of hope for the future mixed with weariness of the present world, dread of judgment, and fear of punishment (Ep. II).
At Lérins, the mood is occasional rather than constant. Vincent says plainly that a solemn expectation of God's coming judgment, together with the danger of new heresies, is exactly what drove him to write his handbook of the faith (Comm. ch. 1).
At Marseilles, the mood shifts from a future expectation to a present fact. Salvian reads the barbarian ruin of the Gallic provinces itself as God's judgment already carried out (Gov. VII.10, VII.12). Cassian, meanwhile, treats fear of hell as only the first and most basic motive a beginner in the ascetic life feels (Conf. XI.6) - not an expectation about the end of the world at all.
This gravity is well attested wherever it appears, but it organizes far less of this world's founding literature than the strength of that evidence might suggest: it is Salvian's own entire book, and it supplies Vincent's stated occasion for writing, but in Sulpitius and Cassian it shows up more as a recurring note than as something that shapes the whole. For that reason it is classified here as a supporting gravity, the weakest and most provisional in this world's whole set, rather than a primary one - not because the evidence for it is thin, but because it never quite organizes as broadly as the strongest gravities do.
Under the pressure of barbarian collapse, judgment changes in kind, not just intensity: it shifts from something still to come to something already happening, in Salvian's own words about the present ruin of the Gallic provinces. That is the one place where the larger world's own catastrophe enters this world's literature directly, and the only gravity that the passing of Roman order touches at all.

use_note.means: Three voices hold time running out in different ways: Antichrist at hand for Sulpitius, awful expectation of judgment for Vincent, and judgment already under way in Gaul's ruin for Salvian.
not_for: one shared apocalyptic doctrine, when the three modes differ
Salvian's present judgment as the monastic houses' teaching, when it is his own voice, as in gallic.term.government-of-god
an Antichrist teaching by Cassian, who has only the fear of hell in what was read

uses.sentence: The fathers of Egypt argued in the open whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty, until one father rose at the Vesper hour, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished.
uses.paragraph: The fathers of Egypt argued in the open whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty, until one father rose at the Vesper hour, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The number was fixed by an angel, not hidden in a cave.

uses.sentence: The archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves.

uses.sentence: And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.paragraph: The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man leaves Caesar's service for Christ's. He fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

uses.sentence: After the cloak he was baptized.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the record is thinner still. Martin himself began as a soldier under oath, still a catechumen, who cut his one cloak in two at a city gate. At ten he had gone to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen, then stayed one for years. After the cloak he was baptized. The brethren gathered around him as disciples around a master. Eighty of them were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. But what a man did to become one of them - whether he too lay outside, whether he was reclothed, how long he was tested - Sulpitius never told.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. uses.sentence: If you dug, we could not tell you what you would find.
uses.paragraph: I cannot say. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Where we gathered is named by place, never described as a building. At Tours, a wooden cell for the saint and caves for the brethren. The island where Honoratus went and Vincent dwelt is a harbour, a camp of God, and a place no one would live before he came - never floor, wall, or roof. Cassian wrote for a bishop founding a new monastery in a province that did not have one, and he wrote of Egypt's customs, not of Gaul's construction. Where the brethren stood to sing the twelve psalms that an angel fixed for the fathers, what covered them or what they stood on - that is not in our record. The one procession we are told of moved on the road, between Tours and the monastery, with two thousand monks and a choir of virgins following the body. If you dug, we could not tell you what you would find.
uses.record_text: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. How do historians know about daily life like ours? From what Cassian said Egypt did, and from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it for a year. From what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

uses.record_text:
Renunciation kept producing bishops. Men renounced the world to become monks, and then the office of bishop overtook them.

Martin shows the pattern. He kept up the position of a bishop properly, yet he did not lay aside the aims and virtues of a monk.

Of the eighty disciples at Marmoutier, numbers were afterwards made bishops (Vita, ch. X). The disciples were trained after their master's example.

Everything Cassian wrote was addressed to bishops, or to men who became bishops. His formation writing was for a bishop's new monastery. Honoratus moves from monk to bishop between two of his dedications (Conferences, prefaces II and III).

Archebius is the Egyptian counter-case. He counted his appointment as expulsion from the monastic system, as unworthy of it. Cassian carried his story west (Conferences XI.2).

Hilary of Arles preached on Honoratus in the south's own Latin. He tells how the priest's headband fastened on a man who fled from it, and how the honor came to him. The Latin is there in the source, but this English wording of it is rated Inferential/Thin.

What sets this world apart is a seminary that looked like a monastery. Every primary voice attests this pattern, and Gennadius confirms it independently. It holds in both north and south, more strongly than any other pattern in this world. It is the only one that a Latin insider in the south, Hilary, attests apart from Cassian.

It explains three things. The withdrawal stayed close to the city. The grace argument reached Rome. The ending was a change in how the institution spoke, not a collapse.

The controversy over grace did not break the pattern. It strengthened it into the Lérins network of bishops. Celestine's letter named Venerius, Cassian's own bishop, first (Gibson's editorial introduction). It warned that priests ought not to teach so as to invade the bishops' rights.

By the 470s a bishop formed at Lérins, Faustus, carried the argument at the commission of synods. Under barbarian pressure this was the institution left standing. Gennadius, writing from the same city about 495, reports two monasteries still standing.

These pressures did not change the pattern. They made it the way the world ended.

use_note.means: Renunciation kept producing bishops, so this world's monks were repeatedly seized into the office they were taught to flee and kept a monk's virtues inside the see.

The fathers taught that a thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. uses.sentence: And where doctrine is contested, the rule is universality, antiquity, and consent - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all.
uses.paragraph: Our approach and purpose in reading the Scriptures is what Cassian set down for the hours and what Vincent held as the rule of understanding. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, and after the psalms came two lessons - one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body. The hours themselves were received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to them by an angel's ministry. Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than sufficient for all things. Yet it needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way and almost as many senses are extracted from it as there are readers. So what we held was this: the Scriptures are read at the hours, daily, by heart, as prayer - not first as a text to be studied but as the voice we speak back to God. And where doctrine is contested, the rule is universality, antiquity, and consent - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, the old, and the consent of the Fathers collated. The Apostle's words were on a monk's lips at the moment he felt his labour had done something: not I, but the grace of God with me. That is purpose: to be turned into prayer, held as one body, and read by the Fathers' consent, never by a man inventing his own sense alone.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

uses.record_text: In those days only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. The perfection of the earliest Church still stood unbroken. The burning faith of the few had not yet cooled by being spread among the many. At that time the honored fathers watchfully made plans for those who would come after them. They met to discuss what plan to adopt for daily worship across the whole community of brothers. A dispute might send out a poisonous root of error, or jealousy, or division among those who came after. Each man judged by the measure of his own zeal, paying no heed to how weak others were. Some were for fifty, others for sixty. Some, not satisfied with that number, thought they really ought to go beyond it. They held a holy difference of opinion in their devout debate over the rule of their religious life. It was so great that the hour for their evening service came before the sacred question was settled. One stood up in their midst to sing the Psalms to the Lord. They were all sitting, their minds closely fixed on the words of the singer. He sang eleven Psalms, with prayers placed between them, each verse sung in an even voice. He ended the twelfth with the response "Alleluia." Then he suddenly vanished from the sight of all. At once this ended both their debate and their service. At this the honored assembly of the Fathers understood that, by God's providence, the angel's guidance had set a general rule for the brothers' communities. So they decreed that this number should be kept in both their evening and their night services. What they added, they added simply as extras, by their own decision.

use_note.means: Cassian, in Institutes II, relates the Egyptian tradition that an angel chanting twelve psalms settled the fathers' dispute over how many psalms the offices should hold.

uses.sentence: He hid that out of grief, not fear.
uses.paragraph: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was - not underground, but in the courts, among bishops who had given way with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue. The violence we knew was heretics driving a bishop into exile, and later bishops handing heretics to the sword. Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt men in the Spains, where a man could be counted a heretic for the clothes he wore. But that was the sword drawn in the Church's cause by bishops, not a persecution that drove believers into hiding. What some of us did hide was different. Martin kept one thing hidden because of the times: that he had gone to the court and yielded once to a communion he abhorred, to save men from being killed. He hid that out of grief, not fear. The hiddenness we valued was the monk's own cell, where a man kept himself from the world he had left. Not catacombs. Wooden cells and caves.
uses.record_text: To stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics in the Spains, Martin yields once to a communion he abhors, is told by an angel that his compunction is just, feels his power diminished, and never attends a synod again.

use_note.means: Gallus tells that Martin yielded once to communion with the Ithacian bishops to save men from the tribunes, then lost power, was told his compunction was just, and shunned synods.

What the brethren at Tours sang, and at what hours, our own record does not dwell on; it dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap. uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.sentence: Our labour is truly ours and truly required.
uses.paragraph: What we argued was this: does the beginning of a good will come from us, or from God? Two friends came back to morning service troubled because an old man had said a man cannot make himself master of the good by his own toil. The elder cut the office short and answered with a field. The husbandman ploughs, sows, and weeds - all truly his labour - and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself alone, yet God does not send it to the idle. From that morning came the teaching: God's grace goes before our will, inspires the beginning, works with us, and crowns the end - and it asks real effort of us every day and hour. Both halves held together. Our labour is truly ours and truly required. The grace that makes it reach its goal is God's.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the power that "always remains free in man" to "neglect or delight in the grace of God." Real enough that a monk's fasting, watching and labour are truly his and truly required. Weak enough that "the assistance and grace of God are necessary to it every day and hour." Never denied, never sufficient.

use_note.means: Free will meant, for Cassian's Marseilles, a real but weak power that always remains in man, which grace strengthens without removing and which never suffices alone.
not_for: a philosophical question about determinism
the Pelagian half of a grace-versus-works binary

uses.sentence: How he works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man.
uses.paragraph: God as we held him is the Lord who never lets go of the tiller and whose hand is on everything. In God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person - that was Vincent's word on the island, and it was not debated among us but confessed as what the Church believes. The Word of God does not change into flesh, and we do not worship a Quaternity. What we called him in our prayers was this: not only Protector and Saviour but Helper and Sponsor - Saviour, because he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. He wills all men to be saved, and to think otherwise was for us grievous blasphemy. Those who perish, perish against his will. He does not will only some instead of all. His grace always works together with our will, going before it and following it, inspiring the first desire and crowning the last perseverance. And at the same time the will always remains free in man, to neglect or delight in that grace, so that a monk's fasting and watching are truly his and truly required. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself; and God does not send rich crops to the idle. Both are held. How he works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. He is the God who judges now, not only at the end - a teaching one of us held, not all. And he is the one met in the beggar at the gate, wearing the half of a cloak.
uses.record_text: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.

use_note.means: Cassian reports Chaeremon teaching that grace kindles desire, enables virtue and preserves it without destroying free will, and that their union exceeds human reason.

uses.sentence: Egypt was our measure, in the south.
uses.paragraph: We held what Egypt handed us and never claimed it went back unbroken to the first days. The psalms and the hours had a story. Among the fathers of Egypt only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. They argued whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupted them. One father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel. That is the rule Cassian brought to Gaul as the fathers' own, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. It is a beginning claimed in Egypt, not in Jerusalem. We never said we had it from the apostles. What we said of ourselves is that we received it from the fathers and kept it where Gaul's cold allowed. Egypt was our measure, in the south. At Tours the highest word spoken was different. Martin had the apostles' own power - over death, over demons, over emperors. That named the kind of power the saint showed, not a line of customs kept. And the test of what was legitimate ran through everything we held. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever has been handed down from antiquity is to be held fast. We did not invent a proof that our hours went back to the first believers. We said Egypt gave them to us, and that an angel gave them to Egypt. The authority was in whose they were, not in how old.
uses.record_text:
This world holds Egypt up as the standard of real monastic life. But the two houses relate to that standard in opposite ways.
In the south, the tie is receptive. Bishop Castor wanted the customs of the East, and especially of Egypt, set up in a province of Gaul that had no monasteries at all. Cassian promises to fix anything founded on one person's own whim, rather than on the Egyptian rule. He will adapt the letter of that rule only where Gaul's climate or circumstances make it truly impossible (Inst. Pref.). Gallic monks are told to take the authors of the Conferences into their own cells, as living teachers (Conf. Pref. III). At Lérins, Eucherius names two Egyptian fathers as the pattern of a life already lived, in effect, in heaven.
In the north, the tie is comparative, even competitive. Gennadius says plainly that the Dialogues set the life of the Eastern monks side by side with the life of Martin. One speaker in the Dialogues concedes to another that Martin surpasses every hermit and solitary of the East. Another passage sends word all the way to Egypt itself. However proud Egypt is of its many saints, Europe need not yield to it, or to all of Asia, since Europe has Martin alone. Gaul is the poorer, colder partner in this comparison.
Both houses organize themselves around the same point: Egypt, as the standard of real monastic life. But they differ in kind. The south receives that standard as a rule to keep. The north measures itself against it as a rival to match. This split shows up everywhere the idea is tested. It repeats across every voice in this world's own literature. The Institutes' whole structure, the Conferences' whole frame, and the shape of the Dialogues all depend on it. In the south, formation itself is nothing but this act of reception. In the north, the fit is only partial. It explains the north's competitive language and the south's own talk of adapting to climate. It explains why Cassian's own text is, at once, desert monasticism's Latin transmission and this world's own founding literature. And it holds up across both houses, in these two different modes, wherever it meets this world's other core ideas. Both halves rest on strong, direct evidence. So this record finds no real doubt about the finding itself. The only open question is what it means for whether this is one world or two - and this record leaves that question open.
The tie to Egypt held steady across this world's whole span. But what Egypt was needed for kept changing. Before Cassian ever wrote, Tours answered the Egyptian standard with rivalry. Marseilles and Lérins answered it, a generation later, with reception and careful adaptation. Once the fight over grace broke out, the receptive mode hardened further. Egypt itself became an authority to plead against Augustine and Rome - the whole line of orthodox teachers on the heart's own perfection, as Cassian frames it. Under the barbarian collapse, Egypt survives as little more than a byword for holiness, in the one place Salvian mentions it. The standard itself never moved. What moved was what this world needed it for.

use_note.means: Egypt stands as the measure of real monastic life, received in the south as a rule from the fathers and matched at Tours by a saint said to outdo it.
