uses.sentence: Then he was lodged a year under the guest-elder.
uses.paragraph: The process among the brethren at Marseilles is Egypt's, and Cassian set it down as the fathers' own. A man came to the door. He was put off and scorned there ten days or more, of set purpose, to prove he meant it. When he was let in, he was searched for even a single hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the garments of the house. Then he was lodged a year under the guest-elder. After that he was handed to a dean over ten, and taught the alphabet, as it were, in the direction of perfection. His old clothes were not thrown away. The steward kept them in his cupboard, and if the man was seen once to cool toward the rule he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the newly received monk as Egypt receives him. Ten days or more at the door "of set purpose repelled and scorned," searched for a hidden coin, stripped and reclothed "by the Abbot's hands," lodged a year under the guest-Elder, then handed to a dean over ten and taught "the alphabet ... in the direction of perfection." And Cassian's own admission: no one in our monasteries has kept it up "unbroken even for a year."

use_note.means: The junior meant the monk newly received as Egypt receives him, scorned at the door and taught to conquer his wishes, a standard Cassian says Gallic houses did not keep.

uses.sentence: On the island the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive and took him off to a see.
uses.paragraph: What belongs with that is the shape of what happened next. The churches came for the men who had left them. A bishop's see was capture, not achievement. Martin was lured out of his monastery by a man pretending his wife was ill, escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and taken into an office he had not sought. The Egyptian bishop Archebius told two Gallic travellers that he had been carried off to a town after thirty-seven years among the anchorites, and that he counted it as being expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it. On the island the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive and took him off to a see. So what a man gave up to join us did not mean he was done with the world's claims on him.
uses.record_text: Honoratus goes unafraid onto an island shunned for its squalor and serpents, carrying a psalm; the serpents give way, a camp of God rises where no one would live - and there "the priestly fillet fastens on its fugitive."

use_note.means: Hilary of Arles preached that Honoratus went unafraid onto a serpent-shunned island carrying a psalm, the serpents gave way, and the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive.

uses.sentence: Scripture was not ours to read alone, and a book dull on the page is not dull at the hours.
uses.paragraph: Scripture was not ours to read alone, and a book dull on the page is not dull at the hours. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers taught a man to learn the psalter by heart so that his mind at the work might always turn on it, and after the psalms at each hour came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. What is read together at a fixed time, standing, is not the same thing as what is read alone in a chair. The whole day's labour sat inside that frame. At Tours Martin kept his mind on prayer through other work, the way a blacksmith beats his anvil between the strokes of what he is making. So the first thing you are missing is the hours themselves - not a private quiet time, but the mill that feeds the wheel.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk at Tours and Marseilles, served at Marseilles by a received Egyptian system of psalms at fixed hours said to be an angel's.

uses.sentence: But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.
uses.paragraph: Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the books, read at the hours. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.
uses.record_text: What did we have of Jesus? The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

use_note.means: The record attests that this world's books never claim a witness to the Lord and never argue the resurrection to a doubter, and it cannot supply either.
not_for: a proof of the resurrection written by this world for a doubter, which the record says is absent

uses.sentence: Marriage was a thing left behind, and its leaving was the renunciation.
uses.paragraph: Marriage was a thing left behind, and its leaving was the renunciation. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that the first stage of a monk's turning was giving up goods, family, and the world's honours - and that this, though it is called leaving all things, was only the first and easiest stage. The act that made a monk was figured as death, and the monk was dead to the world and its deeds and desires. At Tours Martin left Caesar's service at a donative and never married; he gathered brethren, and the bishops who objected to his election said his clothes were mean and his hair disgusting, not that he had taken a wife. The whole of what we marked was the cut, not the bond. For a woman the cut had its own form. A girl was devoted by her father to perpetual virginity, and the bishop placed on her the dress characteristic of that state. At Martin's funeral the consecrated virgins walked as a choir. Cassian taught that marriage may be excused; virginity points to glory. The completed victory is not to be seen.
uses.record_text: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."

use_note.means: Renunciation meant the act that makes a monk, a death to the world of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest of three stages.

uses.sentence: Martin foreknew his own death and still travelled to Condate to restore peace among quarrelling clergy, counting reconciliation a crown for his virtues.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the same question sat elsewhere. Martin foreknew his own death and still travelled to Condate to restore peace among quarrelling clergy, counting reconciliation a crown for his virtues. He kept, as bishop, a monk's own habits - the objects and virtues of a monk in a see. Sulpitius said Martin had apostolic authority, the apostles' own power over death, demons, and emperors. That was the highest word spoken for him, and it was a claim of direct likeness to the first, not to a custom passed through stages.
uses.record_text: I must say, then, that Martin knew the time of his own death long before it came. He told the brothers that he would soon leave his body. Meanwhile, a reason arose that led him to visit the church at Condate. The clergy of that church were quarrelling among themselves. Martin wanted to restore peace there. He knew well that the end of his days was near. Yet he did not shrink from making the journey for such a purpose. In fact, he thought that leaving behind him a church at peace again would be a fine crown to set on his virtues.

use_note.means: Sulpitius writes that Martin foreknew his death yet travelled to Condate to reconcile its quarrelling clergy, counting restored peace a crown for his virtues.
not_for: corroborated fact about the foreknowledge, which rests on Sulpitius alone

uses.sentence: Within the house the place belongs to the senior whose judgment stands in for the junior's own.
uses.paragraph: Within the house the place belongs to the senior whose judgment stands in for the junior's own. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that every itching thought is laid bare to him the moment it rises. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. Abbot is the title of every Egyptian father Cassian reports. At Tours the same place was held by one master, Martin, who himself consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics.

uses.sentence: Cassian said we ought to give loyalty without hesitation to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement, not to customs a few people have introduced.
uses.paragraph: The same grammar ran through everything we held. Cassian said we ought to give loyalty without hesitation to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement, not to customs a few people have introduced. At Tours the saint would not honour a tomb without a steady tradition from antiquity. Pope Stephen's rule was kept as a standing word: let nothing new be brought in, nothing except what has been handed down.
uses.record_text: For we ought to give loyalty without hesitation and obedience without question. But we should not give them to customs and rules that the will of a few has brought in. We should give them to those that long-standing antiquity and many holy fathers have handed on to those who come after. They did so by a unanimous decision.

uses.sentence: Consent means an ancient council's decree, or the ancients collated - the doctors whose agreed writings form "a consentient council".
uses.paragraph: Vincent, on the island, set it down plainly. The canon of Scripture is complete, and more than enough. But Scripture still needs the Church's own line of interpretation, because nearly everyone reads it his own way. So within the Catholic Church itself we take care to hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part of the Church, or a novelty, or a few men dissent, we prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council's decree, or the ancients collated - the doctors whose agreed writings form "a consentient council". A single teacher, be he a bishop, be he a Confessor, be he a martyr, holds only a private fancy of his own.
uses.record_text: The prior generations from whom everything legitimate among us is received and never invented. For Cassian, the Egyptian old men he sat with. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? uses.sentence: But whether they bear guilt from birth, by what they are rather than what they have done, Cassian does not say.
uses.paragraph: We never argued it as a formula, and where Cassian touched it he touched it as Egypt's fathers touched it - as a thing held, not debated. Here is what our record keeps. Among the brethren at Marseilles, Abbot Chaeremon named three stages of the grace by which we are saved: the first kindles our desire toward salvation, the second enables us in the good we wish for, the third preserves us to the end in the virtues. All three are God's gift. And he taught plainly that a newborn has no merits before him - he spoke of "the case even of infants, who have as yet done nothing either good or bad". That is the nearest our record comes to your question's shape: infants with no works of their own, and grace going before every stage. But whether they bear guilt from birth, by what they are rather than what they have done, Cassian does not say. What he does say is this: the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; he does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and it is grievous blasphemy to think otherwise. Free will always remains in a man, and it is weak, and the help of God is necessary to it every day and hour. How both are true - how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. The inherited guilt as a thing confessed apart from the grace that answers it is not in our record to give you.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. Grace "always co-operates with our will"; it goes before the will and follows it; it inspires the first desire and crowns the last perseverance. We hold it together, on purpose, with a will that stays free - in a relation "that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man."

uses.sentence: Four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body.
uses.paragraph: Our approach and purpose in reading the Scriptures is what Cassian set down for the hours and what Vincent held as the rule of understanding. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, and after the psalms came two lessons - one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body. The hours themselves were received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to them by an angel's ministry. Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than sufficient for all things. Yet it needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way and almost as many senses are extracted from it as there are readers. So what we held was this: the Scriptures are read at the hours, daily, by heart, as prayer - not first as a text to be studied but as the voice we speak back to God. And where doctrine is contested, the rule is universality, antiquity, and consent - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, the old, and the consent of the Fathers collated. The Apostle's words were on a monk's lips at the moment he felt his labour had done something: not I, but the grace of God with me. That is purpose: to be turned into prayer, held as one body, and read by the Fathers' consent, never by a man inventing his own sense alone.

At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk at Tours and Marseilles, served at Marseilles by a received Egyptian system of psalms at fixed hours said to be an angel's.

uses.sentence: At the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints.
uses.paragraph: What the reading was for is held at the hours. At the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles. At the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid. At the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. That is what we confessed, at the hours, together.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

So the formation passed by watching a named man. Martin's eighty disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Cassian wrote the conferences so that our monks might receive the fathers into their cells, talking with them after a fashion by daily questions and answers. The books exist to be that example when the man himself is absent.
uses.record_text: For us a conference is an elder's discourse drawn out by disciples' questions. It is the after-supper talk of an Egyptian cell that Cassian writes down so that our monks may receive the fathers "into their cells ... talking with them after a fashion by daily questions and answers." By Gennadius's word, it is also the form in which Sulpitius cast his account of Martin.

uses.paragraph: At Tours the record is thinner still. Martin himself began as a soldier under oath, still a catechumen, who cut his one cloak in two at a city gate. At ten he had gone to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen, then stayed one for years. After the cloak he was baptized. The brethren gathered around him as disciples around a master. Eighty of them were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. But what a man did to become one of them - whether he too lay outside, whether he was reclothed, how long he was tested - Sulpitius never told.

uses.sentence: Cassian wrote for a bishop founding a new monastery in a province that did not have one, and he wrote of Egypt's customs, not of Gaul's construction.
uses.paragraph: I cannot say. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Where we gathered is named by place, never described as a building. At Tours, a wooden cell for the saint and caves for the brethren. The island where Honoratus went and Vincent dwelt is a harbour, a camp of God, and a place no one would live before he came - never floor, wall, or roof. Cassian wrote for a bishop founding a new monastery in a province that did not have one, and he wrote of Egypt's customs, not of Gaul's construction. Where the brethren stood to sing the twelve psalms that an angel fixed for the fathers, what covered them or what they stood on - that is not in our record. The one procession we are told of moved on the road, between Tours and the monastery, with two thousand monks and a choir of virgins following the body. If you dug, we could not tell you what you would find.
uses.record_text: What Cassian carried from Egypt and Palestine to a Gallic bishop's "new monastery." Not a written Rule of his own. Rather, "the customs of the monasteries which we have seen observed" there, "as they were there delivered to us by the Fathers." We keep them where Gaul's cold and our weak bodies allow. Where they do not, we balance them from Pontus and Mesopotamia.

use_note.means: The customs of the monasteries meant what Cassian carried from Egypt to Gaul, received from the fathers and not written as a Rule, kept as far as the cold allowed.
not_for: a codified Rule such as Benedict's, with a canonical abbot and novitiate

uses.sentence: And we spoke of God calling us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, drawing us toward salvation.
uses.paragraph: We spoke of a debt that could not be paid, taken out of the way by Christ's cross. We spoke of free will that always remains in a man, weak but real, able to neglect or delight in the grace of God. And we spoke of God calling us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, drawing us toward salvation. Whether a child not yet able to choose carries guilt from birth - that question as you shape it is not in our record the way it stands in yours.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.

uses.sentence: A newcomer at Marseilles was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house.
uses.paragraph: The path those books took to reach us, our record does not trace. They were already in the churches and the monasteries when Martin first gathered brethren. What our own life added was not the books but what they were read for. A newcomer at Marseilles was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. A week's cook was judged a pilferer for three lentils left on the floor, because everything in the house is consecrated to the Lord. A discharged soldier told Caesar he was now the soldier of Christ and may not fight. The books were read inside that frame - a renunciation of marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter service of Christ. And they were read to be said. The psalter learned by heart, said at the work, kept a man's wheel fed. That is the path as our record keeps it: books received, not invented, read at fixed hours in a house built to hold a man to them.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the newly received monk as Egypt receives him. Ten days or more at the door "of set purpose repelled and scorned," searched for a hidden coin, stripped and reclothed "by the Abbot's hands," lodged a year under the guest-Elder, then handed to a dean over ten and taught "the alphabet ... in the direction of perfection." And Cassian's own admission: no one in our monasteries has kept it up "unbroken even for a year."

use_note.means: The junior meant the monk newly received as Egypt receives him, scorned at the door and taught to conquer his wishes, a standard Cassian says Gallic houses did not keep.

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles a man laid every rising thought bare to the senior the moment it came, before any deed.
uses.paragraph: There was space for the struggle itself - never past the edge of the faith, but within it, yes. Here is what our record shows. Among the brethren at Marseilles a man laid every rising thought bare to the senior the moment it came, before any deed. The fathers taught that a thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. That discipline assumed struggle - the wheel cannot stop turning, and the miller decides what grain goes into it. A monk's cell was the place where everything happened to him: saints came, and the devil came, and the wandering heart was held still inside its walls. At Tours the saint himself, alone in his cell, refused a Christ in purple who showed no wounds. He kept silence a long time, then named what he would not believe. That was held up to us as his own act, not condemned.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, discretion is the virtue by which every other is kept from destroying itself. It is "the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator," the "eye and light of the body," the "royal road" between excess and slackness. It is gained "only ... by true humility." That means testing every thought, like a good money-changer testing coin, against the judgment of the elders.

use_note.means: Discretion meant, for Cassian, the virtue that regulates all others, the royal road between excess and slackness, gained only by humility and by showing thoughts to the elders.
not_for: tact, prudence or confidentiality

uses.sentence: The man had sat down on his wooden seat one day, and Brictio came raging that he was holier than the master who brought him up, calling his visions ridiculous fancies and dreaming that he himself deserved the episcopate.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the record is one named man - Martin, master and bishop both, who kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office. Authority rested where the power was felt. He needed no title. Sulpitius calls him "our master" and says it was unlawful to do anything but acquiesce to him. His disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Yet Martin himself, on a question touching whether a tradition had come down from antiquity, consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics, and would not honour a tomb where no steady tradition supported it. One of those presbyters was Brictio, whom Martin had raised from boyhood and who stormed into the courtyard in a fury. The man had sat down on his wooden seat one day, and Brictio came raging that he was holier than the master who brought him up, calling his visions ridiculous fancies and dreaming that he himself deserved the episcopate. Martin held that demons were driving him, but said he would bear with Brictio the way Christ bore with Judas. He would not remove him. That presbyter's rank came from somewhere, not from Martin alone, but where and how the record does not say.
uses.record_text: Again, one day, he had sat down on that wooden seat of his, which you all know. It stood in the small open yard around his dwelling. From there he saw two demons sitting on the high rock that hangs over the monastery. Then he heard them call out, in eager and joyful voices, ‘Come here, Brictio, come here, Brictio.’ I believe they saw the wretched man coming from far off. They knew how great a frenzy of spirit they had stirred up in him. There is no delay. Brictio rushes in, in utter fury. There, full of madness, he spews out a thousand insults against Martin.

uses.sentence: At Tours the saint would not honour a tomb without a steady tradition from antiquity.
uses.paragraph: The same grammar ran through everything we held. Cassian said we ought to give loyalty without hesitation to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement, not to customs a few people have introduced. At Tours the saint would not honour a tomb without a steady tradition from antiquity. Pope Stephen's rule was kept as a standing word: let nothing new be brought in, nothing except what has been handed down.
uses.record_text: He did this, he said, because he had serious doubts of conscience about these matters. He had these doubts because no steady tradition about them had come down from antiquity.

use_note.means: Sulpitius reports Martin's stated reason for doubting a local martyr cult: no steady tradition about it had come down from antiquity.

uses.sentence: How both are true - how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man.
uses.paragraph: We never argued it as a formula, and where Cassian touched it he touched it as Egypt's fathers touched it - as a thing held, not debated. Here is what our record keeps. Among the brethren at Marseilles, Abbot Chaeremon named three stages of the grace by which we are saved: the first kindles our desire toward salvation, the second enables us in the good we wish for, the third preserves us to the end in the virtues. All three are God's gift. And he taught plainly that a newborn has no merits before him - he spoke of "the case even of infants, who have as yet done nothing either good or bad". That is the nearest our record comes to your question's shape: infants with no works of their own, and grace going before every stage. But whether they bear guilt from birth, by what they are rather than what they have done, Cassian does not say. What he does say is this: the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; he does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and it is grievous blasphemy to think otherwise. Free will always remains in a man, and it is weak, and the help of God is necessary to it every day and hour. How both are true - how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. The inherited guilt as a thing confessed apart from the grace that answers it is not in our record to give you.
uses.record_text: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.

use_note.means: Cassian reports Chaeremon teaching that grace kindles desire, enables virtue and preserves it without destroying free will, and that their union exceeds human reason.
not_for: a settled verdict that the teaching is semi-Pelagian, when that label is contested
the claim that grace looks for human effort, which sits in gallic.quote.chaeremon-grace-requires-our-effort

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles, the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, and after the psalms came two lessons - one from the old books and one from the new.
uses.paragraph: Our approach and purpose in reading the Scriptures is what Cassian set down for the hours and what Vincent held as the rule of understanding. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, and after the psalms came two lessons - one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body. The hours themselves were received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to them by an angel's ministry. Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than sufficient for all things. Yet it needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way and almost as many senses are extracted from it as there are readers. So what we held was this: the Scriptures are read at the hours, daily, by heart, as prayer - not first as a text to be studied but as the voice we speak back to God. And where doctrine is contested, the rule is universality, antiquity, and consent - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, the old, and the consent of the Fathers collated. The Apostle's words were on a monk's lips at the moment he felt his labour had done something: not I, but the grace of God with me. That is purpose: to be turned into prayer, held as one body, and read by the Fathers' consent, never by a man inventing his own sense alone.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk at Tours and Marseilles, served at Marseilles by a received Egyptian system of psalms at fixed hours said to be an angel's.
not_for: the Divine Office as one settled book that all monks everywhere recited

uses.sentence: Grace goes before, works with the will, and crowns it; and still our effort is required.
uses.paragraph: What we never settled, on purpose, was how God's will toward all and a man's own perishing both stay true. Free will always remains in a man to neglect or delight in the grace of God. Grace goes before, works with the will, and crowns it; and still our effort is required. How both are true cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. Grace "always co-operates with our will"; it goes before the will and follows it; it inspires the first desire and crowns the last perseverance. We hold it together, on purpose, with a will that stays free - in a relation "that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man."

use_note.means: Grace meant, for Cassian's Marseilles, God's help without which no effort reaches its goal, going before the will and crowning it, held on purpose with a will that stays free.

uses.sentence: Renunciation - death to the world and its desires - came in three acts, not one.
uses.paragraph: And for the monk the turning had stages. Renunciation - death to the world and its desires - came in three acts, not one. Giving up goods was only the first and easiest. Our record does not speak of being born again. It speaks of turning, of being drawn by grace while still ignorant and unwilling, and of a renunciation that is figured as crucifixion.
uses.record_text: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."

use_note.means: Renunciation meant the act that makes a monk, a death to the world of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest of three stages.

uses.sentence: He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all.
uses.paragraph: On the island Vincent wrote what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.
not_for: a penal substitution doctrine, when the sixth-hour sentence is near it but not the same
anything from Cassian's books against Nestorius, which are unread

uses.sentence: He gives us the Egyptian fathers' unanimous decision on customs, not the mechanism by which one house chose its own.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles leadership was the fathers' structure, received from Egypt. Cassian handed us not a written rule of his own but the customs of the monasteries he had seen kept there, as they were delivered by the Fathers. A congregation was governed by the direction of a single Elder, called Abbot - the Egyptian fathers' own title. Under him were deans, each over ten brothers. Every thought was laid bare to the senior. The junior had no cell key of his own; he could not go out without leave; and it was the Abbot's hands that stripped a newcomer of his old clothes and dressed him in the house's dress. Where that Abbot's own authority came from - election, appointment, seniority - Cassian never says. He gives us the Egyptian fathers' unanimous decision on customs, not the mechanism by which one house chose its own.
uses.record_text:
Antiquity, the Fathers, and consent are the test of legitimacy, set against novelty - applied by all three founding voices to monastic custom, doctrine, and cult alike.
Cassian holds that allegiance is owed not to customs a few people have introduced, but to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement (Inst. I.2). He calls his own Institutes not his but the fathers' (Conf. Pref. I). And he holds up, as a warning, the monk who trusted his own judgment over the Elders' tradition and in the end forsook the desert (Conf. II.24).
Vincent holds that the Catholic faith is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all - tested by universality, antiquity, and consent (Comm. ch. 2). He quotes Pope Stephen's own rule that there should be no innovation, nothing but what has been handed down (ch. 6). And he holds that a guardian of doctrine is not an author but a keeper, not a teacher but a disciple, not a leader but a follower (ch. 22).
Sulpitius tells that Martin, asked to venerate a supposed martyr's tomb, would not lend his own authority to popular opinion, because no reliable tradition about it reached back to antiquity (Vita XI).
This same standard also became a battleground. Prosper reports that the Massilians defended their own obstinacy by antiquity; Celestine, as later editors read him, answered that novelty must cease to assail antiquity; and Vincent read that same letter for his own side (Comm. ch. 32). The rule that was meant to settle disputes became, in the grace controversy, one more thing both sides claimed for themselves.

use_note.means: Antiquity, the fathers and consent are the test of legitimacy against novelty in custom, doctrine and cult, applied by all three founding voices though they never cite one another.
not_for: a conservatism that forbids all growth
the test as consistently applied, when that is contested in gallic.contested.who-holds-antiquity
Cassian's customs as a written Rule
Martin's refusal of an unattested tomb as an application of Vincent's formulated test, which sits in gallic.term.the-rule

uses.sentence: And Martin at Tours refused them communion, judged their yielding to the royal court degenerate submissiveness, held it a foul thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church, and lived sixteen years after Treves without entering a synod again.
uses.paragraph: Authority came, for us, from two directions at once. Vincent on the island held that bishops and ancient councils guard the faith. And Martin at Tours refused them communion, judged their yielding to the royal court degenerate submissiveness, held it a foul thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church, and lived sixteen years after Treves without entering a synod again. We never reconciled the two. Bishops and synods guard the truth, yet the saint keeps fleeing them.
uses.record_text:
Bishops and synods guard the truth, yet the saint keeps fleeing them. The state, in this world's own view, has no right to judge the Church's own causes.
At Tours, the office is the thing fled. Bishops resist Martin's election (Vita IX). Some of Martin's slanderers, Sulpitius says, turned out to be bishops themselves, though very few (Vita XXVII). Before Maximus, Sulpitius writes, apostolic authority held its ground in Martin alone, while the priestly dignity around him bowed to the emperor's court (Vita XX). After the forced communion at Trier, Martin never again attended a synod, and stayed carefully away from every assembly of bishops for the rest of his life (Dial. III.13). Sulpitius calls it a foul, unheard-of wrong for a secular ruler to sit in judgment on a matter belonging to the Church (Sacred History II.50).
At Marseilles, the office is both temptation and a defiance of the Pope. Cassian's Abbot Moses teaches that the devil can push a man to want holy orders under the pretext of doing good for many people (Conf. I.20). Vainglory brings a 'desire for the priesthood or diaconate' (Inst. XI.14). Archebius was 'expelled.' And, as the editor tells it, the Massilians held to their own views even against the authority of the Pope brought to bear on them.
At Lérins, the counter-current runs the other way. Vincent rules that an ancient General Council's decrees should be preferred over the rashness and ignorance of a few (Comm. ch. 3), and names 'the twofold authority of the Apostolic See' (ch. 32). Yet in the same voice, he holds that no rank exempts a lone dissenter: whether a teacher is holy and learned, a bishop, a Confessor, or a martyr, a view held against the consent of all is only his own private fancy (ch. 28).
This tension never resolves evenly. Guarding antiquity by councils while fleeing synods, and producing bishops while distrusting the office, keeps this world from being reducible to a seminary that looked like a monastery. Over time it tips one way: the Lérins network becomes the very episcopate it once fled, and the argument over grace comes to be carried forward by a synodal commission - a shift that marks this world's own ending.

use_note.means: Bishops, synods and emperors are held to guard the truth yet the saint keeps fleeing them, so authority is honoured and refused within the same stories.
not_for: anti-institutionalism, or rejection of bishops as such
Martin's hostility to bishops generalized to every voice, when it rests on Sulpitius

uses.sentence: At Marseilles it was the word for the day a man turned to the monastic life - the early days of their turning were bright, and then they cooled.
uses.paragraph: What we had instead was turning. At Marseilles it was the word for the day a man turned to the monastic life - the early days of their turning were bright, and then they cooled. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, remembered a man named Moses who had fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that forced turning into a willing one. The same word covered what a robber or a rustic did when he turned to Christ.
uses.record_text: For us the typical failure of a monk is not apostasy but cooling. The novice who "grow[s] cold in regard to the rule." The renunciant "turned out a deserter or lukewarm." The elders who "pass their old age in a lukewarmness which they contracted in youth." The Sarabaites "cast down into hell by the lukewarmness of their purpose." A disease of temperature that damns.

use_note.means: Lukewarmness meant the monk's characteristic failure, not apostasy but cooling, a disease of temperature that damns and that a grey head does not cure.
not_for: mild disapproval or half-heartedness

uses.sentence: That Gallic houses lived by Cassian's customs - he says they did not.
uses.paragraph: What would not survive is any claim we made past the record's edge. That Martin's reluctance was total - Sulpitius is no neutral witness, and the objecting bishops never answered. That the island kept what Vincent taught - nothing shows a day there. That Gallic houses lived by Cassian's customs - he says they did not. That a miracle happened as told - our record has reported experience, not assessed fact. That the grace argument has one Catholic answer - Vincent read the Apostolic See's letter for his side, and we never settled which of Chaeremon's two phrasings on the beginning of a good will was his own.
uses.record_text: What "comprehends all universally" - the faith believed everywhere, always, by all. A rule of the many and the old against the few and the new, not a confession.

uses.sentence: The steward kept them in his cupboard against the day he grew cold.
uses.paragraph: He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. The girdle, the hood, the tunic - each was a mystery of the inner life. But his old clothes were not thrown away. The steward kept them in his cupboard against the day he grew cold. They waited there as long as his body advanced in goodness and his mind in humility, and they were kept until the excellence of his progress and his long perseverance in it gave certain proof that he would never return to the world.
uses.record_text: For us the typical failure of a monk is not apostasy but cooling. The novice who "grow[s] cold in regard to the rule." The renunciant "turned out a deserter or lukewarm." The elders who "pass their old age in a lukewarmness which they contracted in youth." The Sarabaites "cast down into hell by the lukewarmness of their purpose." A disease of temperature that damns.

use_note.means: Lukewarmness meant the monk's characteristic failure, not apostasy but cooling, a disease of temperature that damns and that a grey head does not cure.

uses.sentence: At Tours the saint himself began as a soldier under oath, a catechumen not yet baptized, who cut his one cloak in two at a city gate for a beggar while some of the bystanders laughed.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the saint himself began as a soldier under oath, a catechumen not yet baptized, who cut his one cloak in two at a city gate for a beggar while some of the bystanders laughed. He stayed enrolled but not yet baptized for years, into his soldiering. And a soldier could be regarded as a monk even while still in Caesar's service.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.sentence: At Tours the saint himself, alone in his cell, refused a Christ in purple who showed no wounds.
uses.paragraph: There was space for the struggle itself - never past the edge of the faith, but within it, yes. Here is what our record shows. Among the brethren at Marseilles a man laid every rising thought bare to the senior the moment it came, before any deed. The fathers taught that a thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. That discipline assumed struggle - the wheel cannot stop turning, and the miller decides what grain goes into it. A monk's cell was the place where everything happened to him: saints came, and the devil came, and the wandering heart was held still inside its walls. At Tours the saint himself, alone in his cell, refused a Christ in purple who showed no wounds. He kept silence a long time, then named what he would not believe. That was held up to us as his own act, not condemned.

uses.sentence: Cassian wrote the received Egyptian system for the south - twelve psalms, lessons from the old books and the new, unceasing prayer as the aim they served - but what a house in Gaul did with them he never wrote, beyond saying that no one in our monasteries kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even for a year.
uses.paragraph: The limits matter as much as the claims. What the brethren at Tours sang, and at what hours, our own record does not dwell on; it dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap. Cassian wrote the received Egyptian system for the south - twelve psalms, lessons from the old books and the new, unceasing prayer as the aim they served - but what a house in Gaul did with them he never wrote, beyond saying that no one in our monasteries kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even for a year. And of the island's own day - what Lerins kept, how it kept it, an order sung - nothing at all. We carry the founder's coming across the serpents and his going off to a see, and Vincent's own rule against forgetting; we do not carry what a day on the island held.
uses.record_text: What Cassian carried from Egypt and Palestine to a Gallic bishop's "new monastery." Not a written Rule of his own. Rather, "the customs of the monasteries which we have seen observed" there, "as they were there delivered to us by the Fathers." We keep them where Gaul's cold and our weak bodies allow. Where they do not, we balance them from Pontus and Mesopotamia.

use_note.means: The customs of the monasteries meant what Cassian carried from Egypt to Gaul, received from the fathers and not written as a Rule, kept as far as the cold allowed.

uses.sentence: Martin did not.
uses.paragraph: A presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood - a man who owed everything, his formation and his place, to the master who brought him up - came storming into the courtyard. He said he was holier than Martin, called his visions ridiculous fancies, and raged at him. The brethren who heard it thought Martin should have driven him out. Martin did not. He said, if Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio? The man was back within the hour, at Martin's feet in repentance. And Martin bore with him afterward.
uses.record_text: Then the holy man explained, both to him and to all of us, how he had seen demons driving him on. He declared that the insults heaped on him did not move him. In fact, they had hurt the man who spoke them instead. Later, this same Brictio was often accused before Martin of many serious crimes. Yet Martin could not be persuaded to remove him from the priesthood. He did not want to be suspected of taking revenge for the wrong done to himself. And he often repeated this saying: ‘If Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio?’

use_note.means: Gallus, in Sulpitius's Dialogues, reports that Martin refused to remove the accused presbyter Brictio, often saying that if Christ bore with Judas he should bear with Brictio.

uses.sentence: Leaving behind bodily wealth and riches - possessions, kin, the life one had in the world - is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the man who has renounced.
uses.paragraph: Everything, we said - and proved the claim by the life the brethren kept. Among the brethren at Marseilles a man was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the clothing of the house. That is the sign, not the whole list. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, named three renunciations, and giving up one's goods was only the first. Leaving behind bodily wealth and riches - possessions, kin, the life one had in the world - is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the man who has renounced. The second renunciation is of habits, vices, and the mind's former affections - the whole interior road of the faults. The third is drawing the mind away from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come. So the claim was this: marriage, property, honours, secular business, kin. Martin was a soldier in Caesar's service who left it at a donative, saying he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight. The fathers remembered a man who fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that compelled turning into a willing one. And Salvian, who wrote from one of the houses at Marseilles, named those who had taken our way of life as the ones who chose to be lowly, poor, and unesteemed.
uses.record_text: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."

use_note.means: Renunciation meant the act that makes a monk, a death to the world of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest of three stages.

uses.sentence: The authority to teach rests on having seen and heard a named master.
uses.paragraph: The authority to teach rests on having seen and heard a named master. A disciple is made by watching - and, later, by reading - a named man whose life is held up as the thing to copy. Our books exist to be that example when the man himself is absent.
uses.record_text:
Authority to teach or narrate rests on having seen and heard a named master, and formation happens by imitation of a named exemplar. Sulpitius writes 'the life of a most holy man, which shall serve in future as an example to others' (Vita I), and Marmoutier's disciples are 'disciplined after the example of the saintly master' (Vita X), and Martin's last saying is 'I have sinned if I leave you a different example' (Ep. III), and Gallus can say 'I myself am a witness' (Dial. II.4). Cassian writes that 'these things cannot be taught save by one who has had experience of them' (Inst. Pref.). The Conferences are reported speech of named elders whom God 'has deemed us worthy both to see ... and to dwell with'. The novice takes his examples 'from a very few or indeed from one or two only' (Inst. IV.40). At Lérins the value is present as writings collated (Comm. ch. 3, ch. 28). It is also present as a disciple's Life of his master (Hilary's Life of Honoratus, Gennadius ch. LXX).
The texts raise no concern about attestation, but they do raise one about convention: a shared late-antique literary convention, which weakens what convergence proves. The value passes every test applied to it. It repeats across the kinds of evidence tested, one of them by existence alone. The form of both nodes' literature depends on it. The Dialogues are built as eyewitness testimony, and the Conferences are built as heard conferences, and each corpus defends its authority on that ground, while imitation of a named exemplar is the stated way that formation works at both nodes. It explains why Sulpitius writes a Life and why Hilary writes a Life, why Cassian writes reported speech, and why this world's stories are almost entirely first-person-attested. The value persists across nodes, 'with Vincent transforming the value from heard to read.' In the interaction test it passes with one negative cell.
Is this one value? As far as the evidence allows, in the sense the tests measure, yes. It is also a convention shared far beyond this world: 'two unconnected Latin monastic communities in 400 could each have inherited it separately.' The link across nodes is confirmed, but it is discounted as evidence of unity. The value is supporting, not primary. It organizes the literature's form and the formation mechanism, but it works within the context that the monk-bishop and Egypt-as-measure gravities establish, since the exemplar is a monk-bishop or an Egyptian father. A convention that the world shares with its neighbours does not meet the primary bar. The record's confidence and its gravity standing agree.
It held, but it fractured at the edge through transmission. In the grace controversy it becomes a weapon. Cassian's authority is that he heard Chaeremon. Prosper attacks 'a man of priestly rank' without naming him. The eyewitness-teacher's standing survives the attack. The fracture came in transmission, since the excision of Conferences XII and XXII removed two eyewitness conferences from this world's own English text. Gennadius gives 'two divisions' against the three Dialogues in this world's text. This shows that copying split the eyewitness frame itself again.

use_note.means: Authority to teach rests on having seen and heard a named master, so formation is imitation of a named exemplar, shifting at Lerins from men seen to writings read.

uses.sentence: We held that God wills all men to be saved, not some instead of all, and that those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.paragraph: We held that God wills all men to be saved, not some instead of all, and that those who perish, perish against his will. Chaeremon, the elder in Egypt whose teaching Cassian carried to us, set it down plainly: grievous blasphemy it is to say that God does not will all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. He does not want even one of his little ones to perish. That was the southern teaching, received from the fathers. At Tours the record does not raise it as a question.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. Grace "always co-operates with our will"; it goes before the will and follows it; it inspires the first desire and crowns the last perseverance. We hold it together, on purpose, with a will that stays free - in a relation "that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man."

uses.sentence: The customs, the twelve psalms, the teaching on purity of heart - all of it came to us from the fathers, not from us.
uses.paragraph: And the last thing is Egypt. The customs, the twelve psalms, the teaching on purity of heart - all of it came to us from the fathers, not from us. Even the number of psalms was not ours to choose. The fathers of Egypt argued whether it should be fifty or sixty, and the Vesper hour interrupted them; one father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished, and the number was fixed forever by an angel, not by any monk. That is the grammar we stood in. Scripture was not a problem we solved; it was the word we received, read at the hours, learned by heart, and heard through the fathers who had received it before us.

uses.sentence: More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours.
uses.paragraph: Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the books, read at the hours. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.
uses.record_text: What did we have of Jesus? The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

uses.sentence: Two friends came back to morning service troubled because an old man had said a man cannot make himself master of the good by his own toil.
uses.paragraph: What we argued was this: does the beginning of a good will come from us, or from God? Two friends came back to morning service troubled because an old man had said a man cannot make himself master of the good by his own toil. The elder cut the office short and answered with a field. The husbandman ploughs, sows, and weeds - all truly his labour - and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself alone, yet God does not send it to the idle. From that morning came the teaching: God's grace goes before our will, inspires the beginning, works with us, and crowns the end - and it asks real effort of us every day and hour. Both halves held together. Our labour is truly ours and truly required. The grace that makes it reach its goal is God's.
uses.record_text: Two friends come back to morning service troubled by one sentence an old man added the night before - that striving cannot make a man master of the good - and the elder shortens the office to answer them with a husbandman, the rain, and "the initiative ... comes from God."

use_note.means: Cassian records that Germanus's scruple over one sentence of Chaeremon's led the elder to shorten the office and answer that the initiative comes from God.

uses.sentence: He was lodged a year under the elder who kept the gate for guests, learning to conquer his own wishes.
uses.paragraph: He was lodged a year under the elder who kept the gate for guests, learning to conquer his own wishes. Then he was handed to a dean over ten and taught the alphabet, as it were, in the direction of perfection: to lay every itching thought bare to the senior as soon as it arose.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the newly received monk as Egypt receives him. Ten days or more at the door "of set purpose repelled and scorned," searched for a hidden coin, stripped and reclothed "by the Abbot's hands," lodged a year under the guest-Elder, then handed to a dean over ten and taught "the alphabet ... in the direction of perfection." And Cassian's own admission: no one in our monasteries has kept it up "unbroken even for a year."

uses.sentence: The southern teaching - purity of heart as the immediate goal, discretion as its regulator, the eight faults fought in order - stands sentence by sentence in Cassian's two books.
uses.paragraph: The southern teaching - purity of heart as the immediate goal, discretion as its regulator, the eight faults fought in order - stands sentence by sentence in Cassian's two books. The north's power-economy - Martin's felt virtus, the blessed oil and threads, the demon named at exorcism - stands in Sulpitius's Life and Dialogues. Vincent's rule of everywhere-always-all stands in the Commonitory. The grace argument's two-sided teaching, with the field and the husbandman, stands in Conference XIII. Each of those would survive the check on its own ground.
uses.record_text: Purity of heart as the goal, discretion as its regulator, the eight faults as its combats - the whole southern formation program: 'the immediate aim or goal, is purity of heart, without which no one can gain that end' (Conf. I.4); fastings, vigils, and renunciation 'are not perfection, but aids to perfection' (I.7); 'discretion is the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator' (II.4); the eight faults 'and the remedies for them according to their traditions' (Inst. Pref.); vainglory that 'creates a wish to take holy orders' (Inst. XI.14). In Tours, the thing without the vocabulary - Martin's discernment of Anatolius's robe and of the purple-robed 'Christ' (Vita XXIII-XXIV) - but 'no "purity of heart," no "discretion," no fault-list.' Cassian frames every element of this program as received from Egypt, not his own invention; what Gaul contributed was the adaptation - carried west and adapted for a colder climate (Inst. I.10, IV.10-11), its severity sustained by a real fear of spiritual cooling. Two of Cassian's own conferences on this program, on chastity and on nocturnal illusions, and one book of the Institutes, do not survive in the English edition this account draws on.

use_note.means: Purity of heart as goal, discretion as regulator and the eight faults as combats make up the southern formation program, which pulls against office and against the saint's wonders.

uses.sentence: Our approach and purpose in reading the Scriptures is what Cassian set down for the hours and what Vincent held as the rule of understanding.
uses.paragraph: Our approach and purpose in reading the Scriptures is what Cassian set down for the hours and what Vincent held as the rule of understanding. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the psalms learned by heart were said at the work, and after the psalms came two lessons - one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body. The hours themselves were received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to them by an angel's ministry. Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than sufficient for all things. Yet it needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way and almost as many senses are extracted from it as there are readers. So what we held was this: the Scriptures are read at the hours, daily, by heart, as prayer - not first as a text to be studied but as the voice we speak back to God. And where doctrine is contested, the rule is universality, antiquity, and consent - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, the old, and the consent of the Fathers collated. The Apostle's words were on a monk's lips at the moment he felt his labour had done something: not I, but the grace of God with me. That is purpose: to be turned into prayer, held as one body, and read by the Fathers' consent, never by a man inventing his own sense alone.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk at Tours and Marseilles, served at Marseilles by a received Egyptian system of psalms at fixed hours said to be an angel's.

A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. Abbot is the title of every Egyptian father Cassian reports. uses.sentence: Our faith in Jesus as truly God is held as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate.
uses.paragraph: Our faith in Jesus as truly God is held as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, set it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all - a man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused the novelty and innovated nothing. That is the formula as Vincent held it, and it is the whole of our own direct witness on the Trinity as such.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.

uses.sentence: And by our own teaching it was a death to the world, of which giving up goods was only the first and easiest stage.
uses.paragraph: What a man gave up to become one of us had a name: renunciation. And by our own teaching it was a death to the world, of which giving up goods was only the first and easiest stage.
uses.record_text: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."

uses.sentence: At Treves the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, and in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place.
uses.paragraph: The power claimed by bishops when they made common cause with an emperor's court, and the man we remember is the one who said it was a foul thing. Here is what our record holds. At Treves the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, and in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics by bishops in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court. The accuser there was himself a bishop. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. He held that it was punishment enough for the bishops to declare men heretics and put them out of the churches, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went, our record says, to protect even heretics themselves. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin pledged that night that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: The bishops had given way weakly. They let the royal court outrank the priesthood's own dignity. But Martin alone still held the authority handed down from the apostles.

use_note.means: Sulpitius writes in the Life of Martin that while bishops fawned on the emperor Maximus, apostolic authority still asserted itself in Martin alone.
