uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer was held to it by a rule.
uses.paragraph: We did not read them the way you are reading them now. The difference is not what we saw in them but what we did with them. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer was held to it by a rule. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The words were not read once and set aside. They were the grain the mill turned. A man kept praying even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The Apostle's word not I, but the grace of God with me was taught to a monk at the moment he felt his own fasting had done something. At Tours the saint took the Apostle's least of these as the beggar at the gate. And at the election a bystander seized the psalter, read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. So what you are missing is not a key to the text. It is the use the text was put to. You read it to understand it. We said it to feed the wheel that cannot stop turning, and heard it speak into the hour we were standing in.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk at Tours and Marseilles, served at Marseilles by a received Egyptian system of psalms at fixed hours said to be an angel's.

uses.sentence: An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same meeting in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. And the whole of our discipline was held under his word: without him we can do nothing. A monk fasts, watches, keeps his cell, shows every thought to the senior - and at the moment he feels the fast has done something, he is taught to say not I, but the grace of God with me.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

uses.sentence: The discipline for a fault is kept.
uses.paragraph: The discipline for a fault is kept. A brother judged at fault lay on the ground until the abbot bade him rise, or was barred from prayer with the brethren. But that is a house's discipline turned on its own member for a fault, not a reckoning for what the house itself did wrong.

uses.sentence: The grace that makes it reach its goal is God's.
uses.paragraph: What we argued was this: does the beginning of a good will come from us, or from God? Two friends came back to morning service troubled because an old man had said a man cannot make himself master of the good by his own toil. The elder cut the office short and answered with a field. The husbandman ploughs, sows, and weeds - all truly his labour - and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself alone, yet God does not send it to the idle. From that morning came the teaching: God's grace goes before our will, inspires the beginning, works with us, and crowns the end - and it asks real effort of us every day and hour. Both halves held together. Our labour is truly ours and truly required. The grace that makes it reach its goal is God's.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. Grace "always co-operates with our will"; it goes before the will and follows it; it inspires the first desire and crowns the last perseverance. We hold it together, on purpose, with a will that stays free - in a relation "that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man."

uses.sentence: Every place we blurred it would fall.
uses.paragraph: What a scholar would hold us to is the difference between "Cassian says the fathers taught" and "the fathers taught," between "Sulpitius reports Martin raised a man" and "Martin raised a man," between "Vincent gives a rule" and "the island kept it". Every place we kept that difference would stand. Every place we blurred it would fall.
uses.record_text: Purity of heart as the goal, discretion as its regulator, the eight faults as its combats - the whole southern formation program: 'the immediate aim or goal, is purity of heart, without which no one can gain that end' (Conf. I.4); fastings, vigils, and renunciation 'are not perfection, but aids to perfection' (I.7); 'discretion is the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator' (II.4); the eight faults 'and the remedies for them according to their traditions' (Inst. Pref.); vainglory that 'creates a wish to take holy orders' (Inst. XI.14). In Tours, the thing without the vocabulary - Martin's discernment of Anatolius's robe and of the purple-robed 'Christ' (Vita XXIII-XXIV) - but 'no "purity of heart," no "discretion," no fault-list.' Cassian frames every element of this program as received from Egypt, not his own invention; what Gaul contributed was the adaptation - carried west and adapted for a colder climate (Inst. I.10, IV.10-11), its severity sustained by a real fear of spiritual cooling. Two of Cassian's own conferences on this program, on chastity and on nocturnal illusions, and one book of the Institutes, do not survive in the English edition this account draws on.

uses.sentence: He said, if Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio?
uses.paragraph: A presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood - a man who owed everything, his formation and his place, to the master who brought him up - came storming into the courtyard. He said he was holier than Martin, called his visions ridiculous fancies, and raged at him. The brethren who heard it thought Martin should have driven him out. Martin did not. He said, if Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio? The man was back within the hour, at Martin's feet in repentance. And Martin bore with him afterward.
uses.record_text: Then the holy man explained, both to him and to all of us, how he had seen demons driving him on. He declared that the insults heaped on him did not move him. In fact, they had hurt the man who spoke them instead. Later, this same Brictio was often accused before Martin of many serious crimes. Yet Martin could not be persuaded to remove him from the priesthood. He did not want to be suspected of taking revenge for the wrong done to himself. And he often repeated this saying: ‘If Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio?’

use_note.means: Gallus, in Sulpitius's Dialogues, reports that Martin refused to remove the accused presbyter Brictio, often saying that if Christ bore with Judas he should bear with Brictio.
not_for: a verdict that the charges against Brictio were false, which the passage never gives

uses.paragraph: A presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood - a man who owed everything, his formation and his place, to the master who brought him up - came storming into the courtyard. He said he was holier than Martin, called his visions ridiculous fancies, and raged at him. The brethren who heard it thought Martin should have driven him out. Martin did not. He said, if Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio? The man was back within the hour, at Martin's feet in repentance. And Martin bore with him afterward.
uses.record_text: These things filled the wretched man with bitter rage. And, I believe, the urging of those demons drove him most of all. He attacked Martin so fiercely that he barely held back from striking him. The holy man, for his part, kept a calm face and a peaceful mind. With gentle words he tried to hold back the unhappy man's madness. But the spirit of evil had such a grip on him that he could not control even his own mind. That mind was a very foolish one even at the best of times. His lips trembled, and his face changed, pale with rage. He poured out sinful words. He claimed he was a holier man than Martin, who had raised him. From his earliest years, he said, he had grown up in the monastery, trained in the Church's holy ways. Martin, he said, had first been stained by a soldier's life, as Martin could not deny. And now, he said, Martin had sunk completely into old age's foolishness. His groundless superstitions and ridiculous fancies about visions had brought him to it.

use_note.means: Gallus describes Brictio nearly assaulting Martin and claiming to be holier for growing up in the monastery, while Martin answered with gentle words.

uses.sentence: But whether Vincent's reading of that letter stands as ours, or as one voice's act inside an argument still live, our record leaves contested.
uses.paragraph: The evidence that it worked is also the evidence that it did not. On the grace question itself - does our good will begin with us or with God's mercy? - Vincent read the Apostolic See's own letter as written for the side of antiquity, and held that we kept the faith of the fathers. But whether Vincent's reading of that letter stands as ours, or as one voice's act inside an argument still live, our record leaves contested. The fathers of Egypt left it open on purpose: our teacher Chaeremon answered on both sides with Scripture and said no one can fully grasp it. We stopped where the fathers stopped. So what the test gave us was a way to name what binds and what does not, and the refusal of one man's novelty - not one answer forced through to the end.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

use_note.means: The rule meant Vincent's test of the faith, what has been believed everywhere, always, by all, preferring the whole, the old and consent to the part, the new and few.
not_for: the Vincentian canon as a slogan in later polemic over which communion holds the faith

uses.sentence: Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new.
uses.paragraph: We held what Egypt handed us and never claimed it went back unbroken to the first days. The psalms and the hours had a story. Among the fathers of Egypt only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. They argued whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupted them. One father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel. That is the rule Cassian brought to Gaul as the fathers' own, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. It is a beginning claimed in Egypt, not in Jerusalem. We never said we had it from the apostles. What we said of ourselves is that we received it from the fathers and kept it where Gaul's cold allowed. Egypt was our measure, in the south. At Tours the highest word spoken was different. Martin had the apostles' own power - over death, over demons, over emperors. That named the kind of power the saint showed, not a line of customs kept. And the test of what was legitimate ran through everything we held. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever has been handed down from antiquity is to be held fast. We did not invent a proof that our hours went back to the first believers. We said Egypt gave them to us, and that an angel gave them to Egypt. The authority was in whose they were, not in how old.
uses.record_text: The axis on which all three of our founding voices judge what is legitimate. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever "has been handed down" from antiquity is to be held fast. "If novelty is profane, antiquity is sacred."

use_note.means: Novelty and antiquity named the axis on which all three founding voices judged legitimacy: the new is suspect for being new, and what was handed down is held fast.
not_for: novelty as harmless newness or as a virtue

uses.sentence: The brethren gathered around him as disciples around a master.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the record is thinner still. Martin himself began as a soldier under oath, still a catechumen, who cut his one cloak in two at a city gate. At ten he had gone to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen, then stayed one for years. After the cloak he was baptized. The brethren gathered around him as disciples around a master. Eighty of them were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. But what a man did to become one of them - whether he too lay outside, whether he was reclothed, how long he was tested - Sulpitius never told.
uses.record_text: Our formative bond is a named man and those formed by watching him. Martin's "eighty disciples, who were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master"; Clarus, "a disciple of Martin's"; Sulpitius mourning "our master, Martin." The south keeps it as elder and junior. Vincent turns it on doctrine: the true Catholic is "not a teacher but a disciple, not a leader but a follower."

use_note.means: Disciple and master named the bond between a named man and those formed by watching him, which Vincent turned on doctrine: the Catholic is a disciple, not a leader.

uses.sentence: At the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles.
uses.paragraph: What the reading was for is held at the hours. At the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles. At the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid. At the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. That is what we confessed, at the hours, together.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

use_note.means: This witness says this world knew Jesus as the crucified one met in the poor, kept his death and rising at the hours, and preached grace drawing the unwilling.
not_for: a Gallic treatise on the atonement, which no one in this world wrote

uses.sentence: When he was let in, he was searched for even a single hidden coin.
uses.paragraph: The process among the brethren at Marseilles is Egypt's, and Cassian set it down as the fathers' own. A man came to the door. He was put off and scorned there ten days or more, of set purpose, to prove he meant it. When he was let in, he was searched for even a single hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the garments of the house. Then he was lodged a year under the guest-elder. After that he was handed to a dean over ten, and taught the alphabet, as it were, in the direction of perfection. His old clothes were not thrown away. The steward kept them in his cupboard, and if the man was seen once to cool toward the rule he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the newly received monk as Egypt receives him. Ten days or more at the door "of set purpose repelled and scorned," searched for a hidden coin, stripped and reclothed "by the Abbot's hands," lodged a year under the guest-Elder, then handed to a dean over ten and taught "the alphabet ... in the direction of perfection." And Cassian's own admission: no one in our monasteries has kept it up "unbroken even for a year."

use_note.means: The junior meant the monk newly received as Egypt receives him, scorned at the door and taught to conquer his wishes, a standard Cassian says Gallic houses did not keep.

uses.sentence: He does not want even one of his little ones to perish.
uses.paragraph: We held that God wills all men to be saved, not some instead of all, and that those who perish, perish against his will. Chaeremon, the elder in Egypt whose teaching Cassian carried to us, set it down plainly: grievous blasphemy it is to say that God does not will all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. He does not want even one of his little ones to perish. That was the southern teaching, received from the fathers. At Tours the record does not raise it as a question.
uses.record_text: For if He wills none of His little ones to perish, how can we, without grievous blasphemy, imagine He does not will all people's salvation? That He wills only some to be saved, instead of all people in general?

use_note.means: Chaeremon, in Cassian's Conference XIII, argues it would be grievous blasphemy to imagine God wills only some, rather than all, to be saved.
not_for: a separate witness from gallic.quote.grievous-blasphemy-not-all-men-to-be-saved, which carries the same sentence

uses.sentence: He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.paragraph: And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness says Jesus sought the unpitied, citing Martin's cloak, the guest received as Christ and grace calling the unwilling, while naming its thin personal testimony.
not_for: a personal conversion testimony from anyone but Martin, which the record lacks

uses.sentence: The third is withdrawing the mind from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come.
uses.paragraph: Here is what the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, said about it. Renunciation has three stages. The first is giving up one's goods - "of what is not our own," they said, because all things are God's. But that stage alone is not enough to make a man perfect. The second is giving up one's former way of life, its vices and passions of soul and flesh. The third is withdrawing the mind from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come. A professed man had cut himself off from marriage, kin, property, and the life of the world for a stricter life in Christ's service. That cut showed in his body and his dwelling.
uses.record_text: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."

use_note.means: Renunciation meant the act that makes a monk, a death to the world of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest of three stages.

uses.sentence: The third is drawing the mind away from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come.
uses.paragraph: Everything, we said - and proved the claim by the life the brethren kept. Among the brethren at Marseilles a man was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the clothing of the house. That is the sign, not the whole list. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, named three renunciations, and giving up one's goods was only the first. Leaving behind bodily wealth and riches - possessions, kin, the life one had in the world - is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the man who has renounced. The second renunciation is of habits, vices, and the mind's former affections - the whole interior road of the faults. The third is drawing the mind away from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come. So the claim was this: marriage, property, honours, secular business, kin. Martin was a soldier in Caesar's service who left it at a donative, saying he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight. The fathers remembered a man who fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that compelled turning into a willing one. And Salvian, who wrote from one of the houses at Marseilles, named those who had taken our way of life as the ones who chose to be lowly, poor, and unesteemed.

uses.sentence: Martin always kept an event hidden, because of the times.
uses.paragraph: What concealment our record holds is of one kind only. Martin always kept an event hidden, because of the times. He went to the emperor's court at Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent into the Spains to hunt heretics, and to protect even heretics themselves. That silence was a saint's own prudence about power wrongly used, not a believer hiding from arrest.
uses.record_text: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.

use_note.means: Gallus recounts how Maximus shielded Ithacius after Priscillian's death and how Martin went to court to stop tribunes being sent into the Spains.
not_for: a doctrinal ruling on heresy, when Martin's petition concerned lives

uses.sentence: Our age had no persecutor.
uses.paragraph: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was - not underground, but in the courts, among bishops who had given way with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue. The violence we knew was heretics driving a bishop into exile, and later bishops handing heretics to the sword. Martin went to Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt men in the Spains, where a man could be counted a heretic for the clothes he wore. But that was the sword drawn in the Church's cause by bishops, not a persecution that drove believers into hiding. What some of us did hide was different. Martin kept one thing hidden because of the times: that he had gone to the court and yielded once to a communion he abhorred, to save men from being killed. He hid that out of grief, not fear. The hiddenness we valued was the monk's own cell, where a man kept himself from the world he had left. Not catacombs. Wooden cells and caves.
uses.record_text: Hiding in the catacombs? No. Our age had no persecutor. Sulpitius says of Martin that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack; without them, he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding his blood - in hunger, in watchings, in nakedness, in fasting. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was. Did it change what we were? Martin's road began by leaving Caesar's service at a donative: I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. Before he gathered his first brethren, the violence of heretics had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder. And at Treves, where the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place; he held it a foul and unheard-of thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church. He yielded there once, to save lives, and never sat with bishops again. What would an outsider have found strangest? We can only tell you what they laughed at. Some bystanders at a city gate laughed at a soldier walking in half a cloak. Bishops at the election said Martin's person was despicable, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting. Cassian says the Egyptians' sheepskin and little hoods would be a subject for derision in Gaul, so we did not wear them. Our own presbyter, raging in the courtyard, called the saint's visions ridiculous fancies. And what were we accused of? Sulpitius says that some of Martin's calumniators, though very few, were reported to be bishops. Others reported the brethren at Marseilles to Africa and to Rome for what they held about grace. A man of Marseilles wrote that at Carthage a monk, pale, with his hair shaved to the skin, could hardly be looked at without curses, and that servants of God from Egypt were met in the street with hissing. That was Africa, not Gaul. But it is the nearest our record comes to a crowd's own voice.

use_note.means: This witness says the Gallic monks met no persecution but faced derision at dress, hair and visions, and accusation by bishops and reporters to Africa.
not_for: the Carthage crowd's derision as a Gallic town's reaction, when it is Salvian's report of Africa
the objecting bishops as fairly heard, when only Sulpitius speaks for them

uses.sentence: What Cassian set down for a bishop's new house were the customs of Egypt, received from the fathers, not a Rule of his own making.
uses.paragraph: No line runs straight from our houses to any church you know. The monasteries of Gaul, in the span we speak from, had no single rule written and kept across all of them. What Cassian set down for a bishop's new house were the customs of Egypt, received from the fathers, not a Rule of his own making. Vincent on the island wrote a remembrancer against forgetting, not a charter for successors. And of the island's own day - what rule it kept, what a novice was taught, how the hours were sung - our record holds nothing at all.
uses.record_text: What Cassian carried from Egypt and Palestine to a Gallic bishop's "new monastery." Not a written Rule of his own. Rather, "the customs of the monasteries which we have seen observed" there, "as they were there delivered to us by the Fathers." We keep them where Gaul's cold and our weak bodies allow. Where they do not, we balance them from Pontus and Mesopotamia.

use_note.means: The customs of the monasteries meant what Cassian carried from Egypt to Gaul, received from the fathers and not written as a Rule, kept as far as the cold allowed.
not_for: a codified Rule such as Benedict's, with a canonical abbot and novitiate

uses.sentence: All of it serves one mark: purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, at which every fast and vigil is aimed.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set down what he had received from Egypt, the day was built around the hours and the cell. Twelve psalms at evening, twelve at night, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. Between them, labour in the cell without ceasing - basket-work, rope-work, whatever the hands can do while the heart says the psalms learned by heart. The wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. A brother may not go out without the elder's leave. Every thought is laid bare to the senior the moment it arises, before any deed. At the sixth hour comes the danger: a monk hates his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set. The remedy is to stay. All of it serves one mark: purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, at which every fast and vigil is aimed.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the immediate goal of the whole monastic life, as distinct from its end, the kingdom of heaven. It is the "definite mark" at which every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation is aimed, "which is charity." By it all of these are ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself.

use_note.means: Purity of heart meant the monk's immediate goal short of the kingdom, a heart cleared to charity, by which every fast and vigil is ranked as an aid.
not_for: sexual purity or moral spotlessness
sincerity or good intentions

uses.sentence: He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall.
uses.paragraph: The power claimed by bishops when they made common cause with an emperor's court, and the man we remember is the one who said it was a foul thing. Here is what our record holds. At Treves the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, and in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics by bishops in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court. The accuser there was himself a bishop. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. He held that it was punishment enough for the bishops to declare men heretics and put them out of the churches, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went, our record says, to protect even heretics themselves. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin pledged that night that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.
uses.record_text: Meanwhile, the bishops Martin would not share communion with went to the king in terror. They complained that they had been condemned in advance. It was all over for the standing of every one of them, they said, if Martin's authority now backed the stubbornness of Theognitus. He alone had so far condemned them by a sentence given in public. They said the man should never have been let inside the walls. He was now not just the heretics' defender but their champion. And nothing had really been gained by Priscillian's death if Martin was going to play the part of his avenger. At last they threw themselves down, weeping and wailing, and begged the emperor to use his power against this one man. The emperor came close to being forced to give Martin, too, the fate of heretics. Still, although he was inclined to favor the bishops too much, he knew Martin surpassed all others in faith, holiness, and excellence. So he tried another way to get the better of the holy man. First he sent for him in private and spoke to him very kindly. He assured Martin that the heretics had been condemned by regular public trials, not by the priests' persecution. He said there was no reason for Martin to think communion with Ithacius and the rest of that party was something to condemn. He added that Theognitus had caused division out of personal hatred rather than for the cause he stood for. In fact, he said, Theognitus was the only one who had so far cut himself off from communion. The rest had changed nothing. He also pointed out that a synod held a few days before had ruled that Ithacius could not be charged with any fault. When these arguments hardly moved Martin, the king grew furious and hurried out of his presence. Without delay, executioners were appointed for the people Martin had pleaded for. When Martin learned of this, he rushed to the palace, though it was already night. He promised that if these people were spared, he would take communion. He asked only that the tribunes already sent to the Spanish provinces to destroy the churches be called back. There was no delay: Maximus granted everything he asked. The next day, the ordination of Felix as bishop was being arranged. Felix was without doubt a man of great holiness, truly worthy of being made a priest in happier times. Martin took part in the communion that day. He judged it better to give way for the moment than to ignore the safety of those with a sword hanging over their heads. Even so, he would not confirm his communion by signing his name, though the bishops tried their very hardest to make him. The next day he hurried away from that place. On the way back he was filled with grief and mourning that he had been mixed up, even for an hour, in the evil communion. Not far from a village named Andethanna, remote woods stretch far and wide in deep solitude. There he sat down, while his companions went on a little way ahead of him. He sank into deep thought, by turns accusing and defending the cause of his grief and what he had done. Suddenly an angel stood beside him and said, "Martin, you are right to feel remorse, but you had no other way out of your difficulty. Renew your strength and take up your courage again. uses.sentence: Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel.
uses.paragraph: We did not read them the way you are reading them now. The difference is not what we saw in them but what we did with them. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer was held to it by a rule. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The words were not read once and set aside. They were the grain the mill turned. A man kept praying even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The Apostle's word not I, but the grace of God with me was taught to a monk at the moment he felt his own fasting had done something. At Tours the saint took the Apostle's least of these as the beggar at the gate. And at the election a bystander seized the psalter, read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. So what you are missing is not a key to the text. It is the use the text was put to. You read it to understand it. We said it to feed the wheel that cannot stop turning, and heard it speak into the hour we were standing in.

uses.sentence: Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion.
uses.paragraph: The power claimed by bishops when they made common cause with an emperor's court, and the man we remember is the one who said it was a foul thing. Here is what our record holds. At Treves the bishops had bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, and in Martin alone apostolic authority kept its place. A man and his followers had been condemned as heretics by bishops in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court. The accuser there was himself a bishop. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. He held that it was punishment enough for the bishops to declare men heretics and put them out of the churches, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went, our record says, to protect even heretics themselves. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin pledged that night that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. Afterward he sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.

uses.sentence: The north's power-economy - Martin's felt virtus, the blessed oil and threads, the demon named at exorcism - stands in Sulpitius's Life and Dialogues.
uses.paragraph: The southern teaching - purity of heart as the immediate goal, discretion as its regulator, the eight faults fought in order - stands sentence by sentence in Cassian's two books. The north's power-economy - Martin's felt virtus, the blessed oil and threads, the demon named at exorcism - stands in Sulpitius's Life and Dialogues. Vincent's rule of everywhere-always-all stands in the Commonitory. The grace argument's two-sided teaching, with the field and the husbandman, stands in Conference XIII. Each of those would survive the check on its own ground.
uses.record_text:
Miracle, exorcism, and blessed objects hold together the northern literature. The south's teacher refuses this whole approach on principle.
At Tours, power is something Martin bears, and is known by. He prays over a dead catechumen. He senses that God's power is present, and raises the man back to life (Vita VII). Gallus reports that Martin himself used to say something else, too. He sensed less of that power as bishop than he remembered having before he held the office (Dial. II.4). One of Sulpitius's letters defends that same power against a skeptic. Gennadius, writing later, calls Martin a man famous for signs, wonders, and virtues.
Cassian refuses this on principle. He says plainly that he will not try to tell stories about God's wonders, however many he has witnessed himself. Such stories teach a reader nothing about how to live well (Inst. Pref.). Abbot Nesteros goes further still. No one who declared himself an exorcist before an admiring crowd was ever counted a good monk. Whether the devils obeyed him was beside the point (Conf. XV.7). This is the sentence that sets the two literatures directly against each other. Inside the south itself, Eucherius still admires the Egyptian fathers' visible signs of grace. So the real argument runs between Cassian and Sulpitius, not between south and north as a whole. Neither names the other; whether Cassian's refusal is a veiled answer to Sulpitius is not settled.
This gravity organizes the north's literature completely. The Vita, the Letters, and the Dialogues are all built from acts of power. The north's account of the episcopate, power lost through office, depends on it too. But it rests mostly on one voice, Sulpitius's alone. Gennadius confirms only that Martin was famous for signs, not that power organizes a monk's whole life. Cassian refuses the whole approach outright. For that reason, this record holds virtus as a tensional gravity, not a primary one. It is real and unresolved, resting on one voice rather than broad agreement. It is the steady counter-force that keeps this ecology from being reduced to the south's interior program alone. One house's literature is made of exactly what the other house's teacher says a good monk must never proclaim. It does not organize the whole world. But the world cannot be described without it. This record finds no demonstrated link between this gravity and the grace controversy.
Under institutional pressure the gravity shifts rather than holds steady. Martin felt less power as bishop than as monk, by his own account. He felt a further loss after a forced communion with bishops he distrusted. Office itself, in this literature, registers as a real cost to the saint's body. Under barbarian pressure the gravity is touched only twice, and thinly. At the north's ending, it passed from a living saint's power to a relic's, and to a psalm's.

uses.sentence: One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity.
uses.paragraph: On the island Vincent wrote what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

uses.sentence: Free will always remains in a man, and it is weak, and the help of God is necessary to it every day and hour.
uses.paragraph: We never argued it as a formula, and where Cassian touched it he touched it as Egypt's fathers touched it - as a thing held, not debated. Here is what our record keeps. Among the brethren at Marseilles, Abbot Chaeremon named three stages of the grace by which we are saved: the first kindles our desire toward salvation, the second enables us in the good we wish for, the third preserves us to the end in the virtues. All three are God's gift. And he taught plainly that a newborn has no merits before him - he spoke of "the case even of infants, who have as yet done nothing either good or bad". That is the nearest our record comes to your question's shape: infants with no works of their own, and grace going before every stage. But whether they bear guilt from birth, by what they are rather than what they have done, Cassian does not say. What he does say is this: the Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; he does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and it is grievous blasphemy to think otherwise. Free will always remains in a man, and it is weak, and the help of God is necessary to it every day and hour. How both are true - how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. The inherited guilt as a thing confessed apart from the grace that answers it is not in our record to give you.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the power that "always remains free in man" to "neglect or delight in the grace of God." Real enough that a monk's fasting, watching and labour are truly his and truly required. Weak enough that "the assistance and grace of God are necessary to it every day and hour." Never denied, never sufficient.

use_note.means: Free will meant, for Cassian's Marseilles, a real but weak power that always remains in man, which grace strengthens without removing and which never suffices alone.

uses.sentence: Among the fathers of Egypt only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men.
uses.paragraph: We held what Egypt handed us and never claimed it went back unbroken to the first days. The psalms and the hours had a story. Among the fathers of Egypt only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. They argued whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupted them. One father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel. That is the rule Cassian brought to Gaul as the fathers' own, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. It is a beginning claimed in Egypt, not in Jerusalem. We never said we had it from the apostles. What we said of ourselves is that we received it from the fathers and kept it where Gaul's cold allowed. Egypt was our measure, in the south. At Tours the highest word spoken was different. Martin had the apostles' own power - over death, over demons, over emperors. That named the kind of power the saint showed, not a line of customs kept. And the test of what was legitimate ran through everything we held. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever has been handed down from antiquity is to be held fast. We did not invent a proof that our hours went back to the first believers. We said Egypt gave them to us, and that an angel gave them to Egypt. The authority was in whose they were, not in how old.
uses.record_text: In those days only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. The perfection of the earliest Church still stood unbroken. The burning faith of the few had not yet cooled by being spread among the many. At that time the honored fathers watchfully made plans for those who would come after them. They met to discuss what plan to adopt for daily worship across the whole community of brothers. A dispute might send out a poisonous root of error, or jealousy, or division among those who came after. Each man judged by the measure of his own zeal, paying no heed to how weak others were. Some were for fifty, others for sixty. Some, not satisfied with that number, thought they really ought to go beyond it. They held a holy difference of opinion in their devout debate over the rule of their religious life. It was so great that the hour for their evening service came before the sacred question was settled. One stood up in their midst to sing the Psalms to the Lord. They were all sitting, their minds closely fixed on the words of the singer. He sang eleven Psalms, with prayers placed between them, each verse sung in an even voice. He ended the twelfth with the response "Alleluia." Then he suddenly vanished from the sight of all. At once this ended both their debate and their service. At this the honored assembly of the Fathers understood that, by God's providence, the angel's guidance had set a general rule for the brothers' communities. So they decreed that this number should be kept in both their evening and their night services. What they added, they added simply as extras, by their own decision.

use_note.means: Cassian, in Institutes II, relates the Egyptian tradition that an angel chanting twelve psalms settled the fathers' dispute over how many psalms the offices should hold.

uses.paragraph: At Tours the books served the hours of prayer. uses.sentence: He wills all to be saved, and those who perish, perish against his will - to think otherwise is grievous blasphemy.
uses.paragraph: God, as we held him, is the one who calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. uses.sentence: And he held at the same time that Scripture's authority needs the Church's tradition, because of the great depth of Holy Scripture itself - almost everyone does not understand it in one and the same way, so that the same words are understood differently by different people.
uses.paragraph: On the island Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and sufficient. And he held at the same time that Scripture's authority needs the Church's tradition, because of the great depth of Holy Scripture itself - almost everyone does not understand it in one and the same way, so that the same words are understood differently by different people. What guards against that is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. The whole Church's understanding, not one man's.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

uses.sentence: The whole Church's understanding, not one man's.
uses.paragraph: On the island Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and sufficient. And he held at the same time that Scripture's authority needs the Church's tradition, because of the great depth of Holy Scripture itself - almost everyone does not understand it in one and the same way, so that the same words are understood differently by different people. What guards against that is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. The whole Church's understanding, not one man's.
uses.record_text:
Antiquity, the Fathers, and consent are the test of legitimacy, set against novelty - applied by all three founding voices to monastic custom, doctrine, and cult alike.
Cassian holds that allegiance is owed not to customs a few people have introduced, but to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement (Inst. I.2). He calls his own Institutes not his but the fathers' (Conf. Pref. I). And he holds up, as a warning, the monk who trusted his own judgment over the Elders' tradition and in the end forsook the desert (Conf. II.24).
Vincent holds that the Catholic faith is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all - tested by universality, antiquity, and consent (Comm. ch. 2). He quotes Pope Stephen's own rule that there should be no innovation, nothing but what has been handed down (ch. 6). And he holds that a guardian of doctrine is not an author but a keeper, not a teacher but a disciple, not a leader but a follower (ch. 22).
Sulpitius tells that Martin, asked to venerate a supposed martyr's tomb, would not lend his own authority to popular opinion, because no reliable tradition about it reached back to antiquity (Vita XI).
This same standard also became a battleground. Prosper reports that the Massilians defended their own obstinacy by antiquity; Celestine, as later editors read him, answered that novelty must cease to assail antiquity; and Vincent read that same letter for his own side (Comm. ch. 32). The rule that was meant to settle disputes became, in the grace controversy, one more thing both sides claimed for themselves.

uses.sentence: A citizen threw himself at Martin's knees, Martin was escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and he became a bishop who kept the objects and virtues of a monk.
uses.paragraph: And now the limits. At Tours the saint himself began as a soldier still in the ranks, regarded as a monk though he had not yet professed. A citizen threw himself at Martin's knees, Martin was escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and he became a bishop who kept the objects and virtues of a monk. Whether Tours kept any testing at its own door, no one wrote. Of the island's own reception of a newcomer - a rule kept, a novice received - nothing. Not one man who came to our door left an account of how he was met there.
uses.record_text: The office our monks keep being taken into. A monk "carried off," "escorted under guard," "bound to the long-avoided office," who then keeps "the objects and virtues of a monk" in a see. And at the same time our own formation teaching names the desire for that office as vainglory's suggestion and the devil's pretext.

use_note.means: The monk-bishop meant the office into which monks keep being seized and must never seek, kept with a monk's humility though formation teaching names the wish for it vainglory.
not_for: a bishop as administrator or prelate
monk and bishop as opposed careers, so that the office is a promotion or a sell-out
the papacy or Rome, which sits in gallic.term.apostolic-see-pope
the reluctance as total fact in every house, which is contested in gallic.contested.election-as-capture

uses.sentence: A husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; the crop cannot be ascribed to the man's labour alone, and God does not send rich crops to the idle.
uses.paragraph: His grace goes before our will, helps it, and crowns it. The beginning even of our good thoughts comes from God, who inspires a good will to begin with. We call him not only Saviour but Helper - Saviour because he calls us when we are still unwilling, Helper because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Grace kindles the desire, enables the virtue, and preserves it to the end. A husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; the crop cannot be ascribed to the man's labour alone, and God does not send rich crops to the idle. How God works all things in us and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.record_text:
Then Germanus said: "The reward of our efforts is perfect chastity. It is gained by the earnestness of one's own toil. It seems absurd to us not to credit it mainly to the labor of the man who makes the effort. For suppose, for example, that we see a farmer taking the greatest pains to work the ground. It is foolish not to credit the fruits to his labor."
Chaeremon said: "The farmer may take the greatest pains to work the ground. Even so, he cannot at once credit his crops and their rich fruits to his own labor. He finds that his efforts often come to nothing unless timely rains and a quiet, calm winter help them. God's goodness, then, does not grant these rich crops to lazy farmers who do not work their fields by ploughing them often. For a man should think this over and weigh it with the greatest care. By his own strength he could not have made the very efforts he put in so earnestly out of his desire for wealth. He could have made them only if the Lord's protection and mercy had given him strength for all the work of farming. From this we clearly conclude that the first step comes from God. This is true not only of our actions but also of good thoughts. God puts a good will in us to begin with. He gives us the chance to carry out what we rightly desire. But our part is to follow humbly, day by day, the grace of God that is drawing us."

use_note.means: Cassian records Germanus arguing that effort earns its fruit and Chaeremon answering that a husbandman's labour still needs rain and calm weather from God.
not_for: a settled semi-Pelagian position, when its meaning is contested
the night's scruple that prompted the question, which sits in gallic.quote.germanus-troubled-after-the-nights-teaching
Germanus's objection as Chaeremon's own view

uses.sentence: What a scholar would hold us to is the difference between "Cassian says the fathers taught" and "the fathers taught," between "Sulpitius reports Martin raised a man" and "Martin raised a man," between "Vincent gives a rule" and "the island kept it".
uses.paragraph: What a scholar would hold us to is the difference between "Cassian says the fathers taught" and "the fathers taught," between "Sulpitius reports Martin raised a man" and "Martin raised a man," between "Vincent gives a rule" and "the island kept it". Every place we kept that difference would stand. Every place we blurred it would fall.
uses.record_text: The fathers of Egypt argue whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupts them. One father rises to sing, finishes the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanishes. The number is fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel.

use_note.means: Cassian relays the Egyptian fathers' tale that an angel fixed the daily psalms at twelve by singing the twelfth with Alleluia and vanishing.
not_for: Martin's angels, which sit in gallic.term.angels

uses.sentence: What we feared was not the rack but the cooling, the desertion, and the noon assault on a monk alone in his cell.
uses.paragraph: If the question is whether any of our own people wrote under threat, the answer is no - not in what reaches us. Our age had no persecutor. What we feared was not the rack but the cooling, the desertion, and the noon assault on a monk alone in his cell.
uses.record_text: For us the typical failure of a monk is not apostasy but cooling. The novice who "grow[s] cold in regard to the rule." The renunciant "turned out a deserter or lukewarm." The elders who "pass their old age in a lukewarmness which they contracted in youth." The Sarabaites "cast down into hell by the lukewarmness of their purpose." A disease of temperature that damns.

use_note.means: Lukewarmness meant the monk's characteristic failure, not apostasy but cooling, a disease of temperature that damns and that a grey head does not cure.
not_for: mild disapproval or half-heartedness
burnout as an understandable phase
the specific noonday assault on the cell, which sits in gallic.term.accidie
a word for monks only, when Salvian uses it of ordinary Christians

uses.sentence: Among the brethren at Marseilles, the way a newcomer was received was Egypt's way, set down by Cassian as the fathers' own.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, the way a newcomer was received was Egypt's way, set down by Cassian as the fathers' own. The man lay outside the doors ten days or more, put off and scorned on purpose, to give proof that he meant it. He was searched for a single hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. Then he was given for a year to the elder who kept the gate for guests.
uses.record_text: A monk, for us, is a man who has cut himself off from marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter life in Christ's service. The cut shows in his body and his dwelling. But at Tours a soldier still in the ranks could be "regarded as a monk," and so could a bishop in his see.

use_note.means: A monk meant a man cut off from marriage, kin, property and the world for stricter service of Christ, a name a soldier or bishop could bear at Tours.
not_for: a cloistered professional religious under a written Rule and an abbot
someone who by definition is not a soldier, a bishop or a city dweller
Benedictine or later medieval monasticism
why monks became bishops, which sits in gallic.term.monk-bishop

uses.sentence: If one was found hidden, he was not received.
uses.paragraph: Then he was searched. Before he was admitted they checked whether he had kept back a single coin. If one was found hidden, he was not received.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the newly received monk as Egypt receives him. Ten days or more at the door "of set purpose repelled and scorned," searched for a hidden coin, stripped and reclothed "by the Abbot's hands," lodged a year under the guest-Elder, then handed to a dean over ten and taught "the alphabet ... in the direction of perfection." And Cassian's own admission: no one in our monasteries has kept it up "unbroken even for a year."

use_note.means: The junior meant the monk newly received as Egypt receives him, scorned at the door and taught to conquer his wishes, a standard Cassian says Gallic houses did not keep.
not_for: a Benedictine novitiate with a defined year and vows
novice as simply any beginner
the scorning at the door as hazing or abuse
a Tours grade, where disciples appear but no probationary rank, which sits in gallic.term.disciple-master

uses.sentence: Yet Martin himself, on a question touching whether a tradition had come down from antiquity, consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics, and would not honour a tomb where no steady tradition supported it.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the record is one named man - Martin, master and bishop both, who kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office. Authority rested where the power was felt. He needed no title. Sulpitius calls him "our master" and says it was unlawful to do anything but acquiesce to him. His disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Yet Martin himself, on a question touching whether a tradition had come down from antiquity, consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics, and would not honour a tomb where no steady tradition supported it. One of those presbyters was Brictio, whom Martin had raised from boyhood and who stormed into the courtyard in a fury. The man had sat down on his wooden seat one day, and Brictio came raging that he was holier than the master who brought him up, calling his visions ridiculous fancies and dreaming that he himself deserved the episcopate. Martin held that demons were driving him, but said he would bear with Brictio the way Christ bore with Judas. He would not remove him. That presbyter's rank came from somewhere, not from Martin alone, but where and how the record does not say.

uses.sentence: What we held was received, not invented.
uses.paragraph: What we held was received, not invented. The customs of the monasteries were the fathers' own, brought from Egypt, not ours. The faith was what had been believed everywhere, always, by all. We were keepers, not authors - disciples, not teachers - followers, not leaders. That grammar of reception runs through everything: the psalter's number came from an angel the fathers received it from, not from us; the office was not sought but seized; and at the moment a man felt his labour had accomplished something, our discipline taught him to say Not I, but the grace of God with me.

uses.sentence: A presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood stormed into the courtyard, called the master's visions ridiculous fancies, and Martin bore with him afterward the way Christ bore with Judas.
uses.paragraph: So leadership among us was not established. It was capture, and then it was patience. A presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood stormed into the courtyard, called the master's visions ridiculous fancies, and Martin bore with him afterward the way Christ bore with Judas. That is the shape of authority in our record: fled, overtaken, and keeping a monk's humility inside the office it could not refuse.
uses.record_text: A presbyter Martin raised from boyhood storms into the courtyard. He calls his master's visions ridiculous fancies, then repents within the hour. Martin will not remove him, saying he bears with Brictio the way Christ bore with Judas.

use_note.means: Gallus relates that Brictio, raised by Martin, stormed at him and called his visions ridiculous fancies, repented within the hour, and was borne with as Christ bore Judas.
not_for: a neutral report of Brictio's case, when it comes from men hostile to him

uses.sentence: Every thought was laid bare to the senior.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles leadership was the fathers' structure, received from Egypt. Cassian handed us not a written rule of his own but the customs of the monasteries he had seen kept there, as they were delivered by the Fathers. A congregation was governed by the direction of a single Elder, called Abbot - the Egyptian fathers' own title. Under him were deans, each over ten brothers. Every thought was laid bare to the senior. The junior had no cell key of his own; he could not go out without leave; and it was the Abbot's hands that stripped a newcomer of his old clothes and dressed him in the house's dress. Where that Abbot's own authority came from - election, appointment, seniority - Cassian never says. He gives us the Egyptian fathers' unanimous decision on customs, not the mechanism by which one house chose its own.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the practice of laying every "itching thought" bare to the senior as soon as it arises. It is "the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection." The elders' rule: "a thought is from the devil if we are ashamed to disclose it." So "a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment that it is discovered."

use_note.means: Disclosure of thoughts meant laying every rising thought bare to the senior before any deed, the first lesson of Cassian's monastic life and not the later sacrament.
not_for: sacramental confession of sins to a priest with absolution
therapy or optional spiritual accountability
public penance for a committed fault, which sits in gallic.term.penance-satisfaction
a documented Gallic practice, when whether any Gallic house kept it is unrecorded

uses.sentence: The formation that actually passed in a house in Gaul was by example, by the books read in the cell, and by watching the man.
uses.paragraph: So what we hold is Egypt's order, written for Gaul, and Cassian's own admission that we did not keep it. The formation that actually passed in a house in Gaul was by example, by the books read in the cell, and by watching the man. How the watching worked, day by day, our record does not say.
uses.record_text: How formation passes from one person to another among us. A disciple is made by watching - and, later, by reading - a named man whose life is held up as the thing to copy. Our books exist to be that example when the man himself is absent.

use_note.means: Example meant formation by copying a named man, seen or read, which is why the books of this world are Lives.
not_for: an illustration in an argument
a role model freely chosen and admired from a distance
a particular exemplar's deeds, which sit in gallic.term.virtus
the historicity of any one story, which the story records handle

uses.sentence: The miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into the wheel.
uses.paragraph: Your mind is a mill turned by a stream, and the wheel cannot stop turning. That is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of it. Thoughts will come - a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. The miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into the wheel.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, thoughts are the raw material of the interior struggle. "It is impossible for the mind not to be approached by thoughts, but it is in the power of every earnest man either to admit them or to reject them." They come "from God, from the devil, and from ourselves." The mind is a mill-wheel that must grind something; the miller decides "whether he will have wheat or barley or darnel ground by it."

use_note.means: Thoughts meant the raw material of the interior struggle, which cannot stop arriving from God, the devil or ourselves, the monk answering for which he admits.
not_for: intrusive thoughts as symptoms to be managed
the mind as a private space where nothing is a fault
