uses.sentence: The canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough.
uses.paragraph: The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough. And it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness says Jesus sought the unpitied, citing Martin's cloak, the guest received as Christ and grace calling the unwilling, while naming its thin personal testimony.
not_for: a personal conversion testimony from anyone but Martin, which the record lacks
evidence that Gallic houses broke fasts for guests, which Cassian does not say
a settled reading of Conference XIII on grace, which is contested
who Christ was and what his death meant, which sit in gallic.dw.the-christ-who-bears-the-wounds

uses.sentence: What we never settled, on purpose, was how God's will toward all and a man's own perishing both stay true.
uses.paragraph: What we never settled, on purpose, was how God's will toward all and a man's own perishing both stay true. Free will always remains in a man to neglect or delight in the grace of God. Grace goes before, works with the will, and crowns it; and still our effort is required. How both are true cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.
uses.record_text:
Human effort and free choice are real, and they matter. This world argues that point under pressure from Augustine's own later teaching on grace.
Cassian's own text states the position directly. He gives it through the teaching he attributes to Abbot Chaeremon. God's grace always works together with a person's own will, for that will's own good. But it sometimes waits on some real effort from the person before it is given (Conf. XIII.13). To deny that God wants everyone saved, and not just some, Chaeremon says, would be a grave blasphemy (Conf. XIII.7). Neither side of the argument should be pushed too far, Chaeremon warns. Exactly how grace and free will fit together, in the end, is a question human reason cannot fully answer (Conf. XIII.11, XIII.18). Elsewhere, Cassian's own manual for monks, in its climactic book, gives plain advice. A monk who feels he is making progress should credit it all to God's grace, and not to himself (Inst. XII.9).
What the wider Church heard about this teaching came mostly at second hand. Augustine himself reports that the Gallic monks he is answering already grant one point: that God's grace goes ahead of the human will. But they remain unsettled on the question of predestination. That is a report from the other side, not this world's own voice. What is known of Rome's own reply survives only at a distance - Prosper's appeal to the Pope, Celestine's letter to the Gallic bishops, a Roman critique of Cassian's own thirteenth Conference. None of it comes from a text this world wrote itself; it comes through a modern editor's own account of that history. Gennadius, writing on his own, confirms only that a dispute between Cassian and Prosper existed at all. At Tours, there is simply nothing on this question. The corpus there closed before it was ever raised.
At Lérins, the current runs the other way, though how far Vincent himself took part is genuinely disputed. He quotes Pope Celestine's own words, that novelty must give way to old and settled teaching. He reads those words as backing his own side. But nothing in his surviving text names Augustine, or the fight itself, outright.
This argument is Cassian's own, within this world's own voices. No other Native voice in this world independently holds it. Yet it matters enormously wherever it appears. Several other parts of this world's own literature depend on it. It turned one whole Conference, out of twenty-four, into a direct answer to a crisis in formation. And it explains a great deal of what survives about Prosper, Celestine, and a Roman critique of Cassian himself. But it does not appear evenly across this world's whole span. Tours has nothing to say about it, for reasons of plain timing, not disagreement. For that reason, this record calls it a supporting idea at the level of the whole world. Within the southern house alone, though, it is treated as the leading concern. The evidence for the position is strong. Yet its reach across the whole world stays narrow. That gap is itself a real and disclosed tension in how this record is classified. A reader should not mistake the modest classification for any doubt about what Cassian and Chaeremon actually taught.
Under pressure from Rome, the argument grew stronger, and who carried it changed too. It began as monks writing for other monks. It ended, a generation later, with a bishop, trained at Lérins, writing at the order of a church council. Inside this world's own literature, though, it began as something much simpler. It was a remedy for the pride of a monk who feels, at last, that he is making progress - offered long before anyone outside gave it any name at all.

use_note.means: Human effort and free choice are held real and to matter while grace goes before and crowns them, argued under Augustine's pressure in a relation Cassian says reason cannot grasp.
not_for: a settled semi-Pelagian position

uses.sentence: Everything, we said - and proved the claim by the life the brethren kept.
uses.paragraph: Everything, we said - and proved the claim by the life the brethren kept. Among the brethren at Marseilles a man was stripped of his own clothes by the abbot's hands and dressed in the clothing of the house. That is the sign, not the whole list. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, named three renunciations, and giving up one's goods was only the first. Leaving behind bodily wealth and riches - possessions, kin, the life one had in the world - is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the man who has renounced. The second renunciation is of habits, vices, and the mind's former affections - the whole interior road of the faults. The third is drawing the mind away from all present and visible things to contemplate only what is to come. So the claim was this: marriage, property, honours, secular business, kin. Martin was a soldier in Caesar's service who left it at a donative, saying he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight. The fathers remembered a man who fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that compelled turning into a willing one. And Salvian, who wrote from one of the houses at Marseilles, named those who had taken our way of life as the ones who chose to be lowly, poor, and unesteemed.
uses.record_text: The act that makes a monk: "nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification," by which, as Pinufius says, the monk is dead to the world "and its deeds and desires." In the south's received teaching it has three stages. Giving up one's goods, "of what is not our own," is only the first, and "is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant."

use_note.means: Renunciation meant the act that makes a monk, a death to the world of which giving up goods is only the first and easiest of three stages.
not_for: giving things up as the whole monastic act
a heroic once-for-all rejection of society
the day of entry, which sits in gallic.term.conversion
the baptismal renunciation of the devil, which is Salvian's referent

uses.sentence: The one Egyptian bishop Cassian tells of, Archebius, had been carried off from the anchorites and called it expulsion from the life as unworthy.
uses.paragraph: Both houses held one thing the same. The office of bishop was not sought but seized - a man who left the world did not leave the Church, and the churches came for him. Martin was lured out by a lie and escorted under guard. Honoratus on the island fled, and the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive. The one Egyptian bishop Cassian tells of, Archebius, had been carried off from the anchorites and called it expulsion from the life as unworthy. Our own teaching made wanting the office a mark of vainglory and cold pride. Yet bishops were the ones who ordained, judged doctrine, and held councils - and Martin would not sit with them after Trier.
uses.record_text:
This world holds Egypt up as the standard of real monastic life. But the two houses relate to that standard in opposite ways.
In the south, the tie is receptive. Bishop Castor wanted the customs of the East, and especially of Egypt, set up in a province of Gaul that had no monasteries at all. Cassian promises to fix anything founded on one person's own whim, rather than on the Egyptian rule. He will adapt the letter of that rule only where Gaul's climate or circumstances make it truly impossible (Inst. Pref.). Gallic monks are told to take the authors of the Conferences into their own cells, as living teachers (Conf. Pref. III). At Lérins, Eucherius names two Egyptian fathers as the pattern of a life already lived, in effect, in heaven.
In the north, the tie is comparative, even competitive. Gennadius says plainly that the Dialogues set the life of the Eastern monks side by side with the life of Martin. One speaker in the Dialogues concedes to another that Martin surpasses every hermit and solitary of the East. Another passage sends word all the way to Egypt itself. However proud Egypt is of its many saints, Europe need not yield to it, or to all of Asia, since Europe has Martin alone. Gaul is the poorer, colder partner in this comparison.
Both houses organize themselves around the same point: Egypt, as the standard of real monastic life. But they differ in kind. The south receives that standard as a rule to keep. The north measures itself against it as a rival to match. This split shows up everywhere the idea is tested. It repeats across every voice in this world's own literature. The Institutes' whole structure, the Conferences' whole frame, and the shape of the Dialogues all depend on it. In the south, formation itself is nothing but this act of reception. In the north, the fit is only partial. It explains the north's competitive language and the south's own talk of adapting to climate. It explains why Cassian's own text is, at once, desert monasticism's Latin transmission and this world's own founding literature. And it holds up across both houses, in these two different modes, wherever it meets this world's other core ideas. Both halves rest on strong, direct evidence. So this record finds no real doubt about the finding itself. The only open question is what it means for whether this is one world or two - and this record leaves that question open.
The tie to Egypt held steady across this world's whole span. But what Egypt was needed for kept changing. Before Cassian ever wrote, Tours answered the Egyptian standard with rivalry. Marseilles and Lérins answered it, a generation later, with reception and careful adaptation. Once the fight over grace broke out, the receptive mode hardened further. Egypt itself became an authority to plead against Augustine and Rome - the whole line of orthodox teachers on the heart's own perfection, as Cassian frames it. Under the barbarian collapse, Egypt survives as little more than a byword for holiness, in the one place Salvian mentions it. The standard itself never moved. What moved was what this world needed it for.

use_note.means: Egypt stands as the measure of real monastic life, received in the south as a rule from the fathers and matched at Tours by a saint said to outdo it.

uses.sentence: At a donative before battle he told Caesar he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight, offered to stand unarmed before the enemy line, and the enemy surrendered before morning.
uses.paragraph: We kept one story of how it began, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen; he stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. At a donative before battle he told Caesar he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight, offered to stand unarmed before the enemy line, and the enemy surrendered before morning. That was his road. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island.

uses.sentence: And the one Egyptian bishop Cassian chose to tell us of had been carried off from the anchorites and complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it.
uses.paragraph: Leadership was not established among us; it overtook the man who fled it. At Tours a monk was lured from his monastery by a citizen pretending his wife was ill, escorted to the city under a kind of guard, and made bishop though some of the bishops summoned for it said his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, and his hair disgusting. Then the new bishop kept a monk's habits inside the office - the same humility in his heart, sitting on a rude little stool such as those in use by the lowest of servants. Each of our houses told its founder's rise the same way. On the island the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive. And the one Egyptian bishop Cassian chose to tell us of had been carried off from the anchorites and complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it.
uses.record_text:
Renunciation kept producing bishops. Men renounced the world to become monks, and then the office of bishop overtook them.

Martin shows the pattern. He kept up the position of a bishop properly, yet he did not lay aside the aims and virtues of a monk.

Of the eighty disciples at Marmoutier, numbers were afterwards made bishops (Vita, ch. X). The disciples were trained after their master's example.

Everything Cassian wrote was addressed to bishops, or to men who became bishops. His formation writing was for a bishop's new monastery. Honoratus moves from monk to bishop between two of his dedications (Conferences, prefaces II and III).

Archebius is the Egyptian counter-case. He counted his appointment as expulsion from the monastic system, as unworthy of it. Cassian carried his story west (Conferences XI.2).

Hilary of Arles preached on Honoratus in the south's own Latin. He tells how the priest's headband fastened on a man who fled from it, and how the honor came to him. The Latin is there in the source, but this English wording of it is rated Inferential/Thin.

What sets this world apart is a seminary that looked like a monastery. Every primary voice attests this pattern, and Gennadius confirms it independently. It holds in both north and south, more strongly than any other pattern in this world. It is the only one that a Latin insider in the south, Hilary, attests apart from Cassian.

It explains three things. The withdrawal stayed close to the city. The grace argument reached Rome. The ending was a change in how the institution spoke, not a collapse.

The controversy over grace did not break the pattern. It strengthened it into the Lérins network of bishops. Celestine's letter named Venerius, Cassian's own bishop, first (Gibson's editorial introduction). It warned that priests ought not to teach so as to invade the bishops' rights.

By the 470s a bishop formed at Lérins, Faustus, carried the argument at the commission of synods. Under barbarian pressure this was the institution left standing. Gennadius, writing from the same city about 495, reports two monasteries still standing.

These pressures did not change the pattern. They made it the way the world ended.

uses.sentence: Whatever has been handed down from antiquity is to be held fast.
uses.paragraph: We held what Egypt handed us and never claimed it went back unbroken to the first days. The psalms and the hours had a story. Among the fathers of Egypt only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. They argued whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupted them. One father rose to sing, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The number was fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel. That is the rule Cassian brought to Gaul as the fathers' own, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. It is a beginning claimed in Egypt, not in Jerusalem. We never said we had it from the apostles. What we said of ourselves is that we received it from the fathers and kept it where Gaul's cold allowed. Egypt was our measure, in the south. At Tours the highest word spoken was different. Martin had the apostles' own power - over death, over demons, over emperors. That named the kind of power the saint showed, not a line of customs kept. And the test of what was legitimate ran through everything we held. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever has been handed down from antiquity is to be held fast. We did not invent a proof that our hours went back to the first believers. We said Egypt gave them to us, and that an angel gave them to Egypt. The authority was in whose they were, not in how old.
uses.record_text: The axis on which all three of our founding voices judge what is legitimate. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever "has been handed down" from antiquity is to be held fast. "If novelty is profane, antiquity is sacred."

use_note.means: Novelty and antiquity named the axis on which all three founding voices judged legitimacy: the new is suspect for being new, and what was handed down is held fast.

uses.sentence: You are reading it as though you had to settle it yourself, and we were not formed that way.
uses.paragraph: The second is this. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. We were taught not to invent, but to hold what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. That meant Scripture was heard through the fathers, not against them. When a man at our door came in troubled by one sentence - that striving cannot make a man master of the good - the elder answered him with the husbandman and the rain, and told him the initiative comes from God. The question was about what Paul said; the answer was in the elder's mouth, not on the page. You are reading it as though you had to settle it yourself, and we were not formed that way.

"Abbot" is the title of every Egyptian father Cassian reports. At Tours the same place is held by one master, Martin, who himself consults "his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics."

uses.sentence: The same grammar ran through everything we held.
uses.paragraph: The same grammar ran through everything we held. Cassian said we ought to give loyalty without hesitation to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement, not to customs a few people have introduced. At Tours the saint would not honour a tomb without a steady tradition from antiquity. Pope Stephen's rule was kept as a standing word: let nothing new be brought in, nothing except what has been handed down.
uses.record_text:
Antiquity, the Fathers, and consent are the test of legitimacy, set against novelty - applied by all three founding voices to monastic custom, doctrine, and cult alike.
Cassian holds that allegiance is owed not to customs a few people have introduced, but to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have passed on by common agreement (Inst. I.2). He calls his own Institutes not his but the fathers' (Conf. Pref. I). And he holds up, as a warning, the monk who trusted his own judgment over the Elders' tradition and in the end forsook the desert (Conf. II.24).
Vincent holds that the Catholic faith is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all - tested by universality, antiquity, and consent (Comm. ch. 2). He quotes Pope Stephen's own rule that there should be no innovation, nothing but what has been handed down (ch. 6). And he holds that a guardian of doctrine is not an author but a keeper, not a teacher but a disciple, not a leader but a follower (ch. 22).
Sulpitius tells that Martin, asked to venerate a supposed martyr's tomb, would not lend his own authority to popular opinion, because no reliable tradition about it reached back to antiquity (Vita XI).
This same standard also became a battleground. Prosper reports that the Massilians defended their own obstinacy by antiquity; Celestine, as later editors read him, answered that novelty must cease to assail antiquity; and Vincent read that same letter for his own side (Comm. ch. 32). The rule that was meant to settle disputes became, in the grace controversy, one more thing both sides claimed for themselves.

use_note.means: Antiquity, the fathers and consent are the test of legitimacy against novelty in custom, doctrine and cult, applied by all three founding voices though they never cite one another.

uses.sentence: What the reading was for is held at the hours.
uses.paragraph: What the reading was for is held at the hours. At the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles. At the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid. At the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. That is what we confessed, at the hours, together.
uses.record_text: Who was Jesus to us? At Tours the answer is a story. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also the one we met in the poor. Tours remembered a beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the same thing was taught in the fathers' words, from Egypt: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What did he teach that mattered most among us? That what is done to the least of these is done to him - the words Sulpitius set beside the cloak. And that without him we can do nothing - the sentence Cassian sets under every virtue a monk feels he has gained, beside the Apostle's not I, but the grace of God with me. What did his death mean to us? We wrote no treatise on it. We kept its hours. Cassian handed us from Egypt the reason for the hours of prayer: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. What we believed about the resurrection is held there too: dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

use_note.means: This witness says this world knew Jesus as the crucified one met in the poor, kept his death and rising at the hours, and preached grace drawing the unwilling.

uses.sentence: At Tours, a wooden cell for the saint and caves for the brethren.
uses.paragraph: I cannot say. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Where we gathered is named by place, never described as a building. At Tours, a wooden cell for the saint and caves for the brethren. The island where Honoratus went and Vincent dwelt is a harbour, a camp of God, and a place no one would live before he came - never floor, wall, or roof. Cassian wrote for a bishop founding a new monastery in a province that did not have one, and he wrote of Egypt's customs, not of Gaul's construction. Where the brethren stood to sing the twelve psalms that an angel fixed for the fathers, what covered them or what they stood on - that is not in our record. The one procession we are told of moved on the road, between Tours and the monastery, with two thousand monks and a choir of virgins following the body. If you dug, we could not tell you what you would find.
uses.record_text: Foreknowing his death, Martin goes to make peace among quarrelling clerics. He sickens, and refuses straw for his bed of sackcloth and ashes rather than set his disciples a softer example. He is carried to burial by two thousand monks, old men and young soldiers of Christ, and a choir of virgins.

uses.sentence: Our record of the hours kept among us comes from Cassian's own hand, written for a bishop's new monastery: the reason for the third hour, the sixth, the ninth, and the rest, drawn from what he learned in Egypt.
uses.paragraph: Our record of the hours kept among us comes from Cassian's own hand, written for a bishop's new monastery: the reason for the third hour, the sixth, the ninth, and the rest, drawn from what he learned in Egypt. The fathers taught that the number of psalms, twelve at evening and twelve at night, was fixed by an angel's own singing - not invented by men, but received. At Tours the hours themselves are not described, but Martin's practice is: prayer without a gap, like a blacksmith who beats his anvil between strokes.

At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. uses.sentence: The remedy is to stay.
uses.paragraph: Among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set down what he had received from Egypt, the day was built around the hours and the cell. Twelve psalms at evening, twelve at night, brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. Between them, labour in the cell without ceasing - basket-work, rope-work, whatever the hands can do while the heart says the psalms learned by heart. The wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. A brother may not go out without the elder's leave. Every thought is laid bare to the senior the moment it arises, before any deed. At the sixth hour comes the danger: a monk hates his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set. The remedy is to stay. All of it serves one mark: purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, at which every fast and vigil is aimed.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the sixth fault, "which we may term weariness or distress of heart," "especially trying to solitaries." The noon assault that "produces dislike of the place, disgust with the cell, and disdain and contempt of the brethren." It makes the monk gaze at the sun "as if it was too slow in setting," and dresses his escape as pious duty until "the soldier of Christ becomes a runaway from His service, and a deserter."

use_note.means: Accidie meant, for Cassian's Marseilles, the noonday weariness that assails a monk in his cell as the sixth fault and ends in desertion unless he stays.

uses.sentence: Thoughts will come - from God, from the devil, from ourselves - and a man cannot keep them from rising.
uses.paragraph: Yes. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of the mind as a mill that cannot stop turning. Thoughts will come - from God, from the devil, from ourselves - and a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. The mind is a wheel turned by a stream, and the miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, thoughts are the raw material of the interior struggle. "It is impossible for the mind not to be approached by thoughts, but it is in the power of every earnest man either to admit them or to reject them." They come "from God, from the devil, and from ourselves." The mind is a mill-wheel that must grind something; the miller decides "whether he will have wheat or barley or darnel ground by it."

use_note.means: Thoughts meant the raw material of the interior struggle, which cannot stop arriving from God, the devil or ourselves, the monk answering for which he admits.

uses.sentence: One of those presbyters was Brictio, whom Martin had raised from boyhood and who stormed into the courtyard in a fury.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the record is one named man - Martin, master and bishop both, who kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office. Authority rested where the power was felt. He needed no title. Sulpitius calls him "our master" and says it was unlawful to do anything but acquiesce to him. His disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Yet Martin himself, on a question touching whether a tradition had come down from antiquity, consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics, and would not honour a tomb where no steady tradition supported it. One of those presbyters was Brictio, whom Martin had raised from boyhood and who stormed into the courtyard in a fury. The man had sat down on his wooden seat one day, and Brictio came raging that he was holier than the master who brought him up, calling his visions ridiculous fancies and dreaming that he himself deserved the episcopate. Martin held that demons were driving him, but said he would bear with Brictio the way Christ bore with Judas. He would not remove him. That presbyter's rank came from somewhere, not from Martin alone, but where and how the record does not say.
uses.record_text: A presbyter Martin raised from boyhood storms into the courtyard. He calls his master's visions ridiculous fancies, then repents within the hour. Martin will not remove him, saying he bears with Brictio the way Christ bore with Judas.

use_note.means: Gallus relates that Brictio, raised by Martin, stormed at him and called his visions ridiculous fancies, repented within the hour, and was borne with as Christ bore Judas.

uses.sentence: The grace argument's two-sided teaching, with the field and the husbandman, stands in Conference XIII.
uses.paragraph: The southern teaching - purity of heart as the immediate goal, discretion as its regulator, the eight faults fought in order - stands sentence by sentence in Cassian's two books. The north's power-economy - Martin's felt virtus, the blessed oil and threads, the demon named at exorcism - stands in Sulpitius's Life and Dialogues. Vincent's rule of everywhere-always-all stands in the Commonitory. The grace argument's two-sided teaching, with the field and the husbandman, stands in Conference XIII. Each of those would survive the check on its own ground.
uses.record_text:
Then Germanus said: "The reward of our efforts is perfect chastity. It is gained by the earnestness of one's own toil. It seems absurd to us not to credit it mainly to the labor of the man who makes the effort. For suppose, for example, that we see a farmer taking the greatest pains to work the ground. It is foolish not to credit the fruits to his labor."
Chaeremon said: "The farmer may take the greatest pains to work the ground. Even so, he cannot at once credit his crops and their rich fruits to his own labor. He finds that his efforts often come to nothing unless timely rains and a quiet, calm winter help them. God's goodness, then, does not grant these rich crops to lazy farmers who do not work their fields by ploughing them often. For a man should think this over and weigh it with the greatest care. By his own strength he could not have made the very efforts he put in so earnestly out of his desire for wealth. He could have made them only if the Lord's protection and mercy had given him strength for all the work of farming. From this we clearly conclude that the first step comes from God. This is true not only of our actions but also of good thoughts. God puts a good will in us to begin with. He gives us the chance to carry out what we rightly desire. But our part is to follow humbly, day by day, the grace of God that is drawing us."

use_note.means: Cassian records Germanus arguing that effort earns its fruit and Chaeremon answering that a husbandman's labour still needs rain and calm weather from God.
not_for: a settled semi-Pelagian position, when its meaning is contested

uses.sentence: The initiative, before a good will even rises, comes from God.
uses.paragraph: What we held about how a man comes to faith is this: the beginning of it is not ours. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught, and Cassian set it down, that God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. The initiative, before a good will even rises, comes from God. That is not the whole of it, but it is the first thing: the drawing comes before the turning.
uses.record_text:
Human effort and free choice are real, and they matter. This world argues that point under pressure from Augustine's own later teaching on grace.
Cassian's own text states the position directly. He gives it through the teaching he attributes to Abbot Chaeremon. God's grace always works together with a person's own will, for that will's own good. But it sometimes waits on some real effort from the person before it is given (Conf. XIII.13). To deny that God wants everyone saved, and not just some, Chaeremon says, would be a grave blasphemy (Conf. XIII.7). Neither side of the argument should be pushed too far, Chaeremon warns. Exactly how grace and free will fit together, in the end, is a question human reason cannot fully answer (Conf. XIII.11, XIII.18). Elsewhere, Cassian's own manual for monks, in its climactic book, gives plain advice. A monk who feels he is making progress should credit it all to God's grace, and not to himself (Inst. XII.9).
What the wider Church heard about this teaching came mostly at second hand. Augustine himself reports that the Gallic monks he is answering already grant one point: that God's grace goes ahead of the human will. But they remain unsettled on the question of predestination. That is a report from the other side, not this world's own voice. What is known of Rome's own reply survives only at a distance - Prosper's appeal to the Pope, Celestine's letter to the Gallic bishops, a Roman critique of Cassian's own thirteenth Conference. None of it comes from a text this world wrote itself; it comes through a modern editor's own account of that history. Gennadius, writing on his own, confirms only that a dispute between Cassian and Prosper existed at all. At Tours, there is simply nothing on this question. The corpus there closed before it was ever raised.
At Lérins, the current runs the other way, though how far Vincent himself took part is genuinely disputed. He quotes Pope Celestine's own words, that novelty must give way to old and settled teaching. He reads those words as backing his own side. But nothing in his surviving text names Augustine, or the fight itself, outright.
This argument is Cassian's own, within this world's own voices. No other Native voice in this world independently holds it. Yet it matters enormously wherever it appears. Several other parts of this world's own literature depend on it. It turned one whole Conference, out of twenty-four, into a direct answer to a crisis in formation. And it explains a great deal of what survives about Prosper, Celestine, and a Roman critique of Cassian himself. But it does not appear evenly across this world's whole span. Tours has nothing to say about it, for reasons of plain timing, not disagreement. For that reason, this record calls it a supporting idea at the level of the whole world. Within the southern house alone, though, it is treated as the leading concern. The evidence for the position is strong. Yet its reach across the whole world stays narrow. That gap is itself a real and disclosed tension in how this record is classified. A reader should not mistake the modest classification for any doubt about what Cassian and Chaeremon actually taught.
Under pressure from Rome, the argument grew stronger, and who carried it changed too. It began as monks writing for other monks. It ended, a generation later, with a bishop, trained at Lérins, writing at the order of a church council. Inside this world's own literature, though, it began as something much simpler. It was a remedy for the pride of a monk who feels, at last, that he is making progress - offered long before anyone outside gave it any name at all.

uses.sentence: Vincent, on the island, set it down plainly.
uses.paragraph: Vincent, on the island, set it down plainly. The canon of Scripture is complete, and more than enough. But Scripture still needs the Church's own line of interpretation, because nearly everyone reads it his own way. So within the Catholic Church itself we take care to hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part of the Church, or a novelty, or a few men dissent, we prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council's decree, or the ancients collated - the doctors whose agreed writings form "a consentient council". A single teacher, be he a bishop, be he a Confessor, be he a martyr, holds only a private fancy of his own.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

use_note.means: The rule meant Vincent's test of the faith, what has been believed everywhere, always, by all, preferring the whole, the old and consent to the part, the new and few.

uses.sentence: Those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.paragraph: And he was the one without whom we can do nothing. When a monk feels his fasting has accomplished something, he is taught to say *Not I, but the grace of God with me*. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. He calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. Those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness says Jesus sought the unpitied, citing Martin's cloak, the guest received as Christ and grace calling the unwilling, while naming its thin personal testimony.

uses.sentence: At Tours, the same word named what a robber or a rustic did when he turned to Christ.
uses.paragraph: The word we had for turning to the monastic life was *conversion*. At Marseilles, it named the day a man turned from the world to the stricter service: "the early days of their conversion were so bright"; a murderer's "compulsory conversion" turned "into a voluntary one". At Tours, the same word named what a robber or a rustic did when he turned to Christ. It was the act of cutting oneself off - from marriage, from kin, from property, from the life of the world - for Christ's service. A soldier could wear the name while still in the ranks.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, "conversion" is not a change of religion. It is the act of turning to the monastic life: "the early days of their conversion were so bright"; a murderer's "compulsory conversion" turned "into a voluntary one." At Tours the same English word names what a robber or a rustic does when he turns to Christ.

use_note.means: Conversion meant, at Marseilles, the act of turning to the monastic life and not a change of religion, while at Tours it meant turning to Christ.

uses.sentence: The books exist to be that example when the man himself is absent.
uses.paragraph: That is the order Cassian wrote. And in the same book he said plainly that no one who joined our monasteries kept that perseverance unbroken even for a year. So the formation passed by watching a named man. Martin's eighty disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Cassian wrote the conferences so that our monks might receive the fathers into their cells, talking with them after a fashion by daily questions and answers. The books exist to be that example when the man himself is absent.
uses.record_text: How formation passes from one person to another among us. A disciple is made by watching - and, later, by reading - a named man whose life is held up as the thing to copy. Our books exist to be that example when the man himself is absent.

use_note.means: Example meant formation by copying a named man, seen or read, which is why the books of this world are Lives.
not_for: an illustration in an argument
a role model freely chosen and admired from a distance

uses.sentence: It speaks of turning, of being drawn by grace while still ignorant and unwilling, and of a renunciation that is figured as crucifixion.
uses.paragraph: And for the monk the turning had stages. Renunciation - death to the world and its desires - came in three acts, not one. Giving up goods was only the first and easiest. Our record does not speak of being born again. It speaks of turning, of being drawn by grace while still ignorant and unwilling, and of a renunciation that is figured as crucifixion.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, mortification is the state of being dead to the world and its desires, figured as crucifixion. "As then one who is crucified no longer has the power of moving or turning his limbs in any direction as he pleases, so we also ought to affix our wishes and desires." It is read into the monk's very clothes. The girdle of dead skin "signifies that he bears about the mortification of those members in which are contained the seeds of lust."

use_note.means: Mortification meant being already dead to the world as a crucified man cannot move his limbs, the state every practice assumes, worn in the girdle and the tunic.

uses.sentence: The whole was built to serve one aim: prayer that never stops, the way a blacksmith beats his anvil between strokes.
uses.paragraph: A mill-wheel fed and a body held still - that is the shape of a day among the brethren at Marseilles, as Cassian set it down from Egypt. The whole was built to serve one aim: prayer that never stops, the way a blacksmith beats his anvil between strokes. Twelve psalms at evening, learned by heart, and twelve at night - the number an angel fixed when the fathers of Egypt could not settle it themselves. Between those hours, labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. The psalms at the work, too. A man rarely went out except for prayer. The work itself was held sacred: a cook who left three lentils on the floor during his week of duty was judged a pilferer of the Lord's property and suspended from prayer until he did penance, because everything in the house is consecrated to God. That whole order was Egypt's, received from the fathers, not ours. Cassian wrote it out for a bishop's new house and said plainly that no one who joined our monasteries had kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even for a year. What a house in Gaul did instead, day by day, he never wrote.
uses.record_text: Two things at once. At Marseilles, a fixed "canonical system" of psalms and prayers at set hours, received from Egypt as "brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel." At both Tours and Marseilles, the aim that system serves: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith "in the midst of their work" beats his anvil.

use_note.means: Unceasing prayer meant the aim of every monk at Tours and Marseilles, served at Marseilles by a received Egyptian system of psalms at fixed hours said to be an angel's.

uses.sentence: He looked to the decrees of councils - legitimate because they innovate nothing - as guards of the faith.
uses.paragraph: Who settled it? Nobody, when it touched the hardest places. Hear the shape our own record gives it. Vincent, on the island, gave a test: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and the consent of the ancients. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated. He looked to the decrees of councils - legitimate because they innovate nothing - as guards of the faith. That is the theory. What our record shows is a fracture that ran past it.
uses.record_text: The axis on which all three of our founding voices judge what is legitimate. Whatever is new - a doctrine, a monastic custom, a fashion of dress, a cult, an opinion of one's own - is suspect for being new. Whatever "has been handed down" from antiquity is to be held fast. "If novelty is profane, antiquity is sacred."

uses.sentence: He calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation.
uses.paragraph: And he was the one without whom we can do nothing. When a monk feels his fasting has accomplished something, he is taught to say *Not I, but the grace of God with me*. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. He calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. Those who perish, perish against his will.
uses.record_text: Would Jesus have wanted anything to do with someone like you? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were. And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes. How did we come to believe? We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. Who is Jesus to you, not to your church? One man's own word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The rest of us answer as houses answer - in what we did at the gate, and at the hours.

use_note.means: This witness says Jesus sought the unpitied, citing Martin's cloak, the guest received as Christ and grace calling the unwilling, while naming its thin personal testimony.
not_for: a personal conversion testimony from anyone but Martin, which the record lacks
evidence that Gallic houses broke fasts for guests, which Cassian does not say
a settled reading of Conference XIII on grace, which is contested
who Christ was and what his death meant, which sit in gallic.dw.the-christ-who-bears-the-wounds

uses.sentence: We held there was no other way to say it.
uses.paragraph: That is what we said - as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. We held there was no other way to say it.
uses.record_text: Was Jesus God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, did we believe in the Trinity? We held there was no other way to say it. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? Not in those words. What we were taught, at the sixth hour, is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. That is close to what you ask and it is not the same thing, and we will not make it the same. Was he our personal Lord and Saviour? Our Lord and Saviour was our phrase - said at an hour of prayer by a house together. The private form of it is not in our record. One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds.

use_note.means: This witness affirms Jesus as God through Vincent's formula of one substance in three Persons and two substances in one Person, adding Cassian's sixth-hour atonement sentence.
not_for: a penal substitution doctrine, when the sixth-hour sentence is near it but not the same
anything from Cassian's books against Nestorius, which are unread
the bare formula, which sits in gallic.quote.one-substance-three-persons
a private confession of Jesus as personal Lord, which the record lacks

uses.sentence: The same word covered what a robber or a rustic did when he turned to Christ.
uses.paragraph: What we had instead was turning. At Marseilles it was the word for the day a man turned to the monastic life - the early days of their turning were bright, and then they cooled. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, remembered a man named Moses who had fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that forced turning into a willing one. The same word covered what a robber or a rustic did when he turned to Christ.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, "conversion" is not a change of religion. It is the act of turning to the monastic life: "the early days of their conversion were so bright"; a murderer's "compulsory conversion" turned "into a voluntary one." At Tours the same English word names what a robber or a rustic does when he turns to Christ.

use_note.means: Conversion meant, at Marseilles, the act of turning to the monastic life and not a change of religion, while at Tours it meant turning to Christ.
not_for: an inner born-again event of coming to faith
a monk's conversion as his becoming a Christian
the act of giving things up, which sits in gallic.term.renunciation
the mission to the countryside, which sits in gallic.term.heathen-rustics

uses.sentence: Martin held that demons were driving him, but said he would bear with Brictio the way Christ bore with Judas.
uses.paragraph: At Tours the record is one named man - Martin, master and bishop both, who kept the objects and virtues of a monk inside the office. Authority rested where the power was felt. He needed no title. Sulpitius calls him "our master" and says it was unlawful to do anything but acquiesce to him. His disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Yet Martin himself, on a question touching whether a tradition had come down from antiquity, consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics, and would not honour a tomb where no steady tradition supported it. One of those presbyters was Brictio, whom Martin had raised from boyhood and who stormed into the courtyard in a fury. The man had sat down on his wooden seat one day, and Brictio came raging that he was holier than the master who brought him up, calling his visions ridiculous fancies and dreaming that he himself deserved the episcopate. Martin held that demons were driving him, but said he would bear with Brictio the way Christ bore with Judas. He would not remove him. That presbyter's rank came from somewhere, not from Martin alone, but where and how the record does not say.
uses.record_text: Then the holy man explained, both to him and to all of us, how he had seen demons driving him on. He declared that the insults heaped on him did not move him. In fact, they had hurt the man who spoke them instead. Later, this same Brictio was often accused before Martin of many serious crimes. Yet Martin could not be persuaded to remove him from the priesthood. He did not want to be suspected of taking revenge for the wrong done to himself. And he often repeated this saying: ‘If Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio?’

use_note.means: Gallus, in Sulpitius's Dialogues, reports that Martin refused to remove the accused presbyter Brictio, often saying that if Christ bore with Judas he should bear with Brictio.
not_for: a verdict that the charges against Brictio were false, which the passage never gives
a claim about Brictio's later career or status, which nothing at this locus supports
the courtyard tirade and Martin's restraint, which sit in gallic.quote.brictio-tirade-and-martins-restraint
Martin's saying as a verbatim transcript rather than words a narrator reports him repeating

uses.sentence: Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body.
uses.paragraph: The second is this. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. We were taught not to invent, but to hold what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. That meant Scripture was heard through the fathers, not against them. When a man at our door came in troubled by one sentence - that striving cannot make a man master of the good - the elder answered him with the husbandman and the rain, and told him the initiative comes from God. The question was about what Paul said; the answer was in the elder's mouth, not on the page. You are reading it as though you had to settle it yourself, and we were not formed that way.
uses.record_text: What did we have of Jesus? The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims it. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. How do we know the resurrection really happened? We did not ask it that way. We confessed it at the hours: his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. But a proof that the Lord rose, written by one of us for someone who doubts it - that is not in our record.

use_note.means: The record attests that this world's books never claim a witness to the Lord and never argue the resurrection to a doubter, and it cannot supply either.
not_for: a proof of the resurrection written by this world for a doubter, which the record says is absent
the cloak vision or the raised catechumen as evidence that the Lord rose, when they show the saint's power, as in gallic.story.the-cloak-at-amiens and gallic.story.raising-of-the-catechumen
the content of Cassian's seven books against Nestorius, which is unread
a chain of witnesses, when the world's floor stands more than three centuries after the events

uses.sentence: Vincent's rule of everywhere-always-all stands in the Commonitory.
uses.paragraph: The southern teaching - purity of heart as the immediate goal, discretion as its regulator, the eight faults fought in order - stands sentence by sentence in Cassian's two books. The north's power-economy - Martin's felt virtus, the blessed oil and threads, the demon named at exorcism - stands in Sulpitius's Life and Dialogues. Vincent's rule of everywhere-always-all stands in the Commonitory. The grace argument's two-sided teaching, with the field and the husbandman, stands in Conference XIII. Each of those would survive the check on its own ground.
uses.record_text: Vincent's test at Lerins for telling "the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity." Hold "that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all." When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients collated.

use_note.means: The rule meant Vincent's test of the faith, what has been believed everywhere, always, by all, preferring the whole, the old and consent to the part, the new and few.
not_for: the Vincentian canon as a slogan in later polemic over which communion holds the faith
a monastic Rule, whether Cassian's customs or Benedict's
a formula consistently applied, when its use in the live grace dispute is contested in gallic.contested.who-holds-antiquity
novelty as a value in itself, which sits in gallic.term.novelty-antiquity

uses.sentence: Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point.
uses.paragraph: And the mark it all serves: purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, and the archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point.
uses.record_text: In Cassian's Marseilles, the immediate goal of the whole monastic life, as distinct from its end, the kingdom of heaven. It is the "definite mark" at which every fast, vigil, reading and renunciation is aimed, "which is charity." By it all of these are ranked as aids to perfection and never as perfection itself.

use_note.means: Purity of heart meant the monk's immediate goal short of the kingdom, a heart cleared to charity, by which every fast and vigil is ranked as an aid.
not_for: sexual purity or moral spotlessness
sincerity or good intentions
the end, the kingdom, which sits in gallic.term.goal-and-end
the south's own chastity teaching, since Conference XII is excised from the vendored edition

uses.sentence: That Gallic houses lived by Cassian's customs - he says they did not.
uses.paragraph: What would not survive is any claim we made past the record's edge. That Martin's reluctance was total - Sulpitius is no neutral witness, and the objecting bishops never answered. That the island kept what Vincent taught - nothing shows a day there. That Gallic houses lived by Cassian's customs - he says they did not. That a miracle happened as told - our record has reported experience, not assessed fact. That the grace argument has one Catholic answer - Vincent read the Apostolic See's letter for his side, and we never settled which of Chaeremon's two phrasings on the beginning of a good will was his own.
